shelves.title: Pre-emptive pharmacogenomic panels: test once, before the first prescription
shelves.question: Does pre-emptive testing with a multi-gene pharmacogenomic panel, applied before a first prescription, reduce clinically relevant adverse drug reactions compared with standard care?
shelves.mesh: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions · Female · Genetic Testing · Genotype · Humans · Male · Pharmacogenetics · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One large trial carries this shelf. PREPARE, a cluster-randomised crossover implementation study in seven European countries, tested a 12-gene panel before a first prescription and found clinically relevant adverse drug reactions in 21.0% vs 27.7% of patients with an actionable result (OR 0.70) and 21.5% vs 28.6% across all patients (OR 0.70) — about a 30% relative reduction, roughly 7 percentage points absolute in both analyses. The trial was open-label, the outcome was adverse reactions rather than death or hospitalisation, and 97.7% of participants reported European, Mediterranean, or Middle Eastern ethnicity, so the panel's yield in other ancestries is less certain. No second randomized trial of a pre-emptive panel exists yet; the single-gene questions PREPARE bundles are carded on their own shelves in this slate. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: PREPARE (Swen 2023, Lancet): a 12-gene pre-emptive panel cut clinically relevant adverse drug reactions — 21.5% vs 28.6% overall (OR 0.70)
cards.summary: 6,944 adults starting a first prescription for a Dutch Pharmacogenetics Working Group (DPWG) index drug, in 18 hospitals, 9 community health centres and 28 pharmacies across seven European countries, cluster-randomised (crossover) to genotype-guided treatment using a 12-gene, 50-variant panel or standard care. Among patients with an actionable result for the index drug, a clinically relevant adverse drug reaction within 12 weeks occurred in 152 of 725 (21.0%) in the study group vs 231 of 833 (27.7%) in controls (OR 0.70 [95% CI 0.54–0.91]; p=0.0075); across all patients it was 628 of 2,923 (21.5%) vs 934 of 3,270 (28.6%) (OR 0.70 [0.61–0.79]; p<0.0001) — a 30% relative reduction, about 7 percentage points absolute.
cards.type: Open-label, multicentre, controlled, cluster-randomised crossover implementation study, Lancet 2023. Registry ID verified in the record's own databank: NCT03093818.
cards.people: 6,944 patients aged 18 years or older receiving a first prescription for a DPWG index drug (3,342 genotype-guided, 3,602 standard care); 51.4% female; 97.7% self-reported European, Mediterranean, or Middle Eastern ethnicity. The record does not print a mean age.
cards.result: Clinically relevant adverse drug reactions within 12 weeks: in patients with an actionable test result, 21.0% (152/725) on genotype-guided treatment vs 27.7% (231/833) on standard care (OR 0.70 [95% CI 0.54–0.91]; p=0.0075); in all patients, 21.5% (628/2,923) vs 28.6% (934/3,270) (OR 0.70 [0.61–0.79]; p<0.0001).
cards.watchOut: Open-label and cluster-randomised: clinicians knew the assignment, and the endpoint is clinically relevant adverse drug reactions — not mortality or hospitalisation, which the trial was not powered to move. The benefit was concentrated where a DPWG recommendation actually changed treatment, and the population was 97.7% European/Mediterranean/Middle Eastern ancestry; variant frequencies, and therefore panel yield, differ in other populations.
cards.source: Swen JJ et al. A 12-gene pharmacogenetic panel to prevent adverse drug reactions: an open-label, multicentre, controlled, cluster-randomised crossover implementation study. Lancet. 2023;401(10374):347-356. PMID 36739136 · NCT03093818

cards.headline: Synthesis — one trial, one panel, moderate certainty
cards.summary: The shelf rests on a single, large, well-conducted implementation trial. Its result is consistent in the actionable subgroup and in all comers, but it has never been replicated as a panel strategy, and its endpoint is adverse reactions, not hard outcomes.
cards.type: Shelf synthesis — no new trial is carded on this card; it draws only on the cards above and the dated currency sweep recorded in this pack.
cards.people: Not applicable — synthesis card.
cards.result: No second randomized trial of a pre-emptive multi-gene panel was found in the 2024–2026 currency sweep; the panel's individual gene–drug pairs with their own randomized evidence are carded separately in this slate (CYP2C19, warfarin genes, DPYD, HLA-B*57:01).
cards.watchOut: Do not read PREPARE as proof for any single gene–drug pair, and do not read the single-gene shelves as proof for panels: the panel claim and the pair claims are different claims with different evidence.

shelves.title: CYP2C19 testing for clopidogrel after PCI: escalate carriers, or de-escalate everyone else?
shelves.question: After PCI, does CYP2C19 genotype-guided selection of P2Y12 inhibitor therapy improve ischemic outcomes or reduce bleeding compared with a single default strategy?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome · Clopidogrel · Cytochrome P-450 CYP2C19 · Genotype · Hemorrhage · Humans · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Prasugrel Hydrochloride · Purinergic P2Y Receptor Antagonists · ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction · Ticagrelor
shelves.balance: The two trials test opposite directions of the same idea, and they land differently. TAILOR-PCI asked whether escalating CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers from clopidogrel to ticagrelor prevents ischemic events: in carriers the primary endpoint was 4.0% vs 5.9% (HR 0.66 [95% CI 0.43–1.02]; P=.06) — a 34% relative reduction that did not reach significance, in a trial powered for an implausibly large HR of 0.50. POPular Genetics asked the reverse in primary PCI for STEMI — genotype-guided de-escalation, noncarriers to clopidogrel — and met noninferiority for the combined thrombotic outcome (5.1% vs 5.9%) with less bleeding (9.8% vs 12.5%; HR 0.78). Neither trial showed a mortality difference. Proposed split stamp: POSSIBLE for escalation of carriers, LIKELY for de-escalation in STEMI primary PCI — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: TAILOR-PCI (Pereira 2020, JAMA): escalating CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers to ticagrelor — 4.0% vs 5.9% (HR 0.66), P=.06, not significant
cards.summary: 5,302 patients undergoing PCI for acute coronary syndromes (82%) or stable coronary disease (18%) at 40 centres, randomised open-label to point-of-care genotype-guided therapy (loss-of-function carriers prescribed ticagrelor, noncarriers clopidogrel) or conventional clopidogrel for all. In the 1,849 loss-of-function carriers, the primary endpoint (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, stent thrombosis, or severe recurrent ischemia at 12 months) occurred in 35 of 903 (4.0%) genotype-guided vs 54 of 946 (5.9%) conventional (HR 0.66 [95% CI 0.43–1.02]; P=.06). Major or minor bleeding in carriers: 1.9% vs 1.6% (HR 1.22; P=.58). Among all randomized patients the primary endpoint was 4.4% vs 5.3%.
cards.type: Open-label randomized clinical trial, JAMA 2020. Registry ID verified in the record's own databank: NCT01742117.
cards.people: 5,302 patients undergoing PCI (2,652 genotype-guided, 2,650 conventional); median age 62 years; 25% women; 82% acute coronary syndromes, 18% stable coronary artery disease; centres in the US, Canada, South Korea and Mexico.
cards.result: Primary endpoint at 12 months in CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers: 4.0% (35/903) genotype-guided vs 5.9% (54/946) conventional (HR 0.66 [95% CI 0.43–1.02]; P=.06). Major or minor bleeding in carriers: 1.9% vs 1.6% (HR 1.22 [0.60–2.51]; P=.58). None of the 11 prespecified secondary endpoints differed significantly. The trial had 85% power to detect a minimum hazard ratio of 0.50.
cards.watchOut: The headline hazard ratio looks like a win and is not one: P=.06 with a confidence interval crossing 1.0, in a trial powered only for a halving of risk (HR 0.50) that no antiplatelet strategy plausibly delivers. Read this card as 'promising, unproven' — the fence is the power calculation and the interval, both printed on the card's face.
cards.source: Pereira NL et al. Effect of Genotype-Guided Oral P2Y12 Inhibitor Selection vs Conventional Clopidogrel Therapy on Ischemic Outcomes After Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: The TAILOR-PCI Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2020;324(8):761-771. PMID 32840598 · NCT01742117

cards.headline: POPular Genetics (Claassens 2019, NEJM): genotype-guided de-escalation in STEMI primary PCI — thrombotic outcomes noninferior, bleeding lower (9.8% vs 12.5%)
cards.summary: 2,488 patients undergoing primary PCI with stent implantation for STEMI, randomised open-label (assessor-blinded) to CYP2C19 genotype-guided therapy (loss-of-function carriers received ticagrelor or prasugrel; noncarriers received clopidogrel) or standard ticagrelor/prasugrel for 12 months. The primary combined outcome (death from any cause, myocardial infarction, definite stent thrombosis, stroke, or PLATO major bleeding) occurred in 63 patients (5.1%) genotype-guided vs 73 (5.9%) standard (absolute difference −0.7 percentage points [95% CI −2.0 to 0.7]; P<0.001 for noninferiority, margin 2 points). PLATO major or minor bleeding: 122 (9.8%) vs 156 (12.5%) (HR 0.78 [0.61–0.98]; P=0.04).
cards.type: Randomized, open-label, assessor-blinded noninferiority trial, N Engl J Med 2019. Registry IDs verified in the record's own databank: NCT01761786 (Netherlands Trial Register NL2872 also listed).
cards.people: 2,488 patients undergoing primary PCI for ST-elevation myocardial infarction (1,242 genotype-guided, 1,246 standard treatment). The record's abstract does not print a mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Primary combined outcome at 12 months: 5.1% (63/1,242) genotype-guided vs 5.9% (73/1,246) standard (absolute difference −0.7 percentage points [95% CI −2.0 to 0.7]; P<0.001 for noninferiority). Primary bleeding outcome (PLATO major or minor bleeding): 9.8% (122) vs 12.5% (156) (HR 0.78 [95% CI 0.61–0.98]; P=0.04).
cards.watchOut: A noninferiority answer to a de-escalation question, in STEMI primary PCI only: it shows most patients can be stepped down to clopidogrel without a detectable thrombotic penalty and with less bleeding — it does not show genotyping saves lives, and it does not answer TAILOR-PCI's escalation question in broader PCI populations. The 2-percentage-point noninferiority margin is part of the claim and is printed here with it.
cards.source: Claassens DMF et al. A Genotype-Guided Strategy for Oral P2Y12 Inhibitors in Primary PCI. N Engl J Med. 2019;381(17):1621-1631. PMID 31479209 · NCT01761786

cards.headline: Synthesis — the direction of the strategy decides the answer
cards.summary: Genotype guidance after PCI is not one intervention. Escalating carriers to a potent agent (TAILOR-PCI) produced a non-significant trend; de-escalating noncarriers to clopidogrel (POPular Genetics) was noninferior with less bleeding. The shelf's split stamp records exactly that asymmetry.

cards.result: TAILOR-PCI primary endpoint in carriers HR 0.66 [0.43–1.02], P=.06; POPular Genetics combined outcome difference −0.7 points (noninferior) with bleeding HR 0.78. Neither trial reported a mortality benefit.
cards.watchOut: No newer pivotal PCI pharmacogenetic trial appeared in the 2024–2026 sweep. Which P2Y12 inhibitor wins head-to-head without genotyping is a different question, carded on Shelf #269 — not re-carded here.

shelves.title: Pharmacogenetic warfarin dosing: two trials in one journal issue disagreed
shelves.question: Does genotype-guided warfarin dosing (CYP2C9, VKORC1, CYP4F2) improve anticoagulation control or clinical outcomes compared with clinical dosing algorithms or standard loading?
shelves.mesh: Anticoagulants · Aryl Hydrocarbon Hydroxylases · Cytochrome P-450 CYP2C9 · Genotype · Hemorrhage · Humans · International Normalized Ratio · Pharmacogenetics · Vitamin K Epoxide Reductases · Warfarin
shelves.balance: Three randomized trials, three different comparators, and no mortality answer anywhere. COAG (n=1,015), testing genotype-plus-clinical dosing against a clinical algorithm with blinded doses, found no difference in time in therapeutic range at 4 weeks (45.2% vs 45.4%) — and a significant race interaction, with black patients doing worse on genotype guidance (P=0.003 for interaction). EU-PACT (n=455), testing genotype-guided loading against a fixed 3-day loading regimen, found more time in range over 12 weeks (67.4% vs 60.3%) and faster time to a therapeutic INR (21 vs 29 days). GIFT (n=1,650, elective hip/knee arthroplasty, age ≥65) found fewer composite events on genotype guidance (10.8% vs 14.7%), driven by INR ≥4.0 (56 vs 77 events); major bleeding was 2 vs 8 events and there were no deaths in either group. The fairest reading: genotype guidance helps most where the comparator is weakest and the setting is initiation — a process benefit with an unproven clinical dividend, never a demonstrated survival or major-bleeding benefit. Developer's stamp (Nov 8, 2026): MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: COAG (Kimmel 2013, NEJM): genotype-guided vs clinical-algorithm dosing — time in range identical (45.2% vs 45.4%)
cards.summary: 1,015 patients starting warfarin, randomised double-blind to dosing for the first 5 days by an algorithm including clinical variables plus genotype (CYP2C9, VKORC1) or by a clinical-variables-only algorithm; doses blinded for 4 weeks. Primary outcome, percentage of time with INR in the therapeutic range from day 4–5 through day 28: 45.2% genotype-guided vs 45.4% clinically guided (adjusted mean difference −0.2 [95% CI −3.4 to 3.1]; P=0.91). The combined outcome of INR ≥4, major bleeding, or thromboembolism did not differ. A significant interaction with race (P=0.003): among black patients, time in range was lower with genotype-guided dosing.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind trial, N Engl J Med 2013. Registry ID verified in the record's own databank: NCT00839657.
cards.people: 1,015 patients initiating warfarin therapy. The record's abstract does not print a mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Mean percentage of time in the therapeutic INR range through day 28: 45.2% genotype-guided vs 45.4% clinically guided (adjusted difference −0.2 percentage points [95% CI −3.4 to 3.1]; P=0.91). No significant difference in the composite of any INR ≥4, major bleeding, or thromboembolism. Interaction between dosing strategy and race: P=0.003, with black patients faring worse on genotype-guided dosing.
cards.watchOut: COAG's comparator was a good clinical algorithm, not usual care — beating it is the hardest version of this question, and genotype guidance did not. The race interaction matters for any panel built mainly on European-ancestry variant data: in black patients the genotype algorithm performed worse than the clinical algorithm. A null against a strong comparator and a positive against a weak one (Reference 2) is the pattern of this whole shelf.
cards.source: Kimmel SE et al. A pharmacogenetic versus a clinical algorithm for warfarin dosing. N Engl J Med. 2013;369(24):2283-2293. PMID 24251361 · NCT00839657

cards.headline: EU-PACT (Pirmohamed 2013, NEJM): genotype-guided loading beat fixed loading — time in range 67.4% vs 60.3% over 12 weeks
cards.summary: 455 patients with atrial fibrillation or venous thromboembolism starting warfarin, randomised to genotype-guided dosing (point-of-care testing for CYP2C9*2, CYP2C9*3 and VKORC1 −1639G→A; pharmacogenetic algorithm for the first 5 days) or standard care (a 3-day fixed loading-dose regimen). Primary outcome, percentage of time with INR 2.0–3.0 during the first 12 weeks: 67.4% genotype-guided vs 60.3% control (adjusted difference 7.0 percentage points [95% CI 3.3–10.6]; P<0.001). Median time to a therapeutic INR: 21 vs 29 days (P<0.001), with fewer episodes of INR ≥4.0 on genotype guidance.
cards.type: Multicentre randomized controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2013. Registry ID verified in the record's own databank: NCT01119300.
cards.people: 455 patients with atrial fibrillation or venous thromboembolism starting warfarin (227 genotype-guided, 228 control). The record's abstract does not print a mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Percentage of time in the therapeutic INR range (2.0–3.0) over the first 12 weeks: 67.4% genotype-guided vs 60.3% standard dosing (adjusted difference 7.0 percentage points [95% CI 3.3–10.6]; P<0.001). Median time to therapeutic INR 21 vs 29 days (P<0.001); significantly fewer incidences of excessive anticoagulation (INR ≥4.0) in the genotype-guided group.
cards.watchOut: EU-PACT's control was a fixed loading regimen, not a clinical dosing algorithm — the weakest comparator of the three trials on this shelf, and the only clearly positive time-in-range result sits against it. Time in range is a process measure: neither EU-PACT nor COAG showed fewer major bleeds or deaths, and warfarin's shrinking role in the DOAC era narrows where this question still matters.
cards.source: Pirmohamed M et al. A randomized trial of genotype-guided dosing of warfarin. N Engl J Med. 2013;369(24):2294-2303. PMID 24251363 · NCT01119300

cards.headline: GIFT (Gage 2017, JAMA): genotype-guided dosing in arthroplasty patients — composite events 10.8% vs 14.7%, driven by INR ≥4; no deaths
cards.summary: 1,650 patients aged 65 or older initiating warfarin for elective hip or knee arthroplasty at 6 US centres, randomised (2×2 factorial, with INR target 1.8 vs 2.5) to genotype-guided dosing (VKORC1, CYP2C9*2/*3, CYP4F2) or clinically guided dosing on days 1–11. The primary composite (major bleeding, INR ≥4, venous thromboembolism, or death) occurred in 87 patients (10.8%) genotype-guided vs 116 (14.7%) clinically guided (absolute difference 3.9 percentage points [95% CI 0.7–7.2]; P=.02; relative rate 0.73 [0.56–0.95]). Components: major bleeding 2 vs 8, INR ≥4 56 vs 77, VTE 33 vs 38, deaths 0 vs 0.
cards.type: Randomized clinical trial (2×2 factorial), JAMA 2017. Registry ID verified in the record's own databank: NCT01006733.
cards.people: 1,650 randomized patients aged 65 years or older initiating warfarin for elective hip or knee arthroplasty; mean age 72.1 years (SD 5.4); 63.6% women; 91.0% white; 1,597 received at least one warfarin dose and completed the trial.
cards.result: Primary composite endpoint: 10.8% (87 patients) genotype-guided vs 14.7% (116) clinically guided (absolute difference 3.9% [95% CI 0.7%–7.2%]; P=.02; relative rate 0.73 [0.56–0.95]). Individual events, genotype-guided vs clinically guided: major bleeding 2 vs 8 (RR 0.24 [0.05–1.15]); INR ≥4, 56 vs 77 (RR 0.71 [0.51–0.99]); venous thromboembolism 33 vs 38 (RR 0.85 [0.54–1.34]); deaths 0 in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Read the composite before quoting it: the significant difference is carried by INR ≥4.0, a laboratory event — major bleeding (2 vs 8) and VTE (33 vs 38) were not individually significant, and with zero deaths the trial says nothing about mortality. Heart of the fence: genotype guidance made warfarin initiation tidier in older surgical patients; whether it prevents the harms patients feel is unproven.
cards.source: Gage BF et al. Effect of Genotype-Guided Warfarin Dosing on Clinical Events and Anticoagulation Control Among Patients Undergoing Hip or Knee Arthroplasty: The GIFT Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2017;318(12):1115-1124. PMID 28973620 · NCT01006733

cards.headline: Synthesis — comparator-dependent benefit, no hard-outcome win
cards.summary: Across three trials the benefit of genotype-guided warfarin dosing appears against fixed loading (EU-PACT) and on laboratory-heavy composites (GIFT), and disappears against a strong clinical algorithm (COAG). Time in range improves modestly at initiation; major bleeding and mortality benefits have never been shown.
cards.type: Shelf synthesis — no new trial is carded on this card; it draws only on the cards above and the dated currency sweep recorded in this pack.
cards.people: Not applicable — synthesis card.
cards.result: COAG time in range 45.2% vs 45.4% (null); EU-PACT 67.4% vs 60.3%; GIFT composite 10.8% vs 14.7% with major bleeding 2 vs 8 events and no deaths.
cards.watchOut: Any shelf claim for genotype-guided warfarin dosing must name its comparator. A claim stated without one — 'genotyping improves warfarin dosing' — papers over the COAG null and the race interaction, both of which are on this shelf's cards.

shelves.title: DPYD testing before fluoropyrimidines: dose the carriers down, before the first cycle
shelves.question: Does prospective DPYD genotyping with genotype-guided dose reduction reduce severe fluoropyrimidine toxicity in patients starting fluorouracil or capecitabine?
shelves.mesh: Antimetabolites, Antineoplastic · Capecitabine · Case-Control Studies · Dihydrouracil Dehydrogenase (NADP) · Fluorouracil · Gene Frequency · Genetic Testing · Heterozygote · Humans · Neoplasms · Pharmacogenomic Variants · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: There is no randomized trial here, and there will not be one: randomising known DPYD variant carriers to full-dose fluoropyrimidine is not an ethical design. What exists is two large prospective safety studies pointing the same way. Screening for DPYD*2A alone and halving carriers' starting dose cut grade ≥3 toxicity in carriers from 73% in historical full-dose controls to 28%, and drug-induced death from 10% to 0% (Deenen). Screening for four variants and reducing dose cut carriers' relative risk of severe toxicity from 2.87 (historical, full dose) to 1.31 against wild-type patients for DPYD*2A, with the same direction for the other variants (Henricks) — though carriers on reduced doses still had more severe toxicity than wild-type patients (39% vs 23%), and two variants may need a 50% rather than 25% reduction. The comparison is prospective-versus-historical, not randomized, and that fence is on both cards; the size and consistency of the toxicity reduction is why the stamp is not lower. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Deenen 2016 (J Clin Oncol): upfront DPYD*2A genotyping — grade ≥3 toxicity in carriers 28% with dose reduction vs 73% in historical full-dose controls; drug-induced deaths 0% vs 10%
cards.summary: 2,038 patients intended for fluoropyrimidine-based chemotherapy were prospectively genotyped for DPYD*2A before treatment; the 22 carriers (1.1%) received an initial dose reduction of at least 50% with titration by tolerance. Grade ≥3 toxicity in carriers was 28% (95% CI 10%–53%) with genotype-guided dosing vs 73% (58%–85%) in historical controls (n=48 carriers treated at standard dose; P<.001), and drug-induced death fell from 10% to 0%. Carriers' grade ≥3 toxicity (28%) was similar to wild-type patients on standard dose (23%; P=.64), systemic fluorouracil exposure was similar, and screening was cost-saving per patient in the model-based analysis (€2,772 vs €2,817).
cards.type: Prospective safety and cost analysis with historical controls, J Clin Oncol 2016. Registry ID verified in the record's own databank: NCT00838370.
cards.people: 2,038 patients prospectively screened for DPYD*2A before fluoropyrimidine-based chemotherapy in the Netherlands, of whom 22 (1.1%) were heterozygous carriers. The record's abstract does not print a mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Grade ≥3 toxicity in DPYD*2A carriers: 28% (95% CI 10%–53%) with genotype-guided dosing vs 73% (58%–85%) in historical standard-dose controls (P<.001). Drug-induced death: 0% vs 10%. Carriers' toxicity with dose reduction (28%) did not differ significantly from wild-type patients on standard dose (23%; P=.64). Median dose intensity in carriers was 48% (range 17%–91%).
cards.watchOut: The comparator is historical, not randomized: carriers treated at full dose in earlier literature. Secular improvements in supportive care could flatter the guided group, and only 22 carriers were treated — the confidence interval around 28% runs from 10% to 53%. The direction and size of the effect, the mechanistic specificity (DPD deficiency), and the fall in drug-induced deaths are what carry this card; the design is stated here so the reader can weigh them.
cards.source: Deenen MJ et al. Upfront Genotyping of DPYD*2A to Individualize Fluoropyrimidine Therapy: A Safety and Cost Analysis. J Clin Oncol. 2016;34(3):227-234. PMID 26573078 · NCT00838370

cards.headline: Henricks 2018 (Lancet Oncol): four-variant DPYD screening in 1,103 patients — carriers' excess severe-toxicity risk fell sharply vs historical full-dose cohorts, but stayed above wild-type (39% vs 23%)
cards.summary: Prospective multicentre safety analysis in 17 Dutch hospitals: 1,103 evaluable patients starting fluoropyrimidine therapy were genotyped for four DPYD variants (DPYD*2A, c.1679T>G, c.2846A>T, c.1236G>A); the 85 heterozygous carriers (8%) received initial dose reductions of 50% (*2A, c.1679T>G) or 25% (c.2846A>T, c.1236G>A), and 1,018 wild-type patients received standard care. Severe (grade ≥3) fluoropyrimidine-related toxicity occurred in 39% of carriers vs 23% of wild-type patients (p=0.0013). Against historical full-dose cohorts, the relative risk of severe toxicity for DPYD*2A carriers was 1.31 (95% CI 0.63–2.73) with genotype-guided dosing vs 2.87 (2.14–3.86) historically; for c.2846A>T, 2.00 vs 3.11; for c.1236G>A, 1.69 vs 1.72; no severe toxicity occurred in guided c.1679T>G carriers vs a historical RR of 4.30.
cards.type: Prospective, multicentre safety analysis with historical-cohort comparison, Lancet Oncol 2018. Registry ID verified in the record's own databank: NCT02324452.
cards.people: 1,103 evaluable patients (of 1,181 enrolled) aged 18 years or older with cancer starting fluoropyrimidine-based therapy (capecitabine or fluorouracil, alone or in combination) at 17 hospitals in the Netherlands; 85 (8%) heterozygous DPYD variant carriers, 1,018 (92%) wild-type. The record's abstract does not print a mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Severe fluoropyrimidine-related toxicity: 33 of 85 carriers (39%) vs 231 of 1,018 wild-type patients (23%) (p=0.0013). Relative risks of severe toxicity vs the historical full-dose cohort fell with genotype-guided dosing for DPYD*2A (1.31 [95% CI 0.63–2.73] vs 2.87 [2.14–3.86] historical) and c.2846A>T (2.00 [1.19–3.34] vs 3.11 [2.25–4.28]), did not fall for c.1236G>A (1.69 [1.18–2.42] vs 1.72 [1.22–2.42]), and no guided c.1679T>G carrier had severe toxicity (historical RR 4.30 [2.10–8.80]).
cards.watchOut: Two fences. First, the 'improvement' is measured against historical meta-analysis cohorts, not a randomized control group. Second, dose reduction did not normalise risk: carriers still had significantly more severe toxicity than wild-type patients (39% vs 23%), and the authors themselves conclude the 25% reduction for c.2846A>T and c.1236G>A carriers may be too small — a 50% reduction 'requires investigation'. Testing reduces harm; on this evidence it does not eliminate the excess.
cards.source: Henricks LM et al. DPYD genotype-guided dose individualisation of fluoropyrimidine therapy in patients with cancer: a prospective safety analysis. Lancet Oncol. 2018;19(11):1459-1467. PMID 30348537 · NCT02324452

cards.headline: Synthesis — strong prospective signal, historical comparators, no RCT by design
cards.summary: Both prospective studies agree: finding carriers before the first dose and reducing that dose removes most of the excess severe toxicity that full-dose treatment historically caused, including the drug-induced deaths seen in unscreened *2A carriers. The evidence ceiling is set by the comparators — historical cohorts — and by the residual excess risk in carriers even after dose reduction.
cards.type: Shelf synthesis — no new trial is carded on this card; it draws only on the cards above and the dated currency sweep recorded in this pack.
cards.people: Not applicable — synthesis card.
cards.result: Grade ≥3 toxicity in *2A carriers 28% guided vs 73% historical (Deenen); four-variant carriers' severe toxicity 39% vs 23% in wild-type patients despite dose reduction (Henricks).
cards.watchOut: This shelf should not be cited as randomized evidence. Its LIKELY stamp rests on effect size, consistency across two prospective studies and variants, and a specific mechanism — and it falls if a properly controlled comparison ever contradicts it.

shelves.title: Cascade screening for familial hypercholesterolemia: finding relatives is proven — helping them live longer is not
shelves.question: Does cascade screening of relatives of people with familial hypercholesterolemia identify new cases — and does identifying them improve cardiovascular outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Child, Preschool · Cholesterol · Cholesterol, LDL · Female · Humans · Hyperlipoproteinemia Type II · Infant · Male · Mass Screening · Mutation · Parents · Primary Health Care · Preventive Health Services
shelves.balance: Cascade screening does the first half of its job measurably well. Screening toddlers at immunisation visits found familial hypercholesterolemia in 0.4% of children — and, by testing the parents, one affected parent per affected child: 8 people identified per 1,000 children screened (Wald). A 2026 randomized trial of a web-based, patient-mediated cascade programme (CATCH) doubled relatives' testing uptake vs usual care (30.4% vs 16.7%; OR 2.18) and doubled new-case identification (17.0% vs 8.1%). But even the better arm left 70% of eligible relatives untested, and no trial — randomized or otherwise — has shown that cascade screening reduces heart attacks or deaths; the outcome benefit is inferred from the proven benefit of treating FH once found, not demonstrated for the screening strategy itself. Detection is LIKELY real; outcome benefit is unproven. Proposed stamp MAYBE (weak evidence) — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Wald 2016 (NEJM): child–parent screening at immunisation visits — 40 children and 40 parents identified per 10,095 children screened
cards.summary: 10,095 children aged 1–2 years had capillary cholesterol measured and FH mutation testing at routine immunisation visits in UK primary care. With a prespecified cholesterol cutoff of 1.53 multiples of the median plus a mutation or a repeat elevated level, 28 children (0.3%) screened positive; a lower cutoff strategy (1.35 MoM plus mutation, or two values ≥1.50 MoM) identified 40 children (0.4%) and 40 parents with positive results. Overall mutation prevalence was 1 in 273 children (37 in 10,095). For every 1,000 children screened, 8 persons (4 children and 4 parents) were identified as having FH.
cards.type: Prospective screening feasibility and efficacy study in primary care, N Engl J Med 2016. Pre-registration-era screening study: the record carries no registry ID in its databank, and none is printed.
cards.people: 10,095 children aged 1 to 2 years attending routine immunisation visits in primary care, and their parents. The record's abstract does not print the children's sex mix.
cards.result: Positive screening results: 28 children (0.3% [95% CI 0.2–0.4]) at the 1.53 MoM cutoff; 40 children (0.4%) and 40 parents at the 1.35 MoM strategy. FH mutation prevalence 1 in 273 children (37/10,095 [95% CI 1 in 198 to 1 in 388]). Yield: 8 persons identified per 1,000 children screened (4 children, 4 parents). Seventeen children below the 1.53 MoM cholesterol cutoff also carried an FH mutation.
cards.watchOut: This is a detection study, not an outcomes study: it proves screening toddlers finds affected children and parents, not that finding them this way prevents a single heart attack. Cholesterol alone also misses mutation carriers (17 mutation-positive children sat below the higher cutoff), so the strategy's sensitivity depends on pairing the blood test with genetic testing — a cost and consent commitment the yield figures assume.
cards.source: Wald DS et al. Child-Parent Familial Hypercholesterolemia Screening in Primary Care. N Engl J Med. 2016;375(17):1628-1637. PMID 27783906

cards.headline: CATCH (Nanchen 2026, JAMA Network Open): a web platform for patient-mediated cascade screening doubled relatives' testing uptake — 30.4% vs 16.7% (OR 2.18)
cards.summary: Open-label, multicentre, cluster-randomized implementation trial at 7 Swiss lipid clinics: 87 adults with genetically confirmed FH and 359 eligible first-degree relatives were randomized by family to a secure web-based platform (index patients sent preprepared electronic messages inviting relatives to genetic testing) or usual care. Cascade uptake (relatives genetically tested within 6 months) was 30.4% (95% CI 22.0%–40.4%) in the intervention arm vs 16.7% (10.1%–26.3%) in usual care (OR 2.18 [1.06–4.51]; P=.03). New cases identified: 17.0% vs 8.1% (OR 2.32 [1.07–5.05]; P=.03). Overall, 99 of 359 relatives (27.6%) were tested.
cards.type: Open-label, multicentre, cluster-randomized implementation trial, JAMA Netw Open 2026. Registry ID verified in the record's own databank: NCT04419090.
cards.people: 87 index patients with genetically confirmed familial hypercholesterolemia (44 intervention, 43 usual care); median age 49.2 years; 46 (52.9%) female; median highest LDL cholesterol 289.58 mg/dL; and their 359 eligible first-degree relatives living in Switzerland.
cards.result: Cascade screening uptake within 6 months: 30.4% intervention vs 16.7% usual care (OR 2.18 [95% CI 1.06–4.51]; P=.03). New-case identification: 17.0% vs 8.1% (OR 2.32 [1.07–5.05]; P=.03). Newly identified patients were often untreated or had modifiable risk factors.
cards.watchOut: The outcome is testing uptake — a process measure. Doubling a low rate still leaves roughly 70% of eligible relatives untested, follow-up was 6 months, and no cardiovascular events or deaths were (or could be, at this size) assessed. CATCH shows how to run cascade screening better; it cannot show that cascade screening saves lives, and this shelf does not claim it does.
cards.source: Nanchen D et al. Genetic Cascade Screening for Familial Hypercholesterolemia: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Netw Open. 2026;9(4):e266100. PMID 41973423 · NCT04419090

cards.headline: Synthesis — an implementation success resting on an outcomes inference
cards.summary: Cascade screening finds cases (Wald: 8 per 1,000 toddlers screened, counting parents) and digital patient-mediated outreach roughly doubles relative uptake (CATCH: OR 2.18). The chain from 'relative found' to 'heart attack prevented' runs through statin treatment of FH — effective, but carded elsewhere — and has never itself been tested against clinical endpoints.
cards.type: Shelf synthesis — no new trial is carded on this card; it draws only on the cards above and the dated currency sweep recorded in this pack.
cards.people: Not applicable — synthesis card.
cards.result: Detection: 0.4% of toddlers plus one parent each (Wald); uptake 30.4% vs 16.7% and new cases 17.0% vs 8.1% (CATCH). Clinical outcomes of the screening strategy: no data in any carded study.
cards.watchOut: This is the developer-designated MAYBE (weak evidence) shelf for the slate: the stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence) because the shelf's clinical question — do screened families fare better — remains unanswered, however good the detection numbers are.

shelves.title: Aspirin dose in Lynch syndrome: CaPP3 asks whether 100 mg does what 600 mg did
shelves.question: In carriers of Lynch syndrome, are lower daily aspirin doses (100 mg or 300 mg) noninferior to 600 mg for preventing Lynch syndrome cancers — the dose question left open by CAPP2?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aspirin · Colorectal Neoplasms, Hereditary Nonpolyposis · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: This shelf does not re-ask whether aspirin works in Lynch syndrome: that question — CAPP2's 600 mg daily, with colorectal cancer protection emerging at 10 years (ITT HR 0.65) — is home on Shelf #220, and CAPP2 is not re-carded here under the one-home rule. This shelf asks the question CAPP2 left open and Shelf #220 flagged as unreported: the dose. CaPP3 (n=1,866) compared 100 mg and 300 mg against 600 mg and formally concluded noninferiority for NEITHER lower dose: for 100 mg the intention-to-treat estimates sat inside the 1.5 margin (HR 0.97 [95% CI 0.67–1.42]; IRR 0.94 [0.65–1.38]) but the per-protocol time-to-first-cancer analysis did not (HR 1.00 [0.61–1.63]); for 300 mg both analyses missed. What the lower dose clearly bought was safety: serious bleeding events over 5 years occurred in 0 patients on 100 mg, 3 (0.5%) on 300 mg, and 11 (1.5%) on 600 mg. The authors' own reading — 100 mg looked similar for cancer with fewer harms, without formal noninferiority — is the honest summary. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: CaPP3 (Burn 2026, Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology): 100 mg and 300 mg vs 600 mg aspirin in Lynch syndrome — noninferiority formally concluded for neither dose; serious bleeding 0 vs 3 vs 11 patients
cards.summary: 1,879 Lynch syndrome carriers recruited from genetics centres in the UK, Australia, Finland, Israel and Spain were randomised double-blind (3:3:4) to aspirin 100 mg, 300 mg or 600 mg daily for 2 years blinded, then open-label on the same dose for 3 more years; the intention-to-treat population was 1,866. At a median follow-up of 66.4 months, 176 participants had developed 216 Lynch syndrome cancers. For 100 mg vs 600 mg, ITT hazard ratio for time to first Lynch syndrome cancer was 0.97 (95% CI 0.67–1.42) and incidence rate ratio for cancer burden 0.94 (0.65–1.38) — inside the 1.5 noninferiority margin — but per-protocol time-to-first-cancer was not (HR 1.00 [0.61–1.63]). For 300 mg, noninferiority was not established in either population (ITT HR 1.28 [0.91–1.80]). Adverse events of interest rose with dose (25.0%, 26.8%, 31.2%; p=0.03); serious bleeding events over 5 years: 0 (100 mg), 3 (0.5%, 300 mg), 11 (1.5%, 600 mg) (p=0.004).
cards.type: Multicentre, parallel-group, randomised, double-blind, dose non-inferiority trial, Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2026. Registry IDs verified in the record: NCT02497820 (record databank) and ISRCTN16261285 (record text). Ten-year follow-up is planned and has not reported.
cards.people: 1,866 participants in the intention-to-treat population (559 on 100 mg, 562 on 300 mg, 745 on 600 mg), adults older than 18 years with Lynch syndrome recruited from clinical genetics centres in five countries. The record's abstract does not print a mean age or the sex mix. 39.1% stopped aspirin within the 2-year blinded phase; 50.2% completed 5 years.
cards.result: Lynch syndrome cancers, 100 mg vs 600 mg (ITT): HR for time to first cancer 0.97 (95% CI 0.67–1.42); IRR for cancer burden 0.94 (0.65–1.38). Per-protocol: IRR 0.90 (0.55–1.46) noninferior, HR 1.00 (0.61–1.63) not noninferior against the 1.5 margin. 300 mg vs 600 mg (ITT): HR 1.28 (0.91–1.80), IRR 1.12 (0.79–1.61) — noninferiority not established. Serious adverse events due to bleeding over 5 years: 0 patients (100 mg), 3 (0.5%) (300 mg), 11 (1.5%) (600 mg) (p=0.004 for heterogeneity). Authors' interpretation: noninferiority could not formally be concluded for either lower dose, but 100 mg had similar cancer characteristics to 600 mg with fewer side-effects and less bleeding risk.
cards.watchOut: Do not upgrade this card to '100 mg works as well as 600 mg': the trial's own formal conclusion is that noninferiority was NOT established for either dose, because the result split across the four required analyses (ITT/per-protocol × HR/IRR). Add the adherence reality — 39% stopped within the blinded phase — and the still-pending 10-year follow-up, in a syndrome where CAPP2's benefit only became significant at 10 years. The dose answer is genuinely not in yet; the bleeding gradient is the firmest finding on the card.
cards.source: Burn J et al. Aspirin for cancer prevention in individuals with Lynch syndrome: first results from the CaPP3 multicentre, randomised, double-blind, non-inferiority trial. Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2026;11(9):760-774. PMID 42425127 · NCT02497820

shelves.title: Risk-reducing surgery in BRCA carriers: large observational benefits, no randomized trial
shelves.question: In women carrying BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations, do risk-reducing mastectomy and risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy reduce cancer incidence and mortality?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Breast Neoplasms · Fallopian Tubes · Female · Genes, BRCA1 · Genes, BRCA2 · Genetic Predisposition to Disease · Humans · Mastectomy · Middle Aged · Mutation · Ovarian Neoplasms · Ovariectomy · Prospective Studies · Risk
shelves.balance: SLOW-LANE SHELF — flagged for the developer's personal ruling: every mortality figure on this shelf is observational, because randomising BRCA carriers to surgery or no surgery has never been done. The cohorts are large and consistent. In the prospective PROSE consortium cohort (n=2,482), no breast cancers occurred in 247 women after risk-reducing mastectomy vs 98 of 1,372 without it, and salpingo-oophorectomy was associated with lower ovarian cancer (HR 0.14–0.28 by prior-cancer status) and lower all-cause mortality (10% vs 3%; HR 0.40 [95% CI 0.26–0.61]). In an international registry cohort (n=5,783), oophorectomy was associated with an 80% relative reduction in ovarian/fallopian/peritoneal cancer (HR 0.20) and, in women cancer-free at baseline, a 77% relative reduction in all-cause mortality to age 70 (HR 0.23). The earliest matched study (Rebbeck 2002) found the same direction (coelomic cancer HR 0.04; breast cancer HR 0.47). A 2025 international cohort of 5,290 young carriers already diagnosed with breast cancer likewise associated both surgeries with better overall survival (adjusted HR 0.65 and 0.58). Consistency across four cohorts and two decades is real; so is the confounding — women who choose surgery differ from women who do not, and immortal-time and selection biases run in surgery's favour. Proposed grade: POSSIBLE. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: PROSE cohort (Domchek 2010, JAMA): risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy associated with lower all-cause mortality (10% vs 3%; HR 0.40); no breast cancers after risk-reducing mastectomy
cards.summary: Prospective multicentre cohort of 2,482 women with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations at 22 genetics centres in Europe and North America, followed to 2009. No breast cancers were diagnosed among 247 women with risk-reducing mastectomy, vs 98 of 1,372 women without it. Salpingo-oophorectomy vs none: ovarian cancer risk lower in women with prior breast cancer (6% vs 1%; HR 0.14 [95% CI 0.04–0.59]) and without (6% vs 2%; HR 0.28 [0.12–0.69]); first breast cancer lower in BRCA1 (20% vs 14%; HR 0.63) and BRCA2 carriers (23% vs 7%; HR 0.36). All-cause mortality was 10% without vs 3% with salpingo-oophorectomy (HR 0.40 [0.26–0.61]); breast-cancer mortality HR 0.44 and ovarian-cancer mortality HR 0.21.
cards.type: Prospective, multicentre cohort study, JAMA 2010. Observational study: the record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 2,482 women with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations ascertained between 1974 and 2008 at 22 clinical and research genetics centres in Europe and North America. The record's abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: Risk-reducing mastectomy: 0 breast cancers in 247 women vs 98 of 1,372 without mastectomy. Salpingo-oophorectomy: all-cause mortality 10% (no surgery) vs 3% (surgery) (HR 0.40 [95% CI 0.26–0.61]); breast cancer-specific mortality HR 0.44 (0.26–0.76); ovarian cancer-specific mortality HR 0.21 (0.06–0.80); ovarian cancer incidence HR 0.14 (prior breast cancer) and 0.28 (no prior breast cancer).
cards.watchOut: Observational throughout: women chose their surgery, and the comparison groups differ in ways adjustment cannot fully remove — including immortal time (a woman must survive to have surgery) and the healthier-user pattern. The mortality hazard ratios (0.40, 0.44, 0.21) are exactly the size that residual confounding manufactures in surgical cohorts, and there is no randomized trial to check them against. This card is the shelf's best evidence and its central fence at once.

cards.headline: Finch 2014 (J Clin Oncol): preventive oophorectomy — ovarian/fallopian/peritoneal cancer HR 0.20; all-cause mortality to age 70 HR 0.23 in women cancer-free at baseline
cards.summary: International registry cohort of 5,783 women with a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation completing baseline and follow-up questionnaires, followed a mean of 5.6 years; 186 women developed ovarian (132), fallopian (22) or peritoneal (32) cancer, of whom 68 died. Bilateral oophorectomy was associated with a hazard ratio of 0.20 (95% CI 0.13–0.30; P<.001) for ovarian, fallopian tube or peritoneal cancer — an 80% relative reduction — and, among women with no history of cancer at baseline, a hazard ratio of 0.23 (0.13–0.39; P<.001) for all-cause mortality to age 70 — a 77% relative reduction.
cards.type: International registry cohort study with time-dependent survival analysis, J Clin Oncol 2014. Observational study: the record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 5,783 women with a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation identified from an international registry. The record's abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: Hazard ratio for ovarian, fallopian tube or peritoneal cancer associated with bilateral oophorectomy: 0.20 (95% CI 0.13–0.30; P<.001). Hazard ratio for all-cause mortality to age 70, in women with no cancer history at baseline: 0.23 (0.13–0.39; P<.001). Over a mean 5.6 years of follow-up, 186 of 5,783 women developed an ovarian, fallopian or peritoneal cancer.
cards.watchOut: A hazard ratio of 0.23 for all-cause mortality from an observational registry is precisely where this library's observational floor bites: effects this large in non-randomized surgical comparisons should be read as 'associated, plausibly inflated'. Women who had oophorectomy also differ by age at testing, country, and prior cancer (the mortality analysis is restricted to women cancer-free at baseline for exactly this reason). The cancer-incidence result (HR 0.20) is mechanistically direct; the mortality result is the claim to hold at arm's length.

cards.headline: Rebbeck 2002 (NEJM): prophylactic oophorectomy in 551 carriers — coelomic epithelial cancer HR 0.04; breast cancer HR 0.47 (matched controls)
cards.summary: 551 women with germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations from registries: 259 who had bilateral prophylactic oophorectomy and 292 matched controls who had not, followed at least 8 years after surgery. Ovarian cancer was diagnosed in 58 controls (19.9%) after a mean 8.8 years; in the surgery group, 6 women (2.3%) had stage I ovarian cancer found at operation and 2 (0.8%) developed papillary serous peritoneal carcinoma later. Excluding cancers found at surgery, prophylactic oophorectomy was associated with a hazard ratio of 0.04 (95% CI 0.01–0.16) for coelomic epithelial cancer. In the subgroup without prior breast cancer or mastectomy, breast cancer developed in 21 of 99 women (21.2%) after oophorectomy vs 60 of 142 controls (42.3%) (HR 0.47 [0.29–0.77]).
cards.type: Matched retrospective cohort study, N Engl J Med 2002. Pre-registration-era observational study: the record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 551 women with disease-associated germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations identified from registries (259 bilateral prophylactic oophorectomy, 292 matched controls); postoperative follow-up at least 8 years in both groups.
cards.result: Coelomic epithelial cancer: HR 0.04 (95% CI 0.01–0.16) with prophylactic oophorectomy, excluding 6 stage I cancers found at surgery; 58 of 292 controls (19.9%) developed ovarian cancer. Breast cancer in the subgroup analysed: 21.2% (21/99) after oophorectomy vs 42.3% (60/142) in controls (HR 0.47 [0.29–0.77]). Peritoneal carcinoma still occurred after oophorectomy (2 women, 0.8%).
cards.watchOut: The HR of 0.04 is the shelf's most dramatic number and its oldest design: matched but not randomised, with cancers prevalent at surgery handled by exclusion — a choice that favours the surgery group. Note what surgery did not do even here: peritoneal carcinoma occurred afterwards, so 'risk-reducing' is the right word and 'preventive' is not. All-cause mortality was not this study's endpoint; the mortality claims on this shelf come from Cards 1, 2 and 4, all observational.

cards.headline: BRCA BCY Collaboration (Blondeaux 2025, Lancet Oncol): in 5,290 young carriers with prior breast cancer, risk-reducing mastectomy and salpingo-oophorectomy each associated with better overall survival (adjusted HR 0.65 and 0.58)
cards.summary: International hospital-based retrospective cohort at 109 centres on five continents: 5,290 women with germline BRCA1/BRCA2 pathogenic variants diagnosed with stage I–III invasive breast cancer at age 40 or younger between 2000 and 2020; 2,910 (55.0%) underwent risk-reducing mastectomy and 2,782 (52.6%) risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy. After a median follow-up of 8.2 years, risk-reducing mastectomy was associated with better overall survival (adjusted HR 0.65 [95% CI 0.53–0.78]; 20-year restricted mean survival 17.89 vs 16.65 years) and salpingo-oophorectomy likewise (adjusted HR 0.58 [0.48–0.71]; 17.73 vs 16.67 years).
cards.type: International retrospective cohort study, Lancet Oncol 2025. Registry ID in the record's own databank: NCT03673306 (an observational registry registration).
cards.people: 5,290 women with germline BRCA1 (63.5%), BRCA2 or both pathogenic variants, diagnosed with stage I–III invasive breast cancer at age 40 years or younger, 2000–2020, at 109 centres. Median follow-up 8.2 years (IQR 4.7–12.8).
cards.result: Overall survival, adjusted hazard ratios: risk-reducing mastectomy 0.65 (95% CI 0.53–0.78) vs no mastectomy; risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy 0.58 (0.48–0.71) vs no salpingo-oophorectomy. Twenty-year restricted mean overall survival: 17.89 years with mastectomy vs 16.65 without; 17.73 years with salpingo-oophorectomy vs 16.67 without.
cards.watchOut: The newest cohort and the same old problem, sharpened: these are women who already had breast cancer, and the decision to have further surgery after diagnosis tracks prognosis, treatment era, and access across 109 centres and 20 years. Adjusted hazard ratios of 0.58–0.65 for survival are hypothesis-consistent, not proof. Included because the currency sweep found it and it is the largest young-carrier dataset — flagged, like the whole shelf, slow-lane.

cards.headline: Synthesis — slow-lane: consistent cohorts, structural confounding, developer's personal ruling required
cards.summary: Four cohorts over 23 years, one direction: risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy is associated with far fewer ovarian-type cancers (HR 0.04–0.20) and with lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.23–0.40); mastectomy with near-elimination of subsequent breast cancer in carriers without prior cancer. No randomized trial exists for any of it.

shelves.title: Telling people their APOE result: the REVEAL trials found no psychological harm — in people who asked to know
shelves.question: Does disclosing APOE genotype for Alzheimer's disease risk cause psychological harm — and can disclosure be done safely with brief protocols?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Alzheimer Disease · Anxiety · Apolipoprotein E4 · Apolipoproteins E · Depression · Disclosure · Female · Genetic Counseling · Genetic Predisposition to Disease · Genotype · Humans · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: Two randomized trials from the REVEAL programme agree. In REVEAL I (n=162 asymptomatic adult children of Alzheimer's patients), disclosure of APOE genotype produced no significant differences vs nondisclosure in time-averaged anxiety (4.5 vs 4.4; P=0.84), depression (8.8 vs 8.7; P=0.98) or test-related distress (6.9 vs 7.5; P=0.61) over a year — including in the subgroup who learned they carried ε4; ε4-negative participants had less test-related distress than ε4-positive participants (P=0.01). In the REVEAL follow-on noninferiority trial (n=343), condensed disclosure protocols — by genetic counsellors or by physicians — were noninferior to standard multi-session genetic counselling on anxiety and depression at 12 months, with all mean scores well below clinical concern cut-offs. The fence is selection: participants actively sought testing, were screened, and people with high baseline distress fared worse afterwards regardless of result — baseline anxiety and depression strongly predicted post-disclosure scores. 'No measurable harm in trial volunteers' is the claim; it is LIKELY true there and unproven in unselected direct-to-consumer settings. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: REVEAL I (Green 2009, NEJM): disclosing APOE genotype did not raise anxiety, depression or distress over 12 months — including in ε4 carriers
cards.summary: 162 asymptomatic adults with a parent with Alzheimer's disease were randomised to receive their APOE genotyping results (disclosure) or not (nondisclosure), with anxiety, depression and test-related distress measured at 6 weeks, 6 months and 1 year. Changes in time-averaged measures did not differ: anxiety 4.5 (disclosure) vs 4.4 (nondisclosure) (P=0.84); depression 8.8 vs 8.7 (P=0.98); test-related distress 6.9 vs 7.5 (P=0.61). Comparisons of the ε4-positive disclosure subgroup against nondisclosure also showed no significant differences; the ε4-negative subgroup had significantly lower test-related distress than the ε4-positive subgroup (P=0.01). Baseline anxiety and depression scores strongly predicted post-disclosure scores (P<0.001 for both).
cards.type: Prospective, randomized, controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2009. Registry ID verified in the record's own databank: NCT00571025.
cards.people: 162 asymptomatic adults who had a parent with Alzheimer's disease, randomised to disclosure or nondisclosure of their own APOE genotype. The record's abstract does not print a mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: No significant between-group differences in changes in time-averaged anxiety (4.5 vs 4.4; P=0.84), depression (8.8 vs 8.7; P=0.98), or test-related distress (6.9 vs 7.5; P=0.61) at up to 1 year. No significant differences for the ε4-positive subgroup vs nondisclosure; ε4-negative participants reported lower test-related distress than ε4-positive participants (P=0.01). Clinically meaningful changes were distributed evenly across groups.
cards.watchOut: A harm-null in 162 self-selected volunteers who wanted their result, received structured counselling, and were followed for one year. It does not cover unscreened, unsupported, or direct-to-consumer disclosure, longer horizons, or behaviour harms the trial wasn't built to see (insurance and planning decisions are a different evidence base). The strongest predictor of post-disclosure distress was distress before testing — the fence for any clinic copying this protocol.

cards.headline: REVEAL follow-on (Green 2015, Alzheimer's & Dementia): condensed APOE disclosure protocols were noninferior to standard genetic counselling on anxiety and depression at 12 months
cards.summary: Randomized, multicentre noninferiority trial in 343 asymptomatic adults with a first-degree relative with Alzheimer's disease, comparing standard multi-session disclosure by genetic counsellors (n=115) with condensed protocols delivered by genetic counsellors (n=116) or by physicians (n=112). Mean post-disclosure scores on all outcomes were well below cut-offs for clinical concern across protocols. Condensed-by-counsellor vs standard: the 97.5% upper confidence limits for differences in 12-month anxiety and depression means ranged from 1.2 to 2.0 (all P<.001 on noninferiority tests), establishing noninferiority; results were similar in European American and African American participants.
cards.type: Randomized, multicentre noninferiority trial, Alzheimers Dement 2015. The record's databank carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 343 asymptomatic adults with a first-degree relative with Alzheimer's disease at four sites; mean age 58.3 years (range 33–86); 71% female; 23% African American.
cards.result: Co-primary outcomes (anxiety and depression scales at 12 months): condensed protocols were noninferior to the standard genetic-counselling protocol — 97.5% upper confidence limits for mean differences of 1.2 to 2.0 points (all P<.001, noninferiority tests). All groups' mean scores remained well below clinical concern cut-offs.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority of the delivery format, in the same self-selected, screened population as REVEAL I — the authors limit the conclusion to people 'free of severe anxiety or depression who are actively seeking such information'. It supports briefer disclosure inside a service; it is not evidence that APOE results should be returned without any protocol, and APOE's limited predictive value for an individual is a separate fence this shelf does not adjudicate.

cards.headline: Synthesis — safe disclosure, narrow doorway
cards.summary: Across two randomized trials totalling 505 participants, learning one's APOE genotype through a structured protocol did not measurably increase anxiety, depression, or test-related distress over 12 months, and briefer protocols were noninferior to standard counselling. Both trials enrolled motivated volunteers with an affected relative and screened out severe baseline distress.

cards.people: Not applicable — synthesis card.
cards.result: REVEAL I: anxiety P=0.84, depression P=0.98, distress P=0.61 (all null). Green 2015: noninferiority established for condensed protocols (all P<.001).
cards.watchOut: The LIKELY stamp covers the safety of protocolised disclosure in trial-like populations only. Whether APOE disclosure changes behaviour usefully — or harms outside a protocol — is not what these trials tested, and this shelf makes no claim on it.

shelves.title: Newborn genomic screening: it finds risk standard screening misses — outcome benefit untested
shelves.question: Should genome or exome sequencing be added to standard newborn screening — what does it find, what does it do to families, and does it improve children's outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Disease · Exome Sequencing · Female · Genetic Diseases, Inborn · Genetic Predisposition to Disease · Genetic Testing · Genome, Human · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Male · Neonatal Screening · Parents · Pharmacogenetics · Whole Genome Sequencing
shelves.balance: The yield is real and the outcome evidence is absent — the definition of this slate's second MAYBE (weak evidence) shelf. In the BabySeq randomized pilot, sequencing 159 newborns found a childhood-onset disease risk in 9.4% — none anticipated from clinical or family history — plus carrier status in 88% and pharmacogenomic findings reported in 5%. Its companion randomized analysis found no persistent negative psychosocial effect on families, even in parents whose infant received a monogenic risk finding. The GUARDIAN study showed the model scales: 4,000 diverse New York newborns screened for 156 early-onset actionable conditions (plus an optional 99 neurodevelopmental disorders), 72% of approached families consenting, 99.6% of tests completed, and a 3.7% screen-positive rate including treatable conditions current screening cannot detect. What no study shows is the step that matters: that sequencing newborns makes children healthier than standard screening does. GUARDIAN is a single-group feasibility study still enrolling toward 100,000; BabySeq was a pilot. Proposed stamp MAYBE (weak evidence) — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: BabySeq results (Ceyhan-Birsoy 2019, Am J Hum Genet): sequencing 159 newborns found unanticipated childhood-onset disease risk in 9.4%
cards.summary: In the BabySeq pilot randomized trial, newborn genomic sequencing results were interpreted for 159 newborns from well-baby nurseries and neonatal intensive care. Sequencing revealed a risk of childhood-onset disease in 15 of 159 newborns (9.4%), none anticipated from known clinical or family history; actionable adult-onset disease risk in 3 of 85 newborns (3.5%) whose parents consented to that information; carrier status for recessive diseases in 88% and pharmacogenomics variants reported in 5%. Indication-based reanalysis in 29 of 32 NICU and 6 of 127 healthy newborns with later presentations found no variant that sufficiently explained the presentation, though uncertain suspicious results were reported in five. Parental samples aided interpretation in 13 of 159 (8%).
cards.type: Randomized clinical trial (pilot) — results and interpretation report, Am J Hum Genet 2019. The record carries no registry ID in its databank; the BabySeq trial registration (NCT02422511) is verified on the companion card below, not assumed for this one.
cards.people: 159 newborns whose sequencing was interpreted in the BabySeq Project — 127 healthy newborns and 32 admitted to a neonatal intensive care unit (per the indication-based analysis counts in the record). The record does not print a sex mix for the sequenced cohort.
cards.result: Childhood-onset disease risk identified: 15/159 (9.4%), none anticipated clinically. Actionable adult-onset risk: 3/85 (3.5%) among those consenting. Carrier status reported in 88% of newborns; pharmacogenomics variants in 5%. No disease-explaining variant was found in any of the 35 indication-based reanalyses.
cards.watchOut: Yield is not benefit. Most findings were risks and carrier states, not diagnoses of present disease; the NICU reanalyses — the cases where an answer was actually needed — explained none of the presentations, and five families received uncertain results. A 9.4% 'risk found' rate multiplied across all births is also a follow-up, counselling and false-alarm commitment this pilot was not designed to cost or to follow to outcomes.
cards.source: Ceyhan-Birsoy O et al. Interpretation of Genomic Sequencing Results in Healthy and Ill Newborns: Results from the BabySeq Project. Am J Hum Genet. 2019;104(1):76-93. PMID 30609409

cards.headline: BabySeq psychosocial RCT (Pereira 2021, JAMA Pediatrics): no persistent negative psychosocial effect of newborn genomic sequencing on families
cards.summary: Randomized analysis within BabySeq: 325 infants (well-baby and NICU) were randomised to standard newborn screening plus a family-history report, or the same plus a genomic sequencing report; 519 parents completed surveys at enrolment, disclosure, and 3 and 10 months after disclosure. Modelled comparisons showed no meaningful differences between groups in parent–child relationship (Mother-to-Infant Bonding Scale joint P=.57) or parents' psychological distress (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale anxiety subscale joint P=.80), and no persistent negative effect in any domain — including among parents whose infant received a monogenic disease-risk finding. One parents'-relationship measure differed transiently (joint P=.02) with the effect decreasing over time.
cards.type: Randomized clinical trial, JAMA Pediatr 2021. Registry ID verified in the record's own databank: NCT02422511.
cards.people: 519 parents (275 women [53.0%]; mean age 35.1 years [SD 4.5]) of 325 infants from well-baby nurseries and intensive care units at three Boston-area hospitals.
cards.result: No meaningful between-group differences over time in parent–child bonding (joint P=.57) or parental psychological distress (joint P=.80); no evidence of persistent negative psychosocial effect in any domain, in the sequencing group overall or in the subgroup receiving a monogenic disease-risk finding.
cards.watchOut: Reassurance with fences: survey volunteers in a research protocol with genetic-counselling support, followed for 10 months, measuring average scores — averages can hide a distressed minority, and a consented research setting is not a universal state programme. This card answers 'does it visibly harm families on average?' (no signal) — not 'is population screening wise?', which also turns on yield, cost, and outcomes this trial did not measure.

cards.headline: GUARDIAN interim (Ziegler 2025, JAMA): genome screening of 4,000 newborns — 72% of families consented, 99.6% completed, 3.7% screen-positive
cards.summary: Single-group prospective observational study in 6 New York City hospitals, adjunct to the state newborn screening programme: genome sequencing screened 156 early-onset genetic conditions with established interventions (plus 99 optional neurodevelopmental disorders with seizures). Of 5,555 families approached, 4,000 (72.0%) consented; enrolled newborns were diverse by parent-reported race (Asian 16.5%, Black 25.1%, White 44.7%, ≥2 races 13.0%) and ethnicity (Hispanic 44.0%). cards.headline: Synthesis — MAYBE (weak evidence) shelf: feasibility proven at scale, outcomes unproven anywhere
cards.summary: In-flight and ongoing evidence, named as required for a thin shelf: GUARDIAN continues toward its planned 100,000 newborns (NCT05990179) with outcome follow-up still to report; BabySeq remains the only randomized programme, at pilot size. shelves.title: HLA-B*57:01 before abacavir: the pharmacogenetic test that eliminated its reaction
shelves.question: Does prospective HLA-B*57:01 screening before starting abacavir prevent abacavir hypersensitivity reactions in people with HIV-1?
shelves.mesh: Abacavir · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Dideoxynucleosides · Double-Blind Method · Drug Hypersensitivity · Female · Genetic Markers · Genetic Testing · Genotype · HIV Infections · HIV-1 · HLA-B Antigens · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patch Tests · Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors
shelves.balance: The cleanest result in pharmacogenetics. PREDICT-1 (n=1,956, double-blind, randomized) screened prospectively for HLA-B*57:01 and excluded carriers from abacavir: immunologically confirmed hypersensitivity fell to 0% with screening vs 2.7% without (P<0.001), clinically diagnosed hypersensitivity fell from 7.8% to 3.4% (P<0.001), and the test's negative predictive value was 100% (positive predictive value 47.9% — about half of carriers would have reacted). A prospective Western Australian cohort had already shown the same pattern in practice: no hypersensitivity cases among 148 allele-negative recipients after screening was introduced. The fence is ancestry and era: the trial population was 84% white, allele prevalence (5.6% here) and predictive values differ across populations, and abacavir is a smaller part of modern HIV therapy than in 2008. Within its question, though, the evidence is a definitive randomized elimination of the immunologically confirmed reaction. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: PREDICT-1 (Mallal 2008, NEJM): prospective HLA-B*57:01 screening eliminated immunologically confirmed abacavir hypersensitivity — 0% vs 2.7%
cards.summary: 1,956 patients with HIV-1 infection from 19 countries, abacavir-naive, randomised double-blind to prospective HLA-B*57:01 screening (carriers excluded from abacavir) or standard care (abacavir without screening), observed for 6 weeks after starting abacavir, with epicutaneous patch testing to immunologically confirm hypersensitivity. HLA-B*57:01 prevalence was 5.6% (109/1,956). Immunologically confirmed hypersensitivity: 0% in the prospective-screening group vs 2.7% in controls (P<0.001); negative predictive value 100%, positive predictive value 47.9%. Clinically diagnosed hypersensitivity: 3.4% vs 7.8% (P<0.001).
cards.type: Double-blind, prospective, randomized study, N Engl J Med 2008. Registry ID verified in the record's own databank: NCT00340080.
cards.people: 1,956 patients infected with HIV-1 who had not previously received abacavir, from 19 countries. Of patients receiving abacavir, 72% were men, 84% were white, and 18% had not previously received antiretroviral therapy. The record's abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: Immunologically confirmed hypersensitivity reaction: 0% (prospective screening) vs 2.7% (control) (P<0.001). Clinically diagnosed hypersensitivity: 3.4% vs 7.8% (P<0.001). HLA-B*57:01 prevalence 5.6% (109/1,956); negative predictive value 100%; positive predictive value 47.9%.
cards.watchOut: Two fences, both printed by the trial itself. Population: predominantly white (84%), and the allele's prevalence and the test's predictive values vary by ancestry — the 100% negative predictive value is this population's number. Meaning of a positive: with a positive predictive value of 47.9%, screening denies abacavir to roughly one non-reactor for every reactor protected — an acceptable trade for a preventable, potentially fatal reaction with alternatives available, but it is a trade, and it is why the claim is 'screen before abacavir', not 'the allele equals the reaction'.
cards.source: Mallal S et al. HLA-B*5701 screening for hypersensitivity to abacavir. N Engl J Med. 2008;358(6):568-579. PMID 18256392 · NCT00340080

cards.headline: Rauch 2006 (Clin Infect Dis): prospective screening in Western Australian practice — no hypersensitivity cases among 148 HLA-B*57:01-negative recipients
cards.summary: Prospective cohort study of 260 abacavir-naive individuals in Western Australia, of whom 7.7% were HLA-B*57:01-positive, confirming the retrospective genetic association in routine practice: after prospective genetic risk stratification, no cases of abacavir hypersensitivity occurred among the 148 HLA-B*57:01-negative recipients treated. Published two years before PREDICT-1, this was the practice-based evidence that screening worked outside a trial.
cards.type: Prospective cohort study, Clin Infect Dis 2006. Pre-registration-era observational study: the record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 260 abacavir-naive individuals in Western Australia, 7.7% of them positive for HLA-B*57:01; 148 allele-negative recipients were treated with abacavir after screening. The record's abstract does not print a mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Abacavir hypersensitivity cases among prospectively screened HLA-B*57:01-negative recipients: 0 of 148. Allele prevalence in the cohort: 7.7% of 260 individuals.
cards.watchOut: A small, single-region cohort with a short abstract: it confirms direction, not precision — 0 events in 148 patients excludes only very common reactions in negatives, and the record prints no comparator incidence for the pre-screening era in the same clinic. Its role on this shelf is corroboration of PREDICT-1, in real practice, two years earlier; the randomized card carries the claim.

shelves.title: Population BRCA testing in Ashkenazi Jewish populations
shelves.question: Does offering BRCA testing to an entire (unselected by family history) Ashkenazi Jewish population find more carriers cost-effectively versus family-history-based testing — the GCaPPS randomised trial?
shelves.mesh: Anxiety/etiology · BRCA1 Protein/genetics · BRCA2 Protein/genetics · Decision Support Techniques · Depression/etiology · Early Detection of Cancer/methods · Founder Effect
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: A single randomised trial (GCaPPS; 1,034 Ashkenazi Jewish adults in North London) with two reports — the primary psychological-outcomes report (Manchanda 2015) and the 3-year follow-up (Manchanda 2020) — counted once as evidence. Testing everyone, rather than only those meeting family-history criteria, found carriers that criteria missed: 56% of carriers in the primary report and 60% in the long-term report did not fulfil clinical criteria for testing, at a total BRCA prevalence of 2.45% and 2.9% respectively. Psychological outcomes were not worse with population testing at 7 days, 3 months, or over 3 years (anxiety decreased more in the population arm over 3 years, P=0.046). A single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and the shelf claims detection and psychological safety only — not cancer prevented, which this trial does not measure. Family cascade testing (Shelf #476) and risk-reducing surgery after a positive result (Shelf #478) are neighbouring questions, not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Manchanda 2015 (GCaPPS primary): population testing found that 56% of carriers missed family-history criteria, with no worse psychological outcomes
cards.summary: Manchanda 2015 (GCaPPS primary, pinned at build): population testing found that 56% of carriers missed family-history criteria, with no worse psychological outcomes.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (population screening vs family-history-based testing)
cards.people: 1,034 Ashkenazi Jewish individuals older than 18 years recruited by self-referral after pretest genetic counseling in North London, randomly assigned to population screening (testing all participants) or family-history-based testing (691 women, 343 men), with 1,017 eligible for analysis; mean age 54.3 (SD 14.66) years, as stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Thirteen BRCA1/2 carriers were identified in the population screening arm and nine in the family history arm; five more carriers were detected among family-history-negative participants in the family history arm following study completion. Overall, 56% of carriers did not fulfil clinical criteria for genetic testing, and the BRCA1/2 prevalence was 2.45%. There were no statistically significant differences between the family-history and population-screening arms at seven days or three months on measures of anxiety, depression, health anxiety, distress, uncertainty, and quality of life. Overall anxiety (P=.0001) and uncertainty (P=.005) associated with genetic testing decreased over time, and positive experience scores increased (P=.0001).
cards.watchOut: Self-referred volunteers in one city's Ashkenazi Jewish community, testing founder mutations: psychological safety in motivated volunteers does not automatically transfer to unselected population offers or to full sequencing panels.

shelves.title: Pegvaliase for phenylketonuria (PKU) with uncontrolled phenylalanine
shelves.question: In adults with PKU and blood phenylalanine above target despite prior management, does pegvaliase vs control lower blood phenylalanine?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Phenylalanine/blood · Phenylalanine Ammonia-Lyase/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Phenylketonurias/drug therapy · Recombinant Proteins/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — with two corrections to the topic file on the card's face. First, attribution: the pinned record (PMID 29653686) is Thomas et al., Molecular Genetics and Metabolism 2018, reporting the PRISM programme — not 'Harding et al., Genet Med 2018' as the topic file states. Second, design: although the question asks 'versus control', the carded report is a long-term phase 3 programme summary (PRISM-1 randomised patients between two pegvaliase maintenance doses, 20 vs 40 mg/day — not drug vs placebo — and PRISM-2 was largely open-label extension); there is no placebo-controlled comparison in this record. Among 261 treated adults with baseline blood phenylalanine 1,232.7 µmol/L, mean Phe fell to 564.5 µmol/L at 12 months (−51.1%) and 311.4 µmol/L at 24 months (−68.7%); within 24 months, 68.4% reached Phe ≤600 µmol/L, 60.7% ≤360 µmol/L and 51.2% ≤120 µmol/L. Falls of this size in patients uncontrolled on prior management are unlikely to be spontaneous, which earns POSSIBLE despite the uncontrolled design; the price is immunogenicity — arthralgia 70.5%, injection-site reaction 62.1%, headache 47.1%, and acute systemic hypersensitivity events meeting anaphylaxis criteria in 12 participants (17 events), all resolving without sequelae. Phe is a surrogate endpoint, as the topic file flags.

cards.headline: PRISM programme (Thomas 2018): pegvaliase lowered mean blood Phe by 51.1% at 12 months and 68.7% at 24 months in 261 adults — an uncontrolled long-term programme report, not a placebo-controlled trial
cards.summary: PRISM programme (Thomas 2018): pegvaliase lowered mean blood Phe by 51.1% at 12 months and 68.7% at 24 months in 261 adults — an uncontrolled long-term programme report, not a placebo-controlled trial
cards.type: Phase 3 clinical trial programme report (PRISM-1 dose-randomised; PRISM-2 four-part trial with open-label long-term extension)
cards.people: 261 adults with PKU who received pegvaliase treatment; PRISM-1 enrolled pegvaliase-naïve participants with blood Phe above 600 µmol/L, randomised 1:1 to a maintenance dose of 20 mg/day or 40 mg/day after induction/titration, and PRISM-1 participants continued into PRISM-2 (including an open-label long-term extension with doses of 5–60 mg/day). 72.0% reached at least 12 months and 32.6% at least 24 months of treatment; 65% were still actively receiving treatment at the report. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean (SD) blood Phe was 1,232.7 (386.4) µmol/L at baseline, 564.5 (531.2) µmol/L at 12 months, and 311.4 (427) µmol/L at 24 months — decreases from baseline of 51.1% and 68.7% respectively. Within 24 months, 68.4% of participants achieved blood Phe ≤600 µmol/L, 60.7% achieved ≤360 µmol/L (below the upper limit recommended in the ACMG PKU guidelines), and 51.2% achieved ≤120 µmol/L (below the upper limit of normal in unaffected people). Improvements in neuropsychiatric outcomes were associated with Phe reductions and were sustained with long-term treatment. Adverse events were more frequent in the first 6 months; 99% of adverse events were mild or moderate and 96% resolved without dose interruption or reduction. The most common were arthralgia (70.5%), injection-site reaction (62.1%), injection-site erythema (47.9%) and headache (47.1%). Acute systemic hypersensitivity events meeting NIAID/FAAN anaphylaxis criteria occurred in 12 participants (17 events); six remained on treatment; events were not associated with IgE and all resolved without sequelae.
cards.watchOut: No untreated control group and heavy attrition (only 32.6% reached 24 months) mean the mean Phe falls describe patients who stayed on treatment, not an intention-to-treat effect; responder proportions use the treated population as published. The topic file's authorship and journal for this PMID were wrong and are corrected on this card.
