shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One phase III double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Levy 2007, 89 patients with PKU; mean age 20 years) found six weeks of sapropterin 10 mg/kg daily reduced mean blood phenylalanine by 236 µmol/L while placebo rose by 3 µmol/L (P<0.0001), with 44% of sapropterin patients versus 9% on placebo achieving a reduction of at least 30% from baseline. The response concentrated in BH4-responsive patients — the authors frame sapropterin as an adjunct to (and in some cases possible replacement for) the low-phenylalanine diet in responsive patients only. A single 6-week trial on a surrogate endpoint (blood Phe, not clinical outcomes), in a responder-defined condition: POSSIBLE. The topic file's DOUBLE-A label was not matched by a second pinned trial at build.

cards.headline: Levy 2007: sapropterin lowered blood Phe by 236 µmol/L vs a 3 µmol/L rise on placebo at 6 weeks; ≥30% reduction in 44% vs 9%
cards.summary: Levy 2007: sapropterin lowered blood Phe by 236 µmol/L vs a 3 µmol/L rise on placebo at 6 weeks; ≥30% reduction in 44% vs 9%
cards.type: Phase III, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
cards.people: 89 patients with phenylketonuria enrolled (mean age 20 [SD 9.7] years); 42 were assigned to oral sapropterin 10 mg/kg once daily and 47 to placebo for 6 weeks; 88 received at least one dose and 87 attended the week 6 visit. Baseline mean blood phenylalanine was 843 (SD 300) µmol/L on sapropterin and 888 (SD 323) µmol/L on placebo.
cards.result: After 6 weeks, patients given sapropterin had a decrease in mean blood phenylalanine of 236 (SD 257) µmol/L, compared with a 3 (SD 240) µmol/L increase in the placebo group (P<0.0001). A reduction of 30% or more from baseline was achieved by 18 of 41 patients (44%, 95% CI 28 to 60) in the sapropterin group versus 4 of 47 (9%, 2 to 20) on placebo. Phenylalanine fell by about 200 µmol/L after 1 week and the reduction persisted for the remaining 5 weeks (P<0.0001). Adverse events that might have been drug-related occurred in 11 of 47 patients (23%) in the sapropterin group and 8 of 41 (20%) in the placebo group (P=0.80); upper respiratory tract infections were the most common disorder. The record's group denominators for the adverse-event line (47 sapropterin, 41 placebo) are the reverse of its assignment line (42 sapropterin, 47 placebo) — the abstract is internally inconsistent on these denominators, and the card prints both exactly as they appear rather than resolving them.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks, one surrogate: blood Phe is the accepted treatment target in PKU but this trial shows no dietary, cognitive or quality-of-life outcome. The denominator inconsistency in the abstract's safety line is flagged on the card face — figures are as printed.
cards.source: Levy HL et al. Efficacy of sapropterin dihydrochloride (tetrahydrobiopterin, 6R-BH4) for reduction of phenylalanine concentration in patients with phenylketonuria: a phase III randomised placebo-controlled study. Lancet. 2007. PMID: 17693179. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00104247, from the record's databank fields (the abstract prints NCT00104247 within the registration line for this study programme). cards.headline: Synthesis: a real Phe effect in BH4-responsive PKU, at single-trial strength — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real Phe effect in BH4-responsive PKU, at single-trial strength — POSSIBLE
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Levy 2007 (89 patients with PKU).
cards.result: Sapropterin lowered blood phenylalanine quickly (within 1 week) and substantially (−236 µmol/L vs +3 on placebo), with nearly five times the ≥30%-responder rate (44% vs 9%) and placebo-like tolerability over 6 weeks. Pegvaliase (Shelf #1400) serves the uncontrolled-PKU population by a different mechanism and is not interchangeable evidence.
cards.watchOut: Responsiveness must be established per patient (a BH4-loading assessment in practice); quoting the 44% responder rate as if it applied to all PKU patients misstates a responder-enriched result.

shelves.title: Eliglustat (substrate reduction) for Gaucher disease type 1
shelves.question: In treatment-naïve adults with Gaucher disease type 1, does oral eliglustat vs placebo reduce splenomegaly and improve haematological measures?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Double-Blind Method · Enzyme Inhibitors/pharmacology,therapeutic use · Female · Gaucher Disease/complications,drug therapy · Glucosyltransferases/antagonists & inhibitors · Humans · Male · Organ Size/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The pinned trial (ENGAGE, Mistry 2015, 40 previously untreated adults with Gaucher disease type 1) found nine months of oral eliglustat significantly improved every measured disease parameter versus placebo: spleen volume changed by −27.77% versus +2.26% (absolute treatment difference −30.03%, 95% CI −36.82% to −23.24%; P<0.001), haemoglobin rose by an adjusted 1.22 g/dL (P<0.001), liver volume fell by 6.64% (P=0.007) and platelet count rose by 41.06% (P<0.001), with no serious adverse events and one non-treatment-related withdrawal. Forty patients is a pivotal-trial sample for a rare disease, and the authors themselves caution that clinical significance is uncertain and that comparison with enzyme replacement therapy plus longer follow-up are required; the ENCORE non-inferiority trial named in the topic file was not pinned at build. Single carded trial: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ENGAGE 2015: eliglustat shrank spleen volume by 27.8% vs a 2.3% increase on placebo at 9 months, with haemoglobin +1.22 g/dL and platelets +41% adjusted differences
cards.summary: ENGAGE 2015: eliglustat shrank spleen volume by 27.8% vs a 2.3% increase on placebo at 9 months, with haemoglobin +1.22 g/dL and platelets +41% adjusted differences
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (18 sites, 12 countries)
cards.people: 40 previously untreated adults with Gaucher disease type 1 and splenomegaly plus thrombocytopenia and/or anaemia (of 72 patients screened), stratified by spleen volume and randomised 1:1 to eliglustat 50 or 100 mg twice daily (20) or placebo (20) for 9 months. All patients had baseline splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia (mostly moderate or severe), most had mild or moderate hepatomegaly, and 20% had mild anaemia.
cards.result: Least-square mean spleen volume decreased by 27.77% (95% CI −32.57% to −22.97%) on eliglustat (from 13.89 to 10.17 multiples of normal) versus an increase of 2.26% (−2.54% to 7.06%) on placebo (from 12.50 to 12.84 multiples of normal) — an absolute treatment difference of −30.03% (−36.82% to −23.24%; P<0.001). Secondary differences all favoured eliglustat: haemoglobin level +1.22 g/dL (0.57 to 1.88; P<0.001), liver volume −6.64% (−11.37% to −1.91%; P=0.007), platelet count +41.06% (23.95% to 58.17%; P<0.001). No serious adverse events occurred; one eliglustat patient withdrew for a non-treatment-related reason, and 39 of 40 patients entered the open-label extension. The authors state the clinical significance of these findings is uncertain and that comparison with standard enzyme replacement therapy and longer follow-up are needed for definitive conclusions.
cards.watchOut: Organ volumes and blood counts are disease-activity measures, not patient outcomes: nine months in 40 patients cannot speak to bone disease, bleeding events or quality of life, and the trial's comparator is placebo in untreated patients — not the enzyme replacement most eligible patients would otherwise receive.
cards.source: Mistry PK et al. Effect of oral eliglustat on splenomegaly in patients with Gaucher disease type 1: the ENGAGE randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2015. PMID: 25688781. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00891202, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: every disease parameter improved on one small pivotal trial — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: every disease parameter improved on one small pivotal trial — POSSIBLE
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: ENGAGE 2015 (40 treatment-naïve adults with Gaucher disease type 1).
cards.result: Oral substrate-reduction therapy reversed the direction of splenomegaly (−27.8% vs +2.3%), anaemia and thrombocytopenia over 9 months with no serious adverse events — a coherent multi-parameter result. The ENCORE trial (eliglustat versus imiglucerase enzyme replacement) named in the topic file is fenced here, not carded; this shelf establishes eliglustat against placebo only.
cards.watchOut: CYP2D6 metaboliser status governs eliglustat dosing and eligibility in practice — a pharmacogenetic gate that a placebo trial's average effect does not capture.

shelves.title: Migalastat (pharmacological chaperone) for Fabry disease with amenable GLA variants
shelves.question: In patients with Fabry disease and amenable mutations, does migalastat vs placebo (FACETS) or vs enzyme replacement (ATTRACT) reduce substrate deposition?
shelves.mesh: 1-Deoxynojirimycin/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Diarrhea/drug therapy,etiology · Double-Blind Method · Fabry Disease/complications,drug therapy · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — with the primary-result correction stated plainly: the topic file says FACETS showed migalastat 'reduced kidney capillary GL-3 inclusions and plasma lyso-Gb3 vs placebo in the amenable-mutation subgroup'. The record's primary analysis says more and less than that: in ALL randomised patients, the proportion achieving a ≥50% reduction in kidney interstitial-capillary GL-3 inclusions at 6 months was 41% on migalastat versus 28% on placebo — NOT significant (P=0.30). The amenable-mutation framing rests on a validated assay substituted before unblinding, which reclassified the population (50 of 67 randomised patients had suitable mutant forms); among suitable patients treated up to 24 months, renal function was essentially stable and left-ventricular-mass index fell (−7.7 g/m², 95% CI −15.4 to −0.01). ATTRACT (Hughes 2017, 57 adults previously on enzyme replacement) found migalastat and continued ERT had similar effects on renal function over 18 months in an open-label switch design, with left-ventricular-mass index decreasing significantly on migalastat (−6.6 g/m², −11.0 to −2.2) and plasma lyso-Gb3 remaining low and stable after switching. Two trials, a missed primary endpoint in the placebo trial, an open-label active-comparator trial, and surrogate substrate/organ-mass endpoints: POSSIBLE, and the FACETS primary miss must travel with any citation of this shelf.

cards.headline: FACETS 2016: primary endpoint NOT significant — GL-3 response 41% on migalastat vs 28% on placebo (P=0.30); signals rest on the post-assay amenable subgroup
cards.summary: FACETS 2016: primary endpoint NOT significant — GL-3 response 41% on migalastat vs 28% on placebo (P=0.30); signals rest on the post-assay amenable subgroup
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (stage 1, 6 months) followed by open-label migalastat (stage 2 and extension)
cards.people: 67 patients with Fabry disease were randomised to 6 months of double-blind migalastat or placebo, followed by open-label migalastat from 6 to 12 months plus an additional year. Before unblinding, a new validated assay of mutant α-galactosidase forms showed 50 of the 67 participants had forms suitable for targeting by migalastat. The primary endpoint was the percentage of patients with a response (≥50% reduction in the number of GL-3 inclusions per kidney interstitial capillary) at 6 months.
cards.result: The primary endpoint analysis, involving patients with mutant α-galactosidase forms suitable or not suitable for migalastat, did NOT show a significant treatment effect: 13 of 32 patients (41%) on migalastat and 9 of 32 (28%) on placebo had a response at 6 months (P=0.30). Among patients with suitable mutant forms who received migalastat for up to 24 months, annualised changes in estimated GFR and measured GFR were −0.30 (SE 0.66) and −1.51 (SE 1.33) mL/min/1.73 m², and the left-ventricular-mass index decreased significantly from baseline (−7.7 g/m²; 95% CI −15.4 to −0.01), particularly with baseline hypertrophy (−18.6 g/m²; −38.2 to 1.0). The severity of diarrhoea, reflux, and indigestion decreased. The authors conclude that among all randomly assigned patients, the response percentage did not differ significantly between migalastat and placebo.
cards.watchOut: The mid-trial assay change is the crux: the population in which benefit is claimed was defined by a better test applied before unblinding — methodologically defensible, but it converts the trial's headline from a randomised comparison into a subgroup narrative, and the randomised headline is null. Any summary that opens with the subgroup and omits P=0.30 misstates this trial.
cards.source: Germain DP et al. Treatment of Fabry's Disease with the Pharmacologic Chaperone Migalastat. N Engl J Med. 2016. PMID: 27509102. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00925301 and NCT01458119, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: ATTRACT 2017: switching from enzyme replacement to migalastat gave similar renal function over 18 months in amenable patients (open-label)
cards.summary: ATTRACT 2017: switching from enzyme replacement to migalastat gave similar renal function over 18 months in amenable patients (open-label)
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, active-controlled phase III trial (18 months)
cards.people: 57 adults (56% female) with Fabry disease receiving enzyme replacement therapy (88% had multiorgan disease), randomised 1.5:1, based on a preliminary cell-based assay of migalastat responsiveness, to 18 months of open-label migalastat or continued ERT; four patients found to have non-amenable mutant forms on the validated assay after treatment initiation were excluded from primary efficacy analyses only. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Migalastat and ERT had similar effects on renal function. Left ventricular mass index decreased significantly with migalastat (−6.6 g/m², 95% CI −11.0 to −2.2); there was no significant change with ERT. Predefined renal, cardiac or cerebrovascular events occurred in 29% of migalastat and 44% of ERT patients. Plasma globotriaosylsphingosine remained low and stable following the switch from ERT to migalastat. Patient-reported outcomes were comparable between groups, and migalastat was generally safe and well tolerated. The authors conclude migalastat offers promise as an oral monotherapy alternative to intravenous ERT for patients with amenable mutations. NOTE: this record's abstract text prints registry number NCT00925301 (the FACETS number) while its databank fields carry NCT01218659; the card's source line uses the databank value.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 57 patients, no placebo: 'similar renal effects' over 18 months in already-treated patients is a switch-stability result, not proof of equivalent disease modification — and event rates (29% vs 44%) in groups this small are descriptive, not comparative evidence.
cards.source: Hughes DA et al. Oral pharmacological chaperone migalastat compared with enzyme replacement therapy in Fabry disease: 18-month results from the randomised phase III ATTRACT study. J Med Genet. 2017. PMID: 27834756. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01218659, from the record's databank fields (the abstract text prints NCT00925301 — an internal inconsistency in the record, flagged on this card). cards.headline: Synthesis: an oral option for amenable mutations, resting on a missed primary and a switch study — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: an oral option for amenable mutations, resting on a missed primary and a switch study — POSSIBLE
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: FACETS 2016 (67 randomised) and ATTRACT 2017 (57 adults switching from ERT).
cards.result: For Fabry patients whose GLA variant is amenable, migalastat offers oral dosing with stable renal function and falling left-ventricular mass in follow-up data, and switch-stability against continued enzyme replacement — but the only placebo-controlled primary endpoint in the programme missed (41% vs 28%, P=0.30). shelves.title: Alglucosidase alfa enzyme replacement for late-onset Pompe disease (LOTS)
shelves.question: In ambulatory adults with late-onset Pompe disease, does alglucosidase alfa vs placebo improve walking distance and respiratory function?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age of Onset · Aged · Child · Drug Hypersensitivity/etiology · Female · Glycogen Storage Disease Type II/drug therapy,physiopathology · Humans · Male · alpha-Glucosidases/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The single pivotal trial (LOTS, van der Ploeg 2010, 90 patients aged 8 years and older, ambulatory and free of invasive ventilation) found 78 weeks of biweekly alglucosidase alfa improved both co-primary endpoints versus placebo: an estimated mean increase of 28.1 m (SE 13.1) in 6-minute walk distance and an absolute increase of 3.4 (SE 1.2) percentage points in percent-predicted forced vital capacity (P=0.03 and P=0.006). Adverse events, serious adverse events and infusion-associated reactions occurred in similar proportions overall; events seen only on active drug included anaphylactic reactions and infusion reactions (urticaria, flushing, sweating, chest discomfort, vomiting, raised blood pressure), each in 5–8% of patients. One trial, surrogate-functional endpoints (walk distance and FVC, not survival or ventilation-free survival): POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: LOTS 2010: alglucosidase alfa improved 6-minute walk by an estimated +28.1 m and FVC by +3.4 percentage points vs placebo over 78 weeks
cards.summary: LOTS 2010: alglucosidase alfa improved 6-minute walk by an estimated +28.1 m and FVC by +3.4 percentage points vs placebo over 78 weeks
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial (eight centres, United States and Europe)
cards.people: 90 patients who were 8 years of age or older, ambulatory, and free of invasive ventilation, with late-onset Pompe disease, randomly assigned to biweekly intravenous alglucosidase alfa 20 mg/kg or placebo for 78 weeks. The abstract does not state the per-group numbers, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 78 weeks, the estimated mean changes from baseline in the two primary endpoints favoured alglucosidase alfa: an increase of 28.1 (SE 13.1) m on the 6-minute walk test and an absolute increase of 3.4 (SE 1.2) percentage points in percent-predicted forced vital capacity (P=0.03 and P=0.006, respectively). Similar proportions of patients in the two groups had adverse events, serious adverse events, and infusion-associated reactions; events occurring only in patients who received active drug included anaphylactic reactions and infusion-associated reactions of urticaria, flushing, hyperhidrosis, chest discomfort, vomiting, and increased blood pressure, each in 5 to 8% of patients. The authors conclude treatment was associated with improved walking distance and stabilisation of pulmonary function over 18 months.
cards.watchOut: Standard errors of 13.1 m on a 28.1 m walk estimate mean the true average gain is imprecisely known, and the trial enrolled ambulatory patients only — the result does not extend to ventilator-dependent or non-ambulatory late-onset disease.
cards.source: van der Ploeg AT et al. A randomized study of alglucosidase alfa in late-onset Pompe's disease. N Engl J Med. 2010. PMID: 20393176. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00158600, from the record's databank fields. cards.summary: Synthesis: modest functional gains on the only pivotal trial — POSSIBLE
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: LOTS 2010 (90 patients with late-onset Pompe disease).
cards.result: Enzyme replacement produced statistically significant, clinically modest improvements in walking distance (+28.1 m) and forced vital capacity (+3.4 points of predicted) over 78 weeks in ambulatory late-onset Pompe disease, with anaphylaxis among its drug-specific risks. shelves.title: Idursulfase enzyme replacement for mucopolysaccharidosis II (Hunter syndrome)
shelves.question: In patients with MPS II, does weekly idursulfase vs placebo improve a composite of walking distance and forced vital capacity?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Child · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Drug Tolerance · Glycoproteins/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Humans · Iduronate Sulfatase/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Male · Mucopolysaccharidosis II/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The single pivotal trial (Muenzer 2006, 96 patients with MPS II aged 5–31 years) found one year of idursulfase significantly improved the prespecified composite endpoint (sum of ranks of change in 6-minute walk distance and percent-predicted FVC) versus placebo for both weekly dosing (P=0.0049) and every-other-week dosing (P=0.0416). In the weekly group, 6-minute walk distance rose by 37 m (P=0.013), percent-predicted FVC by 2.7% (P=0.065) and absolute FVC by 160 mL (P=0.001) versus placebo. Infusion reactions occurred, and idursulfase antibodies were detected in 46.9% of patients. One trial in a male-only population (MPS II is X-linked; the record's MeSH and population are male), with composite/endurance endpoints: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Muenzer 2006: weekly idursulfase improved the walk/FVC composite vs placebo (P=0.0049), with +37 m walking distance; antibodies in 46.9%
cards.summary: Muenzer 2006: weekly idursulfase improved the walk/FVC composite vs placebo (P=0.0049), with +37 m walking distance; antibodies in 46.9%
cards.type: Phase II/III, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
cards.people: 96 patients with mucopolysaccharidosis II between 5 and 31 years of age, randomised to placebo infusions, weekly idursulfase 0.5 mg/kg infusions, or every-other-week idursulfase 0.5 mg/kg infusions, for one year. The population is male (X-linked condition; the record's MeSH lists Male only).
cards.result: Patients in the weekly and every-other-week idursulfase groups exhibited significant improvement in the composite endpoint (distance walked in 6 minutes plus percentage of predicted forced vital capacity, combined as the sum of the ranks of change from baseline) compared with placebo (P=0.0049 for weekly and P=0.0416 for every-other-week) after one year. The weekly dosing group experienced a 37-m increase in 6-minute-walk distance (P=0.013), a 2.7% increase in percentage of predicted FVC (P=0.065), and a 160 mL increase in absolute FVC (P=0.001) compared with the placebo group at 53 weeks. Idursulfase was generally well tolerated, but infusion reactions did occur; idursulfase antibodies were detected in 46.9% of patients during the study.
cards.watchOut: A rank-sum composite can be significant while its components are uneven — here the FVC percentage component in the weekly arm was not itself significant (P=0.065). Antibody development in nearly half of patients is reported without a carded efficacy consequence in this record; long-term attenuation is outside this trial.

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The single pivotal trial (Harmatz 2006, 39 patients with MPS VI) found 24 weeks of recombinant human arylsulfatase B (galsulfase) improved endurance versus placebo: patients on active treatment walked on average 92 m more in the 12-minute walk test (P=0.025) and climbed 5.7 more stairs per minute in the 3-minute stair climb (P=0.053 — not significant), while urinary glycosaminoglycan excretion fell by 227 µg/mg more than placebo (P<0.001). shelves.title: Glycerol phenylbutyrate for urea cycle disorders
shelves.question: In patients with urea cycle disorders, does glycerol phenylbutyrate vs sodium phenylbutyrate provide equivalent ammonia control?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Ammonia/blood · Child · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glutamine/blood · Glycerol/analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Urea Cycle Disorders, Inborn/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The pivotal evidence is a randomised, double-blind, crossover phase 3 trial in adults (reported within Diaz 2013) in which glycerol phenylbutyrate was non-inferior to sodium phenylbutyrate for ammonia control: mean 24-hour ammonia AUC was 866 (SD 661) versus 977 (SD 865) µmol·h/L. Across 65 adult and paediatric patients completing three similarly designed short-term comparisons, ammonia AUC was directionally lower on glycerol phenylbutyrate in each study and significantly lower in the pooled analysis, as was plasma glutamine; 12 months of open-label treatment kept average ammonia in the normal range. The paediatric card requires a correction to the topic file: the under-6 study (Smith 2013, 15 children aged 2 months to under 6 years) was an OPEN-LABEL switch-over study, not the randomised trial the topic file describes — it met predefined non-inferiority criteria for daily ammonia exposure (ratio of means 0.79, 95% CI 0.593 to 1.055) after switching from sodium phenylbutyrate. Ammonia is a surrogate endpoint, the samples are small rare-disease samples, and 'equivalent control with a better-behaving formulation' is the claim: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Diaz 2013: glycerol phenylbutyrate was non-inferior to sodium phenylbutyrate for 24-hour ammonia control in the pivotal randomised crossover trial (AUC 866 vs 977 µmol·h/L)
cards.summary: Diaz 2013: glycerol phenylbutyrate was non-inferior to sodium phenylbutyrate for 24-hour ammonia control in the pivotal randomised crossover trial (AUC 866 vs 977 µmol·h/L)
cards.type: Pivotal phase 3, randomised, double-blind, crossover trial (reported together with three short-term comparison studies and 12-month open-label follow-up)
cards.people: The pivotal trial enrolled adult patients with urea cycle disorders; the combined short-term programme comprised 65 adult and paediatric patients (ages 6 and above in the long-term report) completing three similarly designed comparisons of glycerol phenylbutyrate versus sodium phenylbutyrate. The abstract does not state the pivotal trial's own enrolment number, mean age or sex mix, and none are printed here.
cards.result: Glycerol phenylbutyrate was non-inferior to sodium phenylbutyrate for ammonia control in the pivotal study, with mean (SD) 24-hour ammonia AUC of 866 (661) versus 977 (865) µmol·h/L respectively. Among the 65 patients completing the three short-term comparisons, ammonia AUC was directionally lower on glycerol phenylbutyrate in each study and significantly lower in the pooled analysis (P<0.05), as was plasma glutamine; 24-hour ammonia profiles were consistent with slow-release behaviour and better overnight control. During 12 months of open-label glycerol phenylbutyrate treatment, average ammonia was normal in adult and paediatric patients, and executive function among paediatric patients (behavioural regulation, goal setting, planning, self-monitoring) was significantly improved — an uncontrolled observation. Pharmacokinetic results accompanied the clinical report.
cards.watchOut: The executive-function improvement comes from the open-label phase with no comparator and is reported here as the authors' observation, not as trial evidence. Non-inferiority on ammonia AUC over short periods does not by itself prove equal protection against hyperammonaemic crises over years.
cards.source: Diaz GA et al. Ammonia control and neurocognitive outcome among urea cycle disorder patients treated with glycerol phenylbutyrate. Hepatology. 2013. PMID: 22961727. cards.headline: Smith 2013: in children 2 months to under 6 years, switching to glycerol phenylbutyrate met non-inferiority for ammonia exposure (ratio 0.79) — an open-label switch-over study, not an RCT
cards.summary: Smith 2013: in children 2 months to under 6 years, switching to glycerol phenylbutyrate met non-inferiority for ammonia exposure (ratio 0.79) — an open-label switch-over study, not an RCT
cards.type: Open-label switch-over study (single-arm comparison against the patient's own prior sodium phenylbutyrate period)
cards.people: 15 patients aged 2 months through 5 years with urea cycle disorders (8 argininosuccinate lyase deficiency, 3 argininosuccinic acid synthetase deficiency, 3 ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, 1 arginase deficiency), all previously taking sodium phenylbutyrate, who underwent 24-hour blood and urine sampling on sodium phenylbutyrate and again on an equimolar dose of glycerol phenylbutyrate; all 15 completed the study.
cards.result: Daily ammonia exposure (24-hour AUC) was lower on glycerol phenylbutyrate and met predefined non-inferiority criteria (ratio of means 0.79; 95% CI 0.593 to 1.055; P=0.03 by Wilcoxon, 0.07 by t test). Six patients experienced mild adverse events on glycerol phenylbutyrate; there were no serious adverse events or significant laboratory changes. Liver tests and argininosuccinic acid levels in argininosuccinate lyase deficiency were unchanged or improved. Eleven of 15 patients reported 35 symptoms on day 1 (on sodium phenylbutyrate); 23 of these 35 symptoms improved or resolved on glycerol phenylbutyrate. Urinary phenylacetylglutamine output was more evenly distributed over 24 hours on glycerol phenylbutyrate. The topic file describes this study as a paediatric RCT; the record is an open-label switch-over study, and the card corrects that.
cards.watchOut: Fifteen children, no parallel control, symptom reports unblinded: the symptom-resolution figures (23 of 35) are exactly the kind of outcome open-label switching inflates, and the non-inferiority P value differs by test (0.03 Wilcoxon vs 0.07 t test) — both are printed.
cards.source: Smith W et al. Ammonia control in children ages 2 months through 5 years with urea cycle disorders: comparison of sodium phenylbutyrate and glycerol phenylbutyrate. J Pediatr. 2013. shelves.title: Sebelipase alfa for lysosomal acid lipase deficiency (ARISE)
shelves.question: In children and adults with lysosomal acid lipase deficiency, does sebelipase alfa vs placebo improve liver enzymes and lipid profile?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Alanine Transaminase/blood · Biopsy · Child · Child, Preschool · Cholesterol, HDL/blood · Cholesterol, LDL/blood · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Sterol Esterase/therapeutic use · Wolman Disease/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The single pivotal trial (ARISE, Burton 2015, 66 children and adults with lysosomal acid lipase deficiency) found 20 weeks of sebelipase alfa 1 mg/kg every other week normalised alanine aminotransferase in 31% of patients versus 7% on placebo (P=0.03), with mean ALT changes of −58 versus −7 U/L (P<0.001), and prespecified secondary endpoints — lipid levels and hepatic fat content — also improving (P<0.001 for all comparisons except triglycerides, P=0.04). Baseline disease burden was substantial (LDL cholesterol ≥190 mg/dL in 58%; cirrhosis in 31% of those biopsied). Adverse events were similar in number between groups and mostly mild and unrelated. One trial, 20 controlled weeks, surrogate endpoints (enzymes, lipids, liver fat — not fibrosis regression or clinical events): POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ARISE 2015: sebelipase alfa normalised ALT in 31% vs 7% on placebo at 20 weeks, with improved lipids and reduced hepatic fat
cards.summary: ARISE 2015: sebelipase alfa normalised ALT in 31% vs 7% on placebo at 20 weeks, with improved lipids and reduced hepatic fat
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study (20-week controlled phase, then open-label treatment for all)
cards.people: 66 patients (children and adults) with lysosomal acid lipase deficiency, randomised to intravenous sebelipase alfa 1 mg/kg every other week or placebo; 65 of 66 completed the double-blind portion. At baseline, 38 of 66 patients (58%) had LDL cholesterol of at least 190 mg/dL and 10 of 32 biopsied patients (31%) had cirrhosis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 20 weeks, the alanine aminotransferase level was normal in 11 of 36 patients (31%) in the sebelipase alfa group and 2 of 30 (7%) in the placebo group (P=0.03), with mean changes from baseline of −58 U per liter versus −7 U per liter (P<0.001). Prespecified key secondary endpoints improved: lipid levels and reduction in hepatic fat content (P<0.001 for all comparisons, except P=0.04 for triglycerides). The number of patients with adverse events was similar in the two groups; most events were mild and considered unrelated to treatment by the investigator.
cards.watchOut: ALT normalisation was achieved by fewer than a third of treated patients, and no endpoint here measures fibrosis, portal hypertension or survival — the cirrhosis present in a third of biopsied patients is the disease's danger, and 20 weeks of enzyme levels do not show it reversing.

shelves.title: Velmanase alfa for alpha-mannosidosis
shelves.question: In patients with alpha-mannosidosis, does velmanase alfa (enzyme replacement) vs placebo improve serum oligosaccharides, motor function, and immunoglobulin levels?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Child · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Enzyme Replacement Therapy · Europe · Female · Humans · Male · alpha-Mannosidosis/drug therapy
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE (biochemical) · MAYBE (weak evidence) (functional) — with a correction to the topic file, which states velmanase 'improved the trial's biochemical and functional measures'. The record (Borgwardt/Lund 2018, 25 patients randomised to weekly velmanase alfa 1 mg/kg or placebo for 52 weeks) supports only half of that: the biochemical co-primary endpoint moved strongly (serum oligosaccharide mean relative change −77.6% on velmanase versus −24.1% on placebo at week 52), but the functional co-primary endpoint did NOT — the 3-minute stair-climb test changed by −1.1% on velmanase at week 52, versus a placebo figure the record prints incompletely ('− %', 95% CI −13.4 to 6.5), i.e. no separation. After placebo patients switched to active treatment in the extension, their oligosaccharides also fell (−55.7% at last observation) while stair-climb changes remained small and imprecise in both groups (3.9% and 9.0%, intervals spanning zero). A 25-patient rare-disease trial with a strong biomarker result and a null functional co-primary earns a split stamp, and the incomplete placebo stair-climb figure is printed as it appears in the record rather than repaired.

cards.headline: Borgwardt 2018: velmanase alfa cut serum oligosaccharides by 77.6% vs 24.1% on placebo at 52 weeks — but the stair-climb co-primary endpoint did not improve (−1.1% on treatment)
cards.summary: Borgwardt 2018: velmanase alfa cut serum oligosaccharides by 77.6% vs 24.1% on placebo at 52 weeks — but the stair-climb co-primary endpoint did not improve (−1.1% on treatment)
cards.type: Phase III, multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (52 weeks) with extension phase (placebo patients switched to active treatment; compassionate-use/follow-on follow-up)
cards.people: 25 patients with alpha-mannosidosis, randomised to weekly velmanase alfa 1 mg/kg or placebo for 52 weeks; at study conclusion placebo patients switched to velmanase alfa, and 23 patients continued in compassionate-use/follow-on studies, evaluated at last observation. Co-primary endpoints were changes in serum oligosaccharide (S-oligo) and in the 3-minute stair-climb test (3MSCT). The abstract does not state mean age or the per-group numbers.
cards.result: Mean relative change in S-oligo in the velmanase arm was −77.6% (95% CI −81.6 to −72.8) at week 52 and −62.9% (−85.8 to −40.0) at last observation; in the placebo arm it was −24.1% (−40.3 to −3.6) at week 52 and −55.7% (−76.4 to −34.9) at last observation after switching to active treatment. Mean relative change in the 3-minute stair-climb test at week 52 was −1.1% (95% CI −9.0 to 7.6) on velmanase and, as printed in the record, '− %' (95% CI −13.4 to 6.5) on placebo — the point estimate is missing from the record's abstract and is not reconstructed here. At last observation, stair-climb changes were 3.9% (−5.5 to 13.2) in the original velmanase arm and 9.0% (−10.3 to 28.3) in the switched group. Similar improvement patterns were reported for secondary parameters. A post hoc analysis found no baseline factor predictive of treatment response besides age. The authors conclude the findings support the utility of velmanase alfa, with more evident benefit over time and when treatment starts in the paediatric age.
cards.watchOut: The authors' 'support the utility' conclusion runs ahead of their own functional co-primary endpoint, which showed no improvement at 52 weeks; the demonstrated effect is biochemical. With 25 patients, every interval here is wide, and the extension phase is uncontrolled — post-switch falls in oligosaccharides are consistent with treatment effect but cannot prove functional benefit.
cards.source: Borgwardt L et al. Efficacy and safety of Velmanase alfa in the treatment of patients with alpha-mannosidosis: results from the core and extension phase analysis of a phase III multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial. shelves.title: Nusinersen for spinal muscular atrophy (ENDEAR & CHERISH)
shelves.question: In infants with SMA type 1 (ENDEAR) and children with later-onset SMA (CHERISH), does intrathecal nusinersen vs sham control improve motor milestones and motor function?
shelves.mesh: Age of Onset · Disease-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Infant · Injections, Spinal · Male · Motor Skills · Oligonucleotides/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Oligonucleotides, Antisense/adverse effects,therapeutic use · RNA, Messenger/drug effects,metabolism · Respiration, Artificial · Spinal Muscular Atrophies of Childhood/drug therapy,genetics,mortality,physiopathology · Survival Analysis · Survival of Motor Neuron 2 Protein/genetics,metabolism
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: ENDEAR's co-primary endpoint is event-free survival — time to death or permanent assisted ventilation — and its overall-survival result is part of the claim set; the topic file ruled this shelf Tier C No on the grounds that the primary claims are motor outcomes, but the survival endpoint is a prespecified co-primary, so the Tier C flag is applied here and the discrepancy is disclosed). Two randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled phase 3 trials agree. In ENDEAR (infantile-onset SMA), a motor-milestone response occurred in 51% of nusinersen infants versus 0% on sham in the final analysis, event-free survival favoured nusinersen (hazard ratio 0.53 relative for death or permanent assisted ventilation), and overall survival favoured nusinersen (hazard ratio 0.37 relative for death). In CHERISH (later-onset SMA, 126 children), the HFMSE motor score rose by 4.0 points on nusinersen while falling 1.9 points on sham (least-squares mean difference 5.9 points, 95% CI 3.7 to 8.1), and 57% versus 26% gained at least 3 HFMSE points. Both trials were stopped early after positive prespecified interim analyses. Adverse-event incidence and severity were similar to sham in both trials.

cards.headline: ENDEAR (Finkel 2017): nusinersen produced motor-milestone responses in 51% vs 0% on sham, with better event-free survival (HR 0.53 relative) and overall survival (HR 0.37 relative) in infantile-onset SMA
cards.summary: ENDEAR (Finkel 2017): nusinersen produced motor-milestone responses in 51% vs 0% on sham, with better event-free survival (HR 0.53 relative) and overall survival (HR 0.37 relative) in infantile-onset SMA
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled phase 3 trial — stopped early after a positive prespecified interim analysis
cards.people: Infants with infantile-onset spinal muscular atrophy. The abstract reports the interim analysis population (51 nusinersen vs 27 control) and the final analysis population for the motor-milestone endpoint (73 nusinersen vs 37 control); it does not state a single total randomised number, mean age, or sex mix.
cards.result: In the interim analysis, a motor-milestone response (per the Hammersmith Infant Neurological Examination) occurred in 21 of 51 infants (41%) on nusinersen versus 0 of 27 (0%) on sham (P<0.001), prompting early termination. In the final analysis, 37 of 73 infants (51%) on nusinersen versus 0 of 37 (0%) on sham had a motor-milestone response. The likelihood of event-free survival was higher with nusinersen (hazard ratio for death or the use of permanent assisted ventilation 0.53 — a relative measure; P=0.005), and the likelihood of overall survival was higher (hazard ratio for death 0.37 — a relative measure; P=0.004). Infants with a shorter disease duration at screening were more likely to benefit. The incidence and severity of adverse events were similar in the two groups. Absolute death counts are not printed in the abstract, so none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: Early termination after a positive interim analysis can exaggerate effect sizes, and the abstract does not print absolute numbers of deaths or of infants receiving permanent ventilation — the survival claims rest on the hazard ratios as printed. The sham procedure involved intrathecal-style sham administration, so the comparison is against a procedural control, not no treatment.

shelves.title: Patisiran for hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis with polyneuropathy (APOLLO)
shelves.question: In adults with hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis and polyneuropathy, does patisiran vs placebo improve neuropathy impairment scores?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Amyloid Neuropathies, Familial/blood,complications,therapy · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Edema/chemically induced · Female · Gait Disorders, Neurologic/etiology · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous/adverse effects · Least-Squares Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Polyneuropathies/etiology,therapy · Prealbumin/analysis,genetics · Quality of Life · RNA, Small Interfering/adverse effects,therapeutic use · RNAi Therapeutics · Severity of Illness Index · Walk Test
shelves.balance: LIKELY: One large randomised, double-blind phase 3 trial (APOLLO, 225 patients) found patisiran not merely slowed but on average reversed neuropathy impairment over 18 months: the modified Neuropathy Impairment Score+7 changed by −6.0 points on patisiran versus +28.0 points on placebo (least-squares mean difference −34.0 points; P<0.001), with quality of life moving the same way (Norfolk QOL-DN difference −21.1 points; P<0.001), gait speed better by 0.31 m per second, and modified BMI better preserved. A single trial, but large for this rare disease, double-blind, and consistent across every prespecified clinical measure. Mild or moderate infusion-related reactions occurred in about 20% on patisiran versus 10% on placebo. The ATTR cardiomyopathy questions (tafamidis, acoramidis, vutrisiran) are homed on Shelves #556/#1170 and are not re-opened here.

cards.headline: APOLLO (Adams 2018): patisiran improved mNIS+7 by 34.0 points vs placebo at 18 months in hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis with polyneuropathy (225 patients)
cards.summary: APOLLO (Adams 2018): patisiran improved mNIS+7 by 34.0 points vs placebo at 18 months in hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis with polyneuropathy (225 patients)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial
cards.people: 225 patients with hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis with polyneuropathy, randomly assigned 2:1 to intravenous patisiran 0.3 mg/kg (148) or placebo (77) once every 3 weeks. Mean (±SD) baseline mNIS+7 was 80.9±41.5 (patisiran) and 74.6±37.0 (placebo). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 18 months, the least-squares mean (±SE) change in mNIS+7 (range 0–304, higher = more impairment) was −6.0±1.7 on patisiran versus +28.0±2.6 on placebo (difference −34.0 points; P<0.001). The Norfolk QOL-DN score (range −4 to 136, higher = worse) changed by −6.7±1.8 versus +14.4±2.7 (difference −21.1 points; P<0.001). Gait speed changed by +0.08±0.02 m/s versus −0.24±0.04 m/s (difference 0.31 m/s; P<0.001), and modified BMI by −3.7±9.6 versus −119.4±14.5 (difference 115.7; P<0.001). Approximately 20% of patisiran patients and 10% of placebo patients had mild or moderate infusion-related reactions; the overall incidence and types of adverse events were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: A single trial in a rare disease, and the endpoints are impairment and quality-of-life scores rather than survival or disability milestones; the placebo group's rapid progression (+28 points in 18 months) is what makes the between-group gap so large. Mortality is not an endpoint of this trial and no survival claim is made on this shelf.

shelves.title: Vosoritide for achondroplasia
shelves.question: In children with achondroplasia, does daily subcutaneous vosoritide vs placebo increase annualised growth velocity?
shelves.mesh: Absorptiometry, Photon · Achondroplasia/blood,drug therapy · Adolescent · Biomarkers/blood · Body Height · Bone Density · Child · Child, Preschool · Collagen Type X/blood · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Injection Site Reaction · Injections, Subcutaneous · Male · Natriuretic Peptide, C-Type/analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Osteogenesis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (121 children aged 5 to under 18 years) found daily subcutaneous vosoritide increased annualised growth velocity by an adjusted mean of 1.57 cm/year versus placebo over 52 weeks (95% CI 1.22 to 1.93; p<0.0001). Adverse events occurred in 98% of both groups, none of the serious adverse events were judged treatment-related, and no deaths occurred. The stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because growth velocity over one year is a surrogate: the trialists themselves state it is not known whether final adult height will be increased, or what the harms of long-term therapy might be, and there is a single trial.

cards.headline: Savarirayan 2020: vosoritide increased annualised growth velocity by 1.57 cm/year vs placebo over 52 weeks in 121 children with achondroplasia
cards.summary: Savarirayan 2020: vosoritide increased annualised growth velocity by 1.57 cm/year vs placebo over 52 weeks in 121 children with achondroplasia
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre phase 3 trial (24 sites, seven countries)
cards.people: 121 children with a clinical diagnosis of achondroplasia, ambulatory, aged 5 to less than 18 years at enrolment, who had participated for 6 months in a baseline growth study; 60 were assigned to vosoritide 15.0 µg/kg and 61 to placebo, given as daily subcutaneous injections at home by trained caregivers for 52 weeks; 119 completed the trial. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix (randomisation was stratified by sex and Tanner stage).
cards.result: The adjusted mean difference in annualised growth velocity between the vosoritide and placebo groups at 52 weeks was 1.57 cm/year in favour of vosoritide (95% CI 1.22 to 1.93; two-sided p<0.0001). A total of 119 patients had at least one adverse event (59 [98%] vosoritide; 60 [98%] placebo). None of the serious adverse events were considered treatment-related and no deaths occurred.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is one year of growth velocity, not adult height: the authors state explicitly that whether final adult height will be increased, and the harms of long-term therapy, are unknown. Daily injections in children for an uncertain final-height payoff is the family's real decision, and this record does not settle it.

shelves.title: Luspatercept for β-thalassaemia (BELIEVE & BEYOND)
shelves.question: In adults with transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia (BELIEVE) and non-transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia (BEYOND), does luspatercept vs placebo reduce transfusion burden / raise haemoglobin?
shelves.mesh: Activin Receptors, Type II/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Erythrocyte Transfusion/statistics & numerical data · Female · Ferritins/blood · Hematinics/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Humans · Immunoglobulin Fc Fragments/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Intention to Treat Analysis · Least-Squares Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Odds Ratio · Recombinant Fusion Proteins/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Splenectomy · Young Adult · beta-Thalassemia/drug therapy,genetics,surgery,therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in the two β-thalassaemia populations agree. In transfusion-dependent disease (BELIEVE, 336 adults), 21.4% on luspatercept versus 4.5% on placebo achieved the primary endpoint of at least a 33% reduction in transfusion burden plus at least 2 fewer red-cell units during weeks 13–24 (P<0.001), and 70.5% versus 29.5% achieved a ≥33% reduction during any 12-week interval. In non-transfusion-dependent disease (BEYOND, phase 2, 145 adults), 77% on luspatercept versus 0% on placebo achieved a ≥1.0 g/dL rise in mean haemoglobin over weeks 13–24 without transfusions (p<0.0001). The price is transient bone pain, arthralgia, dizziness, hypertension and hyperuricemia, each more common on luspatercept. Luspatercept in myelodysplastic syndromes is Shelf #674 — a different disease, not re-carded here.

cards.headline: BELIEVE (Cappellini 2020): luspatercept achieved ≥33% transfusion-burden reduction in 21.4% vs 4.5% on placebo in transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia (336 adults)
cards.summary: BELIEVE (Cappellini 2020): luspatercept achieved ≥33% transfusion-burden reduction in 21.4% vs 4.5% on placebo in transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia (336 adults)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial
cards.people: 336 adults with transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia, assigned 2:1 to best supportive care plus luspatercept 1.00–1.25 mg/kg (224) or placebo (112) for at least 48 weeks; median treatment duration was approximately 64 weeks in both groups. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — a reduction in transfusion burden of at least 33% from baseline during weeks 13–24 plus a reduction of at least 2 red-cell units over that interval — was achieved by 21.4% on luspatercept versus 4.5% on placebo (P<0.001). During any 12-week interval, a ≥33% reduction occurred in 70.5% versus 29.5%, and a ≥50% reduction in 40.2% versus 6.3%. The least-squares mean difference in serum ferritin at week 48 was −348 µg per liter (95% CI −517 to −179) in favour of luspatercept. Adverse events of transient bone pain, arthralgia, dizziness, hypertension, and hyperuricemia were more common with luspatercept than placebo; few adverse events led to discontinuation.

cards.summary: BEYOND (Taher 2022): luspatercept raised haemoglobin by ≥1.0 g/dL in 77% vs 0% on placebo in non-transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia (145 adults, phase 2)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre phase 2 trial (12 centres, six countries)
cards.people: 145 adults aged 18 years or older with non-transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia (including haemoglobin E/β-thalassaemia) and baseline haemoglobin ≤10.0 g/dL, randomly assigned 2:1 to luspatercept (96) or placebo (49) subcutaneously every 3 weeks for 48 weeks; 82 (57%) were female and 63 (43%) male. shelves.title: Emicizumab prophylaxis for haemophilia A (HAVEN 1 & HAVEN 3)
shelves.question: In people with haemophilia A with inhibitors (HAVEN 1) and without inhibitors (HAVEN 3), does subcutaneous emicizumab prophylaxis vs no prophylaxis / prior factor prophylaxis reduce treated bleeding episodes?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Bispecific/adverse effects,pharmacokinetics,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects,pharmacokinetics,therapeutic use · Blood Coagulation Factors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Child · Drug Therapy, Combination · Factor VIII/immunology,therapeutic use · Factor VIIa/therapeutic use · Hemophilia A/drug therapy,immunology · Hemorrhage/prevention & control · Humans · Injections, Subcutaneous · Isoantibodies/blood · Male · Middle Aged · Recombinant Proteins/therapeutic use · Thrombosis/chemically induced · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised phase 3 trials in the two haemophilia A populations show very large reductions in treated bleeding. In patients with factor VIII inhibitors previously on episodic bypassing-agent treatment (HAVEN 1), the annualised bleeding rate was 2.9 events on emicizumab prophylaxis versus 23.3 on no prophylaxis — 87% lower (relative) — with 63% versus 6% having zero bleeds. In patients without inhibitors previously on episodic factor VIII (HAVEN 3), annualised treated bleeding rates were 1.5 (weekly) and 1.3 (every 2 weeks) versus 38.2 on no prophylaxis — 96–97% lower (relative) — and an intraindividual comparison showed a 68% lower rate than previous factor VIII prophylaxis. The safety flag is real: in HAVEN 1, thrombotic microangiopathy and thrombosis were each reported in 2 participants who had received multiple infusions of activated prothrombin complex concentrate for breakthrough bleeding; HAVEN 3 reported no thrombotic or microangiopathy events. Injection-site reactions were the most frequent adverse event in both trials (15% in HAVEN 1).

cards.headline: HAVEN 1 (Oldenburg 2017): emicizumab cut the annualised bleeding rate by 87% relative vs no prophylaxis in haemophilia A with inhibitors (2.9 vs 23.3 events)
cards.summary: HAVEN 1 (Oldenburg 2017): emicizumab cut the annualised bleeding rate by 87% relative vs no prophylaxis in haemophilia A with inhibitors (2.9 vs 23.3 events)
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, randomised trial (open-label; randomised comparison is prophylaxis vs no prophylaxis in the episodic-treatment stratum)
cards.people: 109 male participants aged 12 years or older with haemophilia A with factor VIII inhibitors. Those previously treated episodically with bypassing agents were randomised 2:1 to emicizumab prophylaxis (group A, 35) or no prophylaxis (group B, 18); participants previously on prophylactic bypassing agents received emicizumab in a non-randomised group C. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The annualised bleeding rate was 2.9 events (95% CI 1.7 to 5.0) in group A versus 23.3 events (95% CI 12.3 to 43.9) in group B — a difference of 87% in favour of emicizumab prophylaxis (a relative measure; P<0.001). Twenty-two participants in group A (63%) had zero bleeding events versus 1 (6%) in group B. In group C's intraindividual comparison, emicizumab prophylaxis gave a bleeding rate 79% lower (relative) than previous bypassing-agent prophylaxis (P<0.001). Overall, 198 adverse events were reported in 103 participants receiving emicizumab; the most frequent were injection-site reactions (15% of participants). Thrombotic microangiopathy and thrombosis were reported in 2 participants each (in the primary analysis) who had received multiple infusions of activated prothrombin complex concentrate for breakthrough bleeding. No antidrug antibodies were detected.
cards.watchOut: The randomised no-prophylaxis comparison rests on 53 participants (35 vs 18); the larger group C comparison is intraindividual, not randomised. The thrombotic microangiopathy/thrombosis signal clustered in patients receiving repeated activated prothrombin complex concentrate for breakthrough bleeds — the interaction, not emicizumab alone in this record, is the caution.

cards.headline: HAVEN 3 (Mahlangu 2018): emicizumab cut annualised treated bleeding by 96–97% relative vs no prophylaxis in haemophilia A without inhibitors, and by 68% vs prior factor VIII prophylaxis
cards.summary: HAVEN 3 (Mahlangu 2018): emicizumab cut annualised treated bleeding by 96–97% relative vs no prophylaxis in haemophilia A without inhibitors, and by 68% vs prior factor VIII prophylaxis
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, randomised trial (open-label)
cards.people: 152 participants aged 12 years or older with haemophilia A without factor VIII inhibitors. Those previously on episodic factor VIII were randomised 2:2:1 to emicizumab 1.5 mg/kg weekly (group A), 3.0 mg/kg every 2 weeks (group B), or no prophylaxis (group C); those previously on factor VIII prophylaxis received weekly emicizumab (group D). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The annualised bleeding rate was 1.5 events (95% CI 0.9 to 2.5) in group A and 1.3 events (95% CI 0.8 to 2.3) in group B versus 38.2 events (95% CI 22.9 to 63.8) in group C — 96% lower in group A and 97% lower in group B (relative measures; P<0.001 for both). In group A, 56%, and in group B, 60%, had no treated bleeding events, versus none in group C. In the intraindividual comparison (48 participants), emicizumab prophylaxis gave an annualised bleeding rate 68% lower (relative) than previous factor VIII prophylaxis (P<0.001). The most frequent adverse event was low-grade injection-site reaction. There were no thrombotic or thrombotic microangiopathy events, no antidrug antibodies, and no new factor VIII inhibitors.
cards.watchOut: Open-label trials with bleeding diaries as the outcome source; the no-prophylaxis control rates (38.2 events/year) reflect an episodically treated population, so the 96–97% relative reductions should be read beside the absolute rates printed on the card, and the comparison against modern factor prophylaxis is the intraindividual 68% figure, not a randomised head-to-head.

shelves.title: Evolocumab for paediatric heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (HAUSER-RCT)
shelves.question: In children and adolescents with heterozygous FH on standard therapy, does evolocumab vs placebo lower LDL cholesterol?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Anticholesteremic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Child · Cholesterol, LDL/blood · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Heterozygote · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Hyperlipoproteinemia Type II/drug therapy,genetics · Lipids/blood · Male · PCSK9 Inhibitors · Treatment Outcome · Proprotein Convertase 9
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (HAUSER-RCT, 157 patients aged 10–17 years with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia on stable lipid-lowering therapy) found monthly evolocumab 420 mg lowered LDL cholesterol by 44.5% at 24 weeks versus 6.2% on placebo (difference −38.3 percentage points; P<0.001), an absolute difference of −68.6 mg per deciliter (−1.8 mmol per liter). Adverse events during treatment were similar between groups. The stamp is POSSIBLE because this is a single trial and LDL cholesterol is a surrogate endpoint — no cardiovascular-event outcome is measured or claimed in children, and no pregnancy-related use is implied (participants were already on standard therapy, which remains the base treatment).

cards.headline: HAUSER-RCT (Santos 2020): evolocumab lowered LDL cholesterol by 38.3 percentage points more than placebo at 24 weeks in paediatric heterozygous FH (157 patients aged 10–17)
cards.summary: HAUSER-RCT (Santos 2020): evolocumab lowered LDL cholesterol by 38.3 percentage points more than placebo at 24 weeks in paediatric heterozygous FH (157 patients aged 10–17)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (24 weeks)
cards.people: 157 patients aged 10 to 17 years with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, on stable lipid-lowering treatment for at least 4 weeks, with LDL cholesterol ≥130 mg per deciliter (3.4 mmol per liter) and triglycerides ≤400 mg per deciliter, randomised 2:1 to monthly subcutaneous evolocumab 420 mg (104) or placebo (53) for 24 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At week 24, the mean percent change in LDL cholesterol was −44.5% on evolocumab versus −6.2% on placebo (difference −38.3 percentage points; P<0.001). The absolute change was −77.5 mg per deciliter (−2.0 mmol per liter) versus −9.0 mg per deciliter (−0.2 mmol per liter) (difference −68.6 mg per deciliter [−1.8 mmol per liter]; P<0.001). All secondary lipid variables were significantly better with evolocumab. The incidence of adverse events during the treatment period was similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: A 24-week surrogate-endpoint trial: the size of LDL lowering matches the adult evolocumab programme, but neither events nor long-term paediatric safety are in this record, and the drug was added to standard therapy rather than tested as a replacement for it.

shelves.title: Everolimus for tuberous sclerosis complex tumours (EXIST-1 & EXIST-2)
shelves.question: In patients with tuberous sclerosis complex, does everolimus vs placebo shrink subependymal giant cell astrocytomas (EXIST-1) and renal angiomyolipomas (EXIST-2)?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Astrocytoma/complications,drug therapy · Child · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Everolimus · Female · Fever/chemically induced · Humans · Infant · Male · Oral Ulcer/chemically induced · Seizures/chemically induced · Sirolimus/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Stomatitis/chemically induced · Treatment Outcome · Tuberous Sclerosis/complications · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials of everolimus in tuberous sclerosis complex both met their primary tumour-response endpoints. In EXIST-1 (117 patients with subependymal giant cell astrocytoma), 35% on everolimus versus 0% on placebo achieved at least a 50% reduction in target SEGA volume (difference 35 percentage points, 95% CI 15 to 52; p<0.0001). In EXIST-2 (118 adults with renal angiomyolipoma), the response rate (≥50% volume reduction) was 42% on everolimus versus 0% on placebo. The price is mTOR-inhibitor toxicity — mouth ulceration and stomatitis prominent in EXIST-1 (32% and 31%) — with adverse events mostly grade 1–2 and no discontinuations for adverse events in EXIST-1. Endpoints are tumour-volume responses, not survival or surgery avoidance, though those are the clinical reasons the responses matter.

cards.headline: EXIST-1 (Franz 2013): everolimus produced ≥50% SEGA volume reduction in 35% vs 0% on placebo in tuberous sclerosis complex (117 patients)
cards.summary: EXIST-1 (Franz 2013): everolimus produced ≥50% SEGA volume reduction in 35% vs 0% on placebo in tuberous sclerosis complex (117 patients)
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial
cards.people: 117 patients aged 0–65 years with definite tuberous sclerosis complex and at least one SEGA lesion ≥1 cm with serial growth, a new lesion ≥1 cm, or new/worsening hydrocephalus, randomised 2:1 to oral everolimus 4.5 mg/m² per day titrated to trough concentrations of 5–15 ng/mL (78) or placebo (39), in 24 centres across ten countries. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Twenty-seven (35%) patients on everolimus had at least a 50% reduction in the volume of subependymal giant cell astrocytomas versus none on placebo (difference 35 percentage points, 95% CI 15 to 52; one-sided exact Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test, p<0.0001). Adverse events were mostly grade 1 or 2 and no patients discontinued treatment because of adverse events. The most common adverse events were mouth ulceration (25 [32%] everolimus vs 2 [5%] placebo), stomatitis (24 [31%] vs 8 [21%]), convulsion (18 [23%] vs 10 [26%]), and pyrexia (17 [22%] vs 6 [15%]).
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is radiological volume response over the trial's treatment period; durability after stopping and the effect on hydrocephalus or surgery rates are not the primary measured outcomes in this abstract.

cards.headline: EXIST-2 (Bissler 2013): everolimus produced a renal angiomyolipoma response in 42% vs 0% on placebo in tuberous sclerosis complex (118 adults)
cards.summary: EXIST-2 (Bissler 2013): everolimus produced a renal angiomyolipoma response in 42% vs 0% on placebo in tuberous sclerosis complex (118 adults)
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial
cards.people: 118 patients aged 18 years or older (median age 31.0 years, IQR 18.0–61.0) with tuberous sclerosis complex or sporadic lymphangioleiomyomatosis and at least one renal angiomyolipoma ≥3 cm in longest diameter, randomised 2:1 to oral everolimus 10 mg/day (79) or placebo (39), at 24 centres in 11 countries. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: The angiomyolipoma response rate — confirmed reduction of at least 50% in the total volume of target angiomyolipomas relative to baseline — was 42% (33 of 79; 95% CI 31 to 53) on everolimus versus 0% (0 of 39; 95% CI 0 to 9) on placebo (response-rate difference 42 percentage points, 95% CI 24 to 58; one-sided Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test p<0.0001). The most common adverse events were stomatitis (48% [38 of 79] everolimus vs 8% [3 of 39] placebo), nasopharyngitis (24% [19 of 79] vs 31% [12 of 39]), and acne-like skin lesions (22% [17 of 79] vs 5% [2 of 39]). shelves.title: Losartan vs atenolol / control for aortic dilatation in Marfan syndrome
shelves.question: In children, young adults, and adults with Marfan syndrome, does losartan vs atenolol (or control) slow aortic-root dilatation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Angiotensin II Type 1 Receptor Blockers/administration & dosage · Aorta, Thoracic/pathology · Aortic Diseases/complications,drug therapy,pathology · Dilatation, Pathologic/complications,drug therapy,pathology · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Humans · Losartan/administration & dosage · Magnetic Resonance Angiography · Male · Marfan Syndrome/complications,pathology · Reoperation · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised trials answer two different halves of the question, and they do not add up to superiority over standard care. In adults (COMPARE, 233 participants, open-label with blinded assessment), losartan versus no additional treatment slowed aortic-root dilatation over about 3 years (0.77±1.36 mm vs 1.35±1.55 mm; P=0.014), and slowed aortic-arch dilatation after prior root replacement (0.50±1.26 vs 1.01±1.31 mm; P=0.033), but dilatation beyond the root was not significantly reduced and no difference in the clinical composite (aortic dissection, elective aortic surgery, cardiovascular death) could be demonstrated. In children and young adults (Pediatric Heart Network, 608 participants aged 6 months–25 years), losartan was NOT superior to atenolol: aortic-root z-score change was −0.107±0.013 versus −0.139±0.013 SD units per year (P=0.08), with no difference in surgery, dissection or death over 3 years. The endpoint throughout is a dilatation-rate surrogate; no trial shows losartan reduces dissection or death, and no event claim is made. Losartan is an ARB: nothing on this shelf supports its initiation in pregnancy, where ARBs are fetotoxic.

cards.headline: COMPARE (Groenink 2013): losartan slowed aortic-root dilatation vs no additional treatment in adults with Marfan syndrome (0.77 vs 1.35 mm over ~3 years), with no clinical-endpoint difference
cards.summary: COMPARE (Groenink 2013): losartan slowed aortic-root dilatation vs no additional treatment in adults with Marfan syndrome (0.77 vs 1.35 mm over ~3 years), with no clinical-endpoint difference
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled trial with blinded endpoint assessment
cards.people: 233 adults with Marfan syndrome (operated and unoperated; 47% female), randomised to losartan (116) or no additional treatment (117) in a multicentre trial; follow-up was 3.1±0.4 years. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Aortic-root dilatation rate was significantly lower on losartan than in controls (0.77±1.36 mm vs 1.35±1.55 mm over the follow-up period; P=0.014). Dilatation rate in the trajectory beyond the aortic root was not significantly reduced. In patients with prior aortic-root replacement, aortic-arch dilatation rate was lower on losartan (0.50±1.26 vs 1.01±1.31 mm; P=0.033). No significant differences in separate clinical endpoints or in the composite endpoint (aortic dissection, elective aortic surgery, cardiovascular death) between the groups could be demonstrated.
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment (only the assessments were blinded) and a no-additional-treatment comparator: the trial shows losartan beats nothing on an imaging surrogate in adults; it does not compare losartan with the beta-blocker standard, and its clinical composite was null.

cards.summary: Pediatric Heart Network (Lacro 2014): losartan was not superior to atenolol for aortic-root dilatation in 608 children and young adults with Marfan syndrome over 3 years
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (21 centres) — active-comparator design, no placebo or untreated arm
cards.people: 608 participants aged 6 months to 25 years (mean age 11.5±6.5 years in the atenolol group and 11.0±6.2 years in the losartan group) with Marfan syndrome and an aortic-root z score above 3.0, enrolled at 21 clinical centres from January 2007 to February 2011. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: The baseline-adjusted rate of change in the mean aortic-root z score did not differ significantly between losartan and atenolol (−0.107±0.013 vs −0.139±0.013 standard-deviation units per year, respectively; P=0.08). Both slopes were significantly less than zero, indicating the aortic-root diameter decreased relative to body-surface area on either treatment. The 3-year rates of aortic-root surgery, aortic dissection, death, and a composite of these events did not differ significantly between the groups.
cards.watchOut: With no untreated arm, the trial cannot show losartan works at all in this age group — only that it did not beat atenolol; the numerically smaller z-score decline was actually in the atenolol group. Importing COMPARE's adult versus-nothing result into children would be exactly the cross-population borrowing this library forbids.

shelves.title: Trofinetide for Rett syndrome (LAVENDER)
shelves.question: In girls and young women with Rett syndrome, does trofinetide vs placebo improve co-primary Rett Syndrome Behaviour Questionnaire and clinician global-impression scores?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Rett Syndrome/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Glutamates · Double-Blind Method
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised, double-blind phase 3 trial (LAVENDER, 187 females with Rett syndrome, 12 weeks) met both co-primary endpoints: the Rett Syndrome Behaviour Questionnaire changed by a least-squares mean of −4.9 on trofinetide versus −1.7 on placebo (P=0.0175; Cohen's d 0.37), and Clinical Global Impression-Improvement was 3.5 versus 3.8 (P=0.0030; d 0.47), with the key secondary communication score also favouring trofinetide (−0.1 vs −1.1; P=0.0064). Effect sizes are small-to-moderate, the endpoints are rating scales over 12 weeks, and the price is diarrhoea in 80.6% on trofinetide versus 19.1% on placebo (mostly mild to moderate). A single trial with scale endpoints earns POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: LAVENDER (Neul 2023): trofinetide met both co-primary endpoints vs placebo at 12 weeks in 187 females with Rett syndrome; diarrhoea in 80.6% vs 19.1%
cards.summary: LAVENDER (Neul 2023): trofinetide met both co-primary endpoints vs placebo at 12 weeks in 187 females with Rett syndrome; diarrhoea in 80.6% vs 19.1%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial
cards.people: 187 females with Rett syndrome, randomised to twice-daily oral trofinetide (93) or placebo (94) for 12 weeks. The abstract does not state the age range or mean age.
cards.result: For the co-primary endpoints, the least-squares mean change from baseline to week 12 in the Rett Syndrome Behaviour Questionnaire was −4.9 on trofinetide versus −1.7 on placebo (P=0.0175; Cohen's d effect size 0.37), and least-squares mean Clinical Global Impression-Improvement at week 12 was 3.5 versus 3.8 (P=0.0030; effect size 0.47). For the key secondary endpoint, the least-squares mean change in the Communication and Symbolic Behavior Scales Developmental Profile Infant-Toddler Checklist Social Composite score was −0.1 versus −1.1 (P=0.0064; effect size 0.43). Common treatment-emergent adverse events included diarrhoea (80.6% trofinetide vs 19.1% placebo), mostly mild to moderate in severity.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks, caregiver- and clinician-rated scales, and effect sizes under half a standard deviation: the trial shows measurable symptomatic benefit, not disease modification, and the very high diarrhoea rate (80.6%) is part of the real-world bargain. The record's MeSH list is short and is reproduced as printed.
cards.source: Neul JL et al. Trofinetide for the treatment of Rett syndrome: a randomized phase 3 study. Nat Med. 2023. PMID: 37291210. shelves.title: Burosumab vs conventional therapy for X-linked hypophosphataemia in children
shelves.question: In children with X-linked hypophosphataemia, does burosumab vs continued conventional therapy (phosphate/active vitamin D) improve rickets severity and growth?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Body Height · Child · Child Development · Child, Preschool · Familial Hypophosphatemic Rickets/diagnosis,drug therapy · Female · Fibroblast Growth Factor-23 · Humans · Immunologic Factors/therapeutic use · Infant · Male · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised, active-controlled, open-label phase 3 trial (61 children aged 1–12 years with X-linked hypophosphataemia already on conventional therapy) found switching to burosumab improved rickets severity at week 40 substantially more than continuing conventional therapy: the Radiographic Global Impression of Change global score rose by a least-squares mean of +1.9 versus +0.8 (difference 1.1, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.5; p<0.0001), with the trial also reporting greater improvements in growth and biochemistries. Treatment-related adverse events were more frequent on burosumab (59% vs 22%); three serious adverse events occurred in each group, all judged unrelated to treatment and all resolved. The stamp is POSSIBLE: a single, small, open-label trial with a radiographic primary endpoint, albeit against the active standard of care rather than placebo.

cards.headline: Imel 2019: burosumab improved rickets severity (RGI-C +1.9 vs +0.8) more than continued conventional therapy in 61 children with X-linked hypophosphataemia
cards.summary: Imel 2019: burosumab improved rickets severity (RGI-C +1.9 vs +0.8) more than continued conventional therapy in 61 children with X-linked hypophosphataemia
cards.type: Randomised, active-controlled, open-label phase 3 trial
cards.people: 61 children aged 1–12 years with X-linked hypophosphataemia, a Thacher rickets severity score of at least 2.0, fasting serum phosphorus below 0.97 mmol/L (3.0 mg/dL), a confirmed PHEX mutation (or variant of unknown significance with appropriate family inheritance), and prior conventional therapy (at least 6 months if under 3 years, at least 12 months if older); 29 were assigned to subcutaneous burosumab starting at 0.8 mg/kg every 2 weeks (16 girls, 13 boys) and 32 to continued conventional therapy — oral phosphate and active vitamin D prescribed by investigators (18 girls, 14 boys) — for 64 weeks, at 16 clinical sites.
cards.result: For the primary endpoint at week 40, the burosumab group had significantly greater improvement in the Radiographic Global Impression of Change global score than the conventional-therapy group (least-squares mean +1.9 [SE 0.1] vs +0.8 [0.1]; difference 1.1, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.5; p<0.0001). Treatment-emergent adverse events considered possibly, probably, or definitely related to treatment occurred more frequently with burosumab (17 [59%] of 29 vs 7 [22%] of 32). Three serious adverse events occurred in each group, all considered unrelated to treatment and all resolved. The authors report significantly greater improvements in rickets severity, growth, and biochemistries with burosumab.
cards.watchOut: Open-label: families and investigators knew who was switched to the new antibody, which can colour adherence and reporting even with radiographic endpoints; the sample is 61 children, and the comparator is investigator-prescribed conventional therapy, whose intensity varies in practice. This trial is in children already established on conventional therapy — it does not answer treatment-naïve questions.
