shelves.title: Vamorolone for Duchenne muscular dystrophy
shelves.question: In boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, is vamorolone non-inferior in efficacy to prednisone with a better bone-safety profile?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones · Adrenal Insufficiency/chemically induced,drug therapy · Adrenocorticotropic Hormone/therapeutic use · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/adverse effects · Biomarkers · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Hydrocortisone/therapeutic use · Male · Muscular Dystrophy, Duchenne/drug therapy · Prednisone/therapeutic use · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — with a correction to the topic file on the card's face: the topic file frames the question as vamorolone's non-inferiority to prednisone, but VBP15-004 was not a non-inferiority trial against prednisone. Its primary endpoint was vamorolone 6 mg/kg/day versus PLACEBO on time-to-stand velocity at 24 weeks, which it met (least-squares mean velocity 0.05 vs −0.01 m/s; 95% CI for the difference 0.02 to 0.10; P=.002), along with its first four sequential secondary endpoints. Prednisone was a parallel control arm, not a non-inferiority comparator. The bone-safety contrast was supportive: height percentile declined on prednisone (−1.88) but not on vamorolone 6 mg/kg (+3.86; P=.02), and bone turnover markers declined with prednisone but not vamorolone — but boys with DMD already had low ACTH-stimulated cortisol and a high incidence of adrenal insufficiency at baseline, and all three treatment groups led to increased adrenal insufficiency. One 24-week trial earns POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: VBP15-004 (Guglieri 2022): vamorolone 6 mg/kg beat placebo on time-to-stand velocity at 24 weeks in steroid-naïve boys with DMD; prednisone was a control arm, not a non-inferiority comparator
cards.summary: VBP15-004 (Guglieri 2022): vamorolone 6 mg/kg beat placebo on time-to-stand velocity at 24 weeks in steroid-naïve boys with DMD; prednisone was a control arm, not a non-inferiority comparator
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo- and prednisone-controlled 24-week trial (33 centres, 11 countries)
cards.people: 133 boys aged 4 to younger than 7 years with genetically confirmed Duchenne muscular dystrophy, not previously treated with corticosteroids, at 33 referral centres in 11 countries; 121 were randomly assigned to placebo, prednisone 0.75 mg/kg/day, vamorolone 2 mg/kg/day, or vamorolone 6 mg/kg/day, and 114 completed the 24-week treatment period. Mean (SD) age was 5.4 (0.9) years.
cards.result: The trial met its primary endpoint: change from baseline to week 24 in time-to-stand velocity for vamorolone 6 mg/kg/day versus placebo (least-squares mean [SE] velocity 0.05 [0.01] m/s vs −0.01 [0.01] m/s; 95% CI 0.02 to 0.10; P=.002), and the first 4 sequential secondary endpoints (time-to-stand velocity for vamorolone 2 mg/kg vs placebo; 6-minute walk distance for both vamorolone doses vs placebo; time to run/walk 10 m velocity for vamorolone 6 mg/kg vs placebo). Height percentile declined in prednisone-treated but not vamorolone-treated participants (change from baseline [SD]: prednisone −1.88 [8.81] percentile vs vamorolone 6 mg/kg +3.86 [6.16] percentile; P=.02). Bone turnover markers declined with prednisone but not with vamorolone. Boys with DMD at baseline showed low ACTH-stimulated cortisol and a high incidence of adrenal insufficiency; all 3 treatment groups led to increased adrenal insufficiency.
cards.watchOut: The topic file's non-inferiority framing is corrected here: no non-inferiority margin against prednisone was tested, so this record cannot support a claim of equal efficacy to prednisone — only efficacy versus placebo over 24 weeks plus favourable growth/bone-marker contrasts. The journal is JAMA Neurology (the topic file said JAMA). Adrenal insufficiency worsened on vamorolone too — 'dissociative' does not mean adrenal-sparing in this record.

shelves.title: Corticosteroid dosing regimens in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (FOR-DMD)
shelves.question: In boys with DMD, do daily prednisone or daily deflazacort vs intermittent prednisone (10 days on/10 days off) improve motor and pulmonary outcomes over 3 years?
shelves.mesh: Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Muscular Dystrophy, Duchenne/drug therapy · Prednisone/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Pregnenediones/adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY: One large double-blind randomised trial (FOR-DMD, 196 steroid-naïve boys aged 4–7, followed for 3 years) settled the regimen question: both daily prednisone 0.75 mg/kg and daily deflazacort 0.90 mg/kg were superior to intermittent prednisone (10 days on/10 days off) on the global primary outcome combining rise-from-floor velocity, forced vital capacity, and treatment satisfaction (P<.001 and P=.017 respectively, Bonferroni-adjusted threshold .017), and the two daily regimens did not differ significantly from each other (P=.38). The differences were driven principally by rise-from-floor velocity (0.06 rise/s for each daily regimen vs intermittent); the pairwise comparisons for forced vital capacity and satisfaction were not statistically significant. The commonest adverse events — abnormal behaviour (34–38%), upper respiratory infection (29–37%) and vomiting (23–29%) — were similar across regimens. Vamorolone is Shelf #1420.

cards.headline: FOR-DMD (Guglieri 2022): daily prednisone and daily deflazacort both beat intermittent prednisone over 3 years in DMD; the two daily regimens did not differ
cards.summary: FOR-DMD (Guglieri 2022): daily prednisone and daily deflazacort both beat intermittent prednisone over 3 years in DMD; the two daily regimens did not differ
cards.type: Double-blind, parallel-group randomised clinical trial (3 years)
cards.people: 196 boys aged 4 to 7 years with Duchenne muscular dystrophy who had not previously been treated with corticosteroids, enrolled at 32 clinic sites in 5 countries between January 2013 and September 2016 and assessed for 3 years; 65 were randomised to daily prednisone 0.75 mg/kg, 65 to daily deflazacort 0.90 mg/kg, and 66 to intermittent prednisone 0.75 mg/kg (10 days on, 10 days off); 164 (84%) completed the trial. Mean age was 5.8 years (SD 1.0).
cards.result: Both daily regimens were more effective than intermittent prednisone for the global primary outcome (rise-from-floor velocity, forced vital capacity, and TSQM treatment satisfaction, each averaged across post-baseline visits): P<.001 for daily prednisone vs intermittent and P=.017 for daily deflazacort vs intermittent (Bonferroni-adjusted significance level .017); daily prednisone vs daily deflazacort did not differ significantly (P=.38). The between-group differences were principally attributable to rise-from-floor velocity: 0.06 rise/s (98.3% CI 0.03 to 0.08) for daily prednisone vs intermittent (P=.003), 0.06 rise/s (98.3% CI 0.03 to 0.09) for daily deflazacort vs intermittent (P=.017), and −0.004 rise/s (98.3% CI −0.03 to 0.02) for daily prednisone vs daily deflazacort (P=.75). Pairwise comparisons for forced vital capacity and satisfaction were not statistically significant. The most common adverse events were abnormal behavior (34%, 38% and 36% in the daily prednisone, daily deflazacort and intermittent groups), upper respiratory tract infection (37%, 29%, 36%), and vomiting (29%, 26%, 23%).
cards.watchOut: The global primary outcome is a composite of three endpoints averaged over visits, and only the motor component separated the groups — the FVC and satisfaction components were not individually significant, so the claim is 'daily beats intermittent overall, driven by motor function', not 'daily improves lung function'. Long-term steroid harms (weight, bone, behaviour) accumulate beyond any regimen comparison here; the trial compares regimens, not steroid versus none.

shelves.title: Growth hormone therapy for Turner syndrome
shelves.question: In girls with Turner syndrome, does growth hormone therapy vs no treatment increase adult height?
shelves.mesh: Anabolic Agents/therapeutic use · Body Height · Child · Child, Preschool · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Growth Hormone/therapeutic use · Humans · Oxandrolone/therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Turner Syndrome/drug therapy,physiopathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — with the design disclosed on the card's face: this was a randomised trial only in its initial 12–24-month phase (70 karyotype-verified girls assigned to observation, oxandrolone, GH, or GH plus oxandrolone); after that phase, girls in the GH-alone group continued GH and ALL other subjects were switched to GH plus oxandrolone, so the adult-height results are not a randomised comparison. The 17 girls who received GH alone throughout reached a mean adult height of 150.4±5.5 cm — 8.4±4.5 cm above their mean projected adult height (95% CI 6.3 to 10.6 cm) — and the 43 who received GH plus oxandrolone reached 152.1±5.9 cm, 10.3±4.7 cm above projected (95% CI 8.9 to 11.7). A comparison group of 25 never-treated historical American subjects reached 144.2±6.0 cm, exactly matching their projected height, which supports (but does not prove, being historical) that the gains are treatment effects rather than projection error. An older programme, a projection-based endpoint and a non-randomised long-term phase hold the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Rosenfeld 1998: growth hormone (± oxandrolone) was associated with adult heights 8.4–10.3 cm above projected in Turner syndrome — but randomisation ended after the initial phase
cards.summary: Rosenfeld 1998: growth hormone (± oxandrolone) was associated with adult heights 8.4–10.3 cm above projected in Turner syndrome — but randomisation ended after the initial phase
cards.type: Multicentre, prospective, randomised trial (initial phase) with a non-randomised treatment phase to adult height and historical controls
cards.people: 70 girls with karyotype-verified Turner syndrome in a multicentre prospective trial, randomly assigned for an initial 12–24-month phase to (1) observation, (2) oxandrolone, (3) growth hormone, or (4) GH plus oxandrolone; thereafter group 3 continued GH only and all other subjects received GH plus oxandrolone until adult height. Sixty completed the trial: 17 received GH alone throughout and 43 received GH plus oxandrolone. A further 25 American historical subjects with Turner syndrome, matched for age, height, parental target height and karyotype and never treated with GH or androgens, served as the adult-height comparison. The abstract does not state mean age at enrolment.
cards.result: The 17 subjects receiving GH alone all completed the trial and reached a height of 150.4±5.5 cm (mean ± SD), 8.4±4.5 cm taller than their mean projected adult height at enrolment (95% CI 6.3 to 10.6 cm). The 43 subjects receiving GH plus oxandrolone attained a mean height of 152.1±5.9 cm, 10.3±4.7 cm taller than projected (95% CI 8.9 to 11.7 cm). The historical control subjects had a mean adult height of 144.2±6.0 cm, precisely matching their original projected adult height of 144.2±6.1 cm.
cards.watchOut: The adult-height claim rests on comparisons with each girl's projected height and with 25 historical controls — not on the randomised groups, which were dissolved after the first phase. Ten of 70 girls did not complete the trial. Projected adult height in Turner syndrome carries its own error; the historical controls matching their projections exactly is reassuring but is not randomisation. The authors' own title asserts a 'beneficial effect'; the design supports that conclusion less strongly than the title implies, and this card grades the design, not the title.
cards.source: Rosenfeld RG et al. Growth hormone therapy of Turner's syndrome: beneficial effect on adult height. J Pediatr. 1998. PMID: 9506648. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: HLA-B*58:01 screening before allopurinol: in Taiwan's national prospective cohort, no screened-negative patient treated with allopurinol developed a severe cutaneous reaction — against seven expected
shelves.question: In patients about to start allopurinol, does HLA-B*58:01 screening prevent severe cutaneous adverse reactions?
shelves.mesh: Allopurinol/adverse effects* · Chronic Disease · Drug Eruptions/genetics/prevention & control* · Exanthema/chemically induced · Female · Genetic Testing · Genotype · Gout Suppressants/adverse effects* · HLA-B Antigens/genetics* · Heterozygote · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Pruritus/chemically induced · Taiwan
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The genetic association is among the strongest in pharmacogenomics, and the one national implementation cohort found the screening strategy worked as designed. In Taiwan, all 51 patients with allopurinol-induced severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs) carried HLA-B*58:01, versus 15% of allopurinol-tolerant controls (odds ratio 580.3, 95% CI 34.4 to 9780.9 — a relative figure with a very wide interval) (Hung SI et al., PMID: 15743917). When Taiwan screened prospectively (Ko TM et al., PMID: 26399967), 571 of 2,910 genotyped patients (19.6%) were carriers and were advised to avoid allopurinol; among the 2,339 screened-negative patients who took allopurinol, no SCAR occurred, against seven cases expected from the historical national incidence of 0.30% per year (P = 0.0026); mild transient rash occurred in 3%. The CPIC guideline on HLA-B genotype and allopurinol dosing was reviewed for its 2015 update and its recommendations left unchanged (Saito Y et al., PMID: 26094938). What is missing is any randomised or concurrently controlled comparison — the cohort's control is historical, the outcome is rare, and carrier frequency (and therefore screening yield) is far lower in most European-ancestry populations than the ~20% seen in this Han Chinese cohort. Tier C: observational-dependent. HLA-B*57:01 screening before abacavir — the pharmacogenetic test with a randomised trial behind it — is shelf #481.

cards.headline: Ko 2015: Taiwan's national screening cohort — 571 carriers steered away from allopurinol, and zero severe reactions among 2,339 screened-negative patients treated, against seven expected
cards.summary: Ko 2015: Taiwan's national screening cohort — 571 carriers steered away from allopurinol, and zero severe reactions among 2,339 screened-negative patients treated, against seven expected
cards.type: National prospective cohort study with historical comparison (Ko 2015)
cards.people: 2,926 allopurinol-naive patients with an indication for allopurinol at 15 Taiwanese medical centres (2009–2014), of whom 2,910 were genotyped for HLA-B*58:01. Carriers (571, 19.6%) were advised to avoid allopurinol and referred to alternative treatment; non-carriers (2,339) received allopurinol and were interviewed weekly for two months to monitor symptoms.
cards.result: No participant who screened negative and received allopurinol developed a severe cutaneous adverse reaction, and none was admitted to hospital for an adverse drug reaction. Seven SCAR cases were expected, from the historical national incidence of 0.30% per year (95% CI 0.28% to 0.31%; P = 0.0026). Mild transient rash without blisters developed in 97 participants (3%).
cards.watchOut: The comparison is a historical national rate, not a concurrent control group, and follow-up was two months — the window in which most allopurinol SCARs occur, but not all. The cohort was Han Chinese, where roughly one in five people carries the allele; where carriage is ~1%, the same programme prevents far fewer cases per thousand tested.

cards.headline: Hung 2005: every one of 51 allopurinol SCAR cases carried HLA-B*5801 — versus 15% of tolerant controls (odds ratio 580, a relative figure)
cards.summary: Hung 2005: every one of 51 allopurinol SCAR cases carried HLA-B*5801 — versus 15% of tolerant controls (odds ratio 580, a relative figure)
cards.type: Case-control genetic association study (Hung 2005)
cards.people: 51 Han Chinese patients with allopurinol-induced severe cutaneous adverse reactions (drug hypersensitivity syndrome, Stevens–Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis) and 228 controls (135 allopurinol-tolerant patients and 93 healthy general-population subjects), genotyped across drug-metabolism and immune-response genes and at the HLA loci.
cards.result: The HLA-B*5801 allele (now written B*58:01) was present in all 51 cases (100%), in 20 of 135 tolerant controls (15%) — odds ratio 580.3 (95% CI 34.4 to 9780.9), a relative measure — and in 19 of 93 healthy subjects (20%; OR 393.51). The linked alleles A*3303, Cw*0302 and DRB1*0301 formed an extended haplotype with B*5801.
cards.watchOut: A case-control association, however extreme, is not screening performance: most carriers tolerate allopurinol (15% of tolerant controls carried the allele), so a positive test marks a risk group, not a destiny. The clinical strategy — give carriers a different drug — is what the Taiwan cohort (card 1) then put into practice.

cards.people: One national prospective implementation cohort (2,910 genotyped; 2,339 treated after a negative test), one case-control association study (51 cases, 228 controls), and the standing CPIC guideline.
cards.result: Association: 100% of SCAR cases vs 15% of tolerant controls carried the allele (OR 580.3, relative). Implementation: 19.6% tested positive and were diverted to other treatment; zero SCARs occurred among treated screen-negative patients versus about seven expected at the historical incidence of 0.30% per year. Mild rash still occurred in 3% of the cohort.
cards.watchOut: No randomised trial of screening exists or is likely (the outcome is rare and the association overwhelming), so the benefit estimate leans on a historical control. Yield depends on ancestry: carrier frequencies near 20% in Han Chinese populations make screening efficient; at the much lower frequencies of many other populations the same test prevents far fewer events per thousand tested.

shelves.title: HNF1A-MODY and gliclazide: fasting glucose fell 4.7 mmol/L (≈85 mg/dL) on gliclazide versus 0.9 on metformin — a 5.2-fold sensitivity in a 36-patient crossover trial
shelves.question: In HNF1A maturity-onset diabetes of the young, are patients unusually sensitive to low-dose gliclazide compared with type 2 diabetes?
shelves.mesh: ATP-Binding Cassette Transporters · Adult · Aged · Blood Glucose · DNA-Binding Proteins · Diabetes Mellitus · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Fasting · Female · Gliclazide · Hepatocyte Nuclear Factor 1 · Hepatocyte Nuclear Factor 1-alpha · Hepatocyte Nuclear Factor 1-beta · Humans · Hyperglycemia · Hypoglycemic Agents · Male · Metformin · Middle Aged · Nuclear Proteins · Potassium Channels · Potassium Channels, Inwardly Rectifying · Receptors, Drug · Sulfonylurea Receptors · Transcription Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a marked, mechanism-backed drug sensitivity shown in one small randomised crossover trial. Pearson ER et al. (PMID: 14575972) randomised 36 patients — HNF1A-mutation diabetes or type 2 diabetes matched for BMI and fasting glucose — to crossover treatment with gliclazide and metformin. Patients with HNF1A diabetes had a 5.2-fold greater response to gliclazide than to metformin (fasting plasma glucose reduction 4.7 versus 0.9 mmol/L (≈85 versus 16 mg/dL), P=0.0007) and a 3.9-fold greater response to gliclazide than patients with type 2 diabetes (P=0.002). The mechanism fitted: a strong insulin secretory response to intravenous tolbutamide despite a small response to intravenous glucose, greater insulin sensitivity than type 2 diabetes, and similar sulfonylurea metabolism in both groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): HNF1A diabetes is unusually sensitive to low-dose gliclazide — one 36-patient crossover trial from 2003, never replicated at scale, so Tier C.

cards.type: Randomised crossover trial (Pearson 2003)
cards.people: 36 patients in a randomised crossover trial of gliclazide and metformin: patients with diabetes caused by HNF1A mutations and patients with type 2 diabetes, matched for body-mass index and fasting plasma glucose; primary outcome reduction in fasting plasma glucose, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: Patients with HNF1A diabetes had a 5.2-fold greater response to gliclazide than to metformin (fasting plasma glucose reduction 4.7 versus 0.9 mmol/L (≈85 versus 16 mg/dL), P=0.0007) and a 3.9-fold greater response to gliclazide than those with type 2 diabetes (P=0.002). Mechanistically, HNF1A patients had a strong insulin secretory response to intravenous tolbutamide despite a small response to intravenous glucose, were more insulin sensitive than the type 2 group, and cleared tolbutamide at a similar rate.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-six patients, short crossover periods, and a fasting-glucose endpoint: the trial proves sensitivity, not the safe starting dose, long-term control, or hypoglycaemia rates in routine care — and the finding is specific to HNF1A, not to MODY in general (GCK-MODY, for example, needs no drug treatment at all).

shelves.title: Screening for HLA-B*1502 before carbamazepine in Taiwan: zero cases of Stevens–Johnson syndrome in 4,877 screened patients, against about 10 expected historically
shelves.question: In populations with high HLA-B*15:02 prevalence, does screening for HLA-B*15:02 before starting carbamazepine prevent Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anticonvulsants/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Asian People/genetics · Carbamazepine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Child · Child, Preschool · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions/genetics/prevention & control · Female · Genetic Testing · Genotype · HLA-B Antigens/genetics · HLA-B15 Antigen · Humans · Incidence · Infant · Male · Middle Aged · Pharmacogenetics · Stevens-Johnson Syndrome/chemically induced/epidemiology/genetics/prevention & control · Taiwan · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large prospective screening programme with a historical comparator, not a randomised trial. In Chen 2011 (PMID: 21428768), 4,877 carbamazepine candidates in Taiwan were genotyped: 372 (7.7%) carried HLA-B*1502 and were advised to avoid carbamazepine, while the 92.3% who tested negative took it. Stevens–Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis developed in none of the screened-negative patients taking carbamazepine, against an estimated historical incidence of 0.23% — about 10 expected cases in this cohort (P < 0.001). Mild transient rash still occurred in 4.3% and a more widespread rash requiring hospitalisation in 0.1%, so screening removes the catastrophic reaction, not all rash. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in a high-prevalence population, pre-treatment HLA-B*1502 screening with avoidance in carriers was associated with eliminating carbamazepine-induced SJS-TEN in nearly 5,000 patients. Tier C is set: the evidence is a single prospective cohort against historical incidence, an observational design.

cards.headline: Chen 2011: 7.7% carried HLA-B*1502 and avoided carbamazepine; SJS-TEN in 0 of the screened-negative patients treated, versus ~10 cases expected (P < 0.001)
cards.summary: Chen 2011: 7.7% carried HLA-B*1502 and avoided carbamazepine; SJS-TEN in 0 of the screened-negative patients treated, versus ~10 cases expected (P < 0.001)
cards.type: Prospective screening cohort with historical control (Chen 2011)
cards.people: 4,877 candidate subjects at 23 hospitals in Taiwan who had not previously taken carbamazepine, genotyped for HLA-B*1502; carriers (7.7%) were advised not to take carbamazepine and given an alternative or continued prestudy medication, non-carriers (92.3%) were advised to take carbamazepine, with weekly telephone monitoring for 2 months. The comparator was the estimated historical incidence of carbamazepine-induced SJS-TEN.
cards.result: SJS-TEN did not develop in any HLA-B*1502-negative subject receiving carbamazepine. The estimated historical incidence of 0.23% would have predicted approximately 10 cases among the study subjects (P < 0.001). Mild transient rash developed in 4.3% of subjects and more widespread rash in 0.1%, who were hospitalised.
cards.watchOut: No randomised or concurrent control group — the comparison is with historical incidence, which can drift; carriers were not exposed to carbamazepine, so the study shows the screening pathway works, and the allele's predictive value is inferred from prior association data rather than re-proven here. Results apply to populations with high HLA-B*1502 prevalence.
cards.source: Chen P et al. Carbamazepine-induced toxic effects and HLA-B*1502 screening in Taiwan. New England Journal of Medicine. 2011. PMID: 21428768. shelves.title: TPMT testing before thiopurines (TOPIC): no overall reduction in blood toxicity (7.4% versus 7.9%) — but variant carriers given a reduced dose had a tenth the events (2.6% versus 22.9%)
shelves.question: In patients with inflammatory bowel disease starting thiopurines, does pre-treatment TPMT genotyping with genotype-guided dosing reduce haematological adverse events versus standard dosing?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/metabolism · Azathioprine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/metabolism · Colitis, Ulcerative/diagnosis/drug therapy/enzymology/genetics · Crohn Disease/diagnosis/drug therapy/enzymology/genetics · Drug Dosage Calculations · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/metabolism · Genetic Testing · Genetic Variation · Heterozygote · Homozygote · Humans · Leukopenia/chemically induced/prevention & control · Male · Mercaptopurine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/metabolism · Methyltransferases/genetics/metabolism · Middle Aged · Netherlands · Pharmacogenetics · Phenotype · Predictive Value of Tests · Prospective Studies · Risk Factors · Thrombocytopenia/chemically induced/prevention & control · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the trial's two answers point opposite ways depending on who you look at. Overall, TOPIC (Coenen 2015, PMID: 26072396) found haematological adverse events in 7.4% of the genotype-guided group versus 7.9% on standard care (relative risk 0.93, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.52) — no benefit, because variant carriers are uncommon. But among carriers themselves, dose reduction worked dramatically: 2.6% of screened carriers developed a haematological event versus 22.9% of unscreened carriers (relative risk 0.11, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.85). Disease activity did not differ between groups (P = .18 for Crohn's disease, P = .14 for ulcerative colitis), so the dose reduction did not cost efficacy. PROPOSED SPLIT: population-level screening did not lower the overall event rate in this trial, while identified carriers who received a reduced starting dose were strongly protected.

cards.headline: TOPIC: overall haematological adverse events 7.4% screened versus 7.9% control (RR 0.93); in variant carriers, 2.6% versus 22.9% (RR 0.11)
cards.summary: TOPIC: overall haematological adverse events 7.4% screened versus 7.9% control (RR 0.93); in variant carriers, 2.6% versus 22.9% (RR 0.11)
cards.type: Randomised prospective trial (Coenen 2015, TOPIC)
cards.people: 783 patients with inflammatory bowel disease at 30 Dutch hospitals randomised to standard thiopurine treatment (n = 378) or pretreatment screening for three TPMT variants (n = 405), in which heterozygous carriers received 50% of the standard dose and homozygous carriers 0–10%; outcomes were assessed over 20 weeks, with disease activity measured in 356 Crohn's and 253 ulcerative colitis patients.
cards.result: Similar proportions developed a haematological adverse event (leukocyte count below 3.0×10⁹/L or platelets below 100×10⁹/L): 7.4% in the intervention group versus 7.9% in controls (relative risk 0.93; 95% confidence interval 0.57 to 1.52). Among variant carriers, however, 2.6% of the screened group developed an event versus 22.9% of controls (relative risk 0.11; 95% CI 0.01 to 0.85). Mean disease activity did not differ significantly (P = .18 Crohn's; P = .14 ulcerative colitis).
cards.watchOut: The carrier subgroup is small, so the striking RR 0.11 has a wide interval (0.01 to 0.85); only three TPMT variants were screened, and TPMT explains only part of thiopurine leukopenia — most events in the trial occurred in non-carriers, which is exactly why the population result is null. Tier C is set: the benefit claim rests on a subgroup of a single trial.
cards.source: Coenen MJH et al. Identification of Patients With Variants in TPMT and Dose Reduction Reduces Hematologic Events During Thiopurine Treatment of Inflammatory Bowel Disease. Gastroenterology. 2015. PMID: 26072396. Registry ID: NCT00521950. shelves.title: UGT1A1-guided irinotecan dosing: febrile neutropenia in 6.5% of dose-reduced poor metabolisers versus 24% in historical full-dose poor metabolisers — and €183 saved per patient
shelves.question: In patients with UGT1A1 poor-metaboliser genotypes starting irinotecan, does pre-emptive genotype-guided dose reduction reduce severe neutropenia and diarrhoea versus standard dosing?
shelves.mesh: Camptothecin/adverse effects · Costs and Cost Analysis · Febrile Neutropenia · Genotype · Glucuronosyltransferase/genetics · Humans · Irinotecan/adverse effects · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a prospective implementation study against historical controls, backed by the genetics of the toxicity. In Hulshof 2022 (PMID: 34998046), 31 of 350 patients (8.9%) were UGT1A1 poor metabolisers and received a median 30% initial dose reduction; febrile neutropenia in the first two cycles occurred in 6.5% of them versus 24% in a historical poor-metaboliser cohort treated at full dose (P = 0.04), a rate comparable to non-poor-metabolisers on full dose. The meta-analysis card (Zhang 2017, PMID: 28585035) confirms the underlying risk the strategy targets: UGT1A1*6 variant carriers had roughly double the odds of severe neutropenia (OR 2.03, 95% CI 1.54 to 2.68; homozygous OR 2.95, 1.83 to 4.75). Dose reduction was cost-saving (€183 per patient). The record reports neutropenia outcomes; a diarrhoea benefit is not quantified in it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pre-emptive genotyping with a 30% starting-dose reduction in poor metabolisers cut febrile neutropenia to the background rate. Tier C is set: the dosing study is non-randomised with a historical comparator.

cards.headline: Hulshof 2022: febrile neutropenia 6.5% in dose-reduced poor metabolisers versus 24% in historical full-dose poor metabolisers (P = 0.04)
cards.summary: Hulshof 2022: febrile neutropenia 6.5% in dose-reduced poor metabolisers versus 24% in historical full-dose poor metabolisers (P = 0.04)
cards.type: Prospective multicentre non-randomised study (Hulshof 2022)
cards.people: 350 evaluable patients intended for irinotecan treatment, pre-therapeutically genotyped for UGT1A1*28 and *93; the 31 poor metabolisers (8.9%) received an initial 30% dose reduction. The primary endpoint was febrile neutropenia in the first two cycles, compared with a historical full-dose poor-metaboliser cohort and with non-poor-metabolisers treated at full dose in the same study.
cards.result: Febrile neutropenia occurred in 6.5% of dose-reduced poor metabolisers versus 24% in historical full-dose poor metabolisers (P = 0.04), and was comparable to the incidence in non-poor-metabolisers on full dose. Systemic SN-38 exposure remained slightly higher than in a standard-dosed cohort (difference +32%), and the cost analysis showed genotype-guided dosing was cost-saving, at €183 per patient.
cards.watchOut: Non-randomised with a historical comparator and only 31 poor metabolisers — the 6.5% is two patients, so the estimate is fragile; diarrhoea, the other classic irinotecan toxicity in the shelf question, is not reported as an outcome in this record, and efficacy (tumour response at the reduced dose) is addressed only through drug-exposure levels.

cards.headline: Zhang 2017 (meta-analysis): UGT1A1*6 carriers had double the odds of severe neutropenia (OR 2.03); homozygous carriers OR 2.95
cards.summary: Zhang 2017 (meta-analysis): UGT1A1*6 carriers had double the odds of severe neutropenia (OR 2.03); homozygous carriers OR 2.95
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Zhang 2017)
cards.people: 12 studies including 746 patients with the wild-type UGT1A1*6 genotype and 394 with variant genotypes (G/A and A/A), examining irinotecan-induced severe neutropenia in cancer patients, largely in Asian populations where the *6 variant is prevalent.
cards.result: Variant carriers (GA + AA versus GG) had an increased risk of severe neutropenia (odds ratio 2.03, 95% confidence interval 1.54 to 2.68; risk difference 0.11, P < 0.001); heterozygous carriers had OR 1.83 (1.36 to 2.46) and homozygous carriers OR 2.95 (1.83 to 4.75). The association held in both Chinese and Japanese subgroups.
cards.watchOut: This card establishes the genotype–toxicity link for the *6 allele; the dosing study carded above genotyped *28 and *93. The alleles differ by ancestry, so the shelf's claim is about the poor-metaboliser strategy, not one universal variant panel.

shelves.title: CYP3A5-guided tacrolimus starting dose: 43.2% in target range at day 3 versus 29.1% with standard dosing — faster to target, fewer dose changes, clinical outcomes unchanged
shelves.question: In kidney transplant recipients, does adapting the starting tacrolimus dose to CYP3A5 genotype get patients into the target range faster versus standard weight-based dosing?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cytochrome P-450 CYP3A/genetics · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Genotype · Graft Rejection/prevention & control · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage/pharmacokinetics · Kidney Transplantation/methods · Male · Middle Aged · Pharmacogenetics/methods · Prospective Studies · Tacrolimus/administration & dosage/pharmacokinetics · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the blood level, not (yet) for the patient. In Thervet 2010 (PMID: 20393454), 280 kidney transplant recipients were randomised to a CYP3A5-adapted or standard starting dose: at day 3, 43.2% of the adapted group were within the target trough range versus 29.1% of controls (P = 0.03), the adapted group needed fewer dose modifications, and 75% of them reached target sooner. Clinical endpoints, however, were similar in the two groups — no rejection or survival advantage was shown. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): genotype-adapted starting doses get tacrolimus into range faster with less titration, a process benefit whose clinical payoff remains unproven. Tier C is set: a single trial carrying a benefit claim.

cards.headline: Thervet 2010: in-range at day 3 in 43.2% (genotype-adapted) versus 29.1% (standard), P = 0.03; fewer dose modifications, faster to target, clinical endpoints similar
cards.summary: Thervet 2010: in-range at day 3 in 43.2% (genotype-adapted) versus 29.1% (standard), P = 0.03; fewer dose modifications, faster to target, clinical endpoints similar
cards.type: Randomised prospective trial (Thervet 2010)
cards.people: 280 renal transplant recipients randomly assigned to tacrolimus dosed according to CYP3A5 genotype or according to the standard daily regimen; the primary endpoint was the proportion within the target trough concentration at day 3 after starting tacrolimus, with secondary endpoints of dose modifications and delay to target.
cards.result: A higher proportion of the adapted-dose group had values within the target trough at day 3 (43.2% versus 29.1%; P = 0.03); they required fewer dose modifications, and the target concentration was achieved by 75% of these patients more rapidly. Clinical endpoints were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is a drug level at day 3 — a surrogate. Even in the adapted group most patients (56.8%) were out of range at day 3, and the trial shows no difference in rejection or other clinical outcomes; whether faster target attainment prevents early rejection needs a larger, outcome-powered trial.
cards.source: Thervet E et al. Optimization of initial tacrolimus dose using pharmacogenetic testing. Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics. 2010. PMID: 20393454. shelves.title: Rapid MT-RNR1 testing before gentamicin in newborn intensive care: 80.6% of antibiotic-treated babies tested in 26 minutes, 3 carriers identified and spared aminoglycosides, no delay to antibiotics
shelves.question: In neonatal intensive care, does a rapid point-of-care test for the MT-RNR1 m.1555A>G variant, used before gentamicin, prevent aminoglycoside-induced hearing loss versus standard prescribing?
shelves.mesh: Aminoglycosides/adverse effects · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects · Genotype · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Intensive Care, Neonatal · Ototoxicity · Point-of-Care Systems · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the pathway works end-to-end; prevented deafness itself is inferred, not counted. In the PALOH implementation study (McDermott 2022, PMID: 35311942), 751 neonates at two UK intensive care units were tested with a point-of-care assay giving a result in 26 minutes, with 100% sensitivity (95% CI 93.9% to 100%) and specificity (98.5% to 100%) on preclinical validation. Three babies carried the m.1555A>G variant and all three avoided aminoglycosides; 424 infants (80.6%) receiving antibiotics were successfully tested, and mean time to antibiotics was equivalent to previous practice. No baby in the study was followed to a hearing outcome — the prevented harm rests on the established variant–ototoxicity link and on those three avoided exposures. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): rapid testing can be integrated without delaying antibiotics and does divert carriers away from aminoglycosides. Tier C is set: a single non-randomised implementation study with a process outcome.

cards.headline: PALOH 2022: genotype in 26 minutes; 3 carriers identified, all avoided aminoglycosides; 80.6% of antibiotic-treated infants tested; time to antibiotics unchanged
cards.summary: PALOH 2022: genotype in 26 minutes; 3 carriers identified, all avoided aminoglycosides; 80.6% of antibiotic-treated infants tested; time to antibiotics unchanged
cards.type: Pragmatic prospective implementation trial (McDermott 2022, PALOH)
cards.people: 751 neonates (median age 2.5 days) admitted to two large UK neonatal intensive care units between January and November 2020, tested for the MT-RNR1 m.1555A>G variant by rapid point-of-care test on admission; the primary outcome was the proportion of antibiotic-prescribed infants successfully tested, with time to antibiotics compared against pre-implementation practice.
cards.result: The test genotyped the variant in 26 minutes, with preclinical validation showing 100% sensitivity (95% confidence interval 93.9% to 100.0%) and 100% specificity (98.5% to 100.0%). Three participants with the variant were identified and all avoided aminoglycoside antibiotics. Overall 424 infants (80.6%) receiving antibiotics were successfully tested, and mean time to antibiotics was equivalent to previous practice.
cards.watchOut: The outcome is implementation success, not hearing: with a variant prevalence around 1 in 500, even 751 babies yield only 3 carriers, and no audiological follow-up is reported — the claim 'prevents hearing loss' is an inference from avoided exposure. About one in five antibiotic-treated infants was still not tested.
cards.source: McDermott JH et al. Rapid Point-of-Care Genotyping to Avoid Aminoglycoside-Induced Ototoxicity in Neonatal Intensive Care. JAMA Pediatrics. 2022. PMID: 35311942. shelves.title: SLCO1B1 and simvastatin myopathy: odds ratio 4.5 per copy of the rs4149056 C allele — 16.9 in CC homozygotes — replicated at the lower dose and in a second genome-wide study
shelves.question: In patients taking high-dose simvastatin, does the SLCO1B1 variant identify who is at high risk of myopathy — and should it change statin choice or dose?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Arterial Occlusive Diseases/drug therapy · Chromosomes, Human, Pair 12 · Diabetes Mellitus/drug therapy · Female · Genetic Markers · Genotype · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/adverse effects/pharmacokinetics/therapeutic use · Liver-Specific Organic Anion Transporter 1 · Male · Middle Aged · Muscular Diseases/chemically induced/genetics · Myocardial Infarction/drug therapy/prevention & control · Organic Anion Transporters/genetics · Polymorphism, Single Nucleotide · Risk · Simvastatin/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — for carrying the variant on high-dose simvastatin; the testing-policy half of the question has no trial. The SEARCH genome-wide study (Link 2008, PMID: 18650507) found myopathy odds rising 4.5-fold per copy of the SLCO1B1 rs4149056 C allele (95% CI 2.6 to 7.7), and 16.9-fold (4.7 to 61.1) in CC versus TT homozygotes, with more than 60% of myopathy cases in the 80 mg trial attributable to the variant; the association replicated in a 40 mg simvastatin trial. An independent genome-wide study (Carr 2019, PMID: 31220337) again found only this variant genome-wide significant for severe myopathy (OR 5.15, 95% CI 3.13 to 8.45). No record carded here randomised patients to genotype-guided statin choice, so 'should it change prescribing' is answered by risk magnitude, not by an outcomes trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): the C allele identifies a genuinely high-risk group for simvastatin myopathy, strongest at 80 mg. Tier C is set: observational genetic association evidence behind a harm claim.

cards.headline: SEARCH 2008: myopathy odds ratio 4.5 per C allele and 16.9 for CC versus TT on simvastatin 80 mg; over 60% of cases attributable to the variant
cards.summary: SEARCH 2008: myopathy odds ratio 4.5 per C allele and 16.9 for CC versus TT on simvastatin 80 mg; over 60% of cases attributable to the variant
cards.type: Genome-wide association study with replication (Link 2008, SEARCH Collaborative Group)
cards.people: 85 patients with definite or incipient myopathy and 90 controls, all taking simvastatin 80 mg daily within a trial of about 12,000 participants, scanned at roughly 300,000 markers with fine-mapping; replication was tested in a separate trial of simvastatin 40 mg daily involving about 20,000 participants. The C allele prevalence in the population was 15%.
cards.result: A single strong association emerged: the rs4363657 SNP within SLCO1B1 (in near-complete linkage disequilibrium with the nonsynonymous rs4149056, r² = 0.97) at P = 4×10⁻⁹. The odds ratio for myopathy was 4.5 (95% confidence interval 2.6 to 7.7) per copy of the rs4149056 C allele and 16.9 (4.7 to 61.1) in CC compared with TT homozygotes; more than 60% of myopathy cases could be attributed to the C variant. The association replicated at the 40 mg dose, which also showed an association with cholesterol-lowering effect.
cards.watchOut: A case-control genetic association, not a trial of testing: absolute myopathy risk on modern simvastatin doses (80 mg is now rarely used) is far lower than in this high-dose trial population, and the shelf cannot say from these records whether genotype-guided switching improves outcomes.
cards.source: Link E et al. SLCO1B1 variants and statin-induced myopathy--a genomewide study. New England Journal of Medicine. 2008. PMID: 18650507. Registry ID: ISRCTN74348595. cards.summary: Carr 2019: independent genome-wide study — rs4149056 again the only genome-wide signal for severe myopathy (OR 5.15)
cards.type: Genome-wide association study with validation cohorts (Carr 2019)
cards.people: 135 patients with statin myopathy recruited through the UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink, compared with 2,501 population controls, with nominally significant signals evaluated in independent cohorts comprising 332 cases and 449 drug-tolerant controls, across several statins in real-world practice.
cards.result: Only the SLCO1B1 rs4149056 (c.521T>C) SNP was genome-wide significant in the severe myopathy group (creatine kinase above 10 times the upper limit of normal or rhabdomyolysis): P = 2.55×10⁻⁹, odds ratio 5.15 (95% confidence interval 3.13 to 8.45). The association was present for several statins and replicated in the independent validation cohorts; no other novel genetic risk factor of similar effect size was identified.
cards.watchOut: Real-world case ascertainment through records is noisier than trial adjudication, and effect sizes for milder muscle symptoms are smaller than for the severe-myopathy group analysed here; the study identifies risk, it does not test a prescribing strategy.
cards.source: Carr DF et al. Genomewide Association Study of Statin-Induced Myopathy in Patients Recruited Using the UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink. Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics. 2019. PMID: 31220337. cards.headline: Synthesis: one variant, two genome-wide studies, odds ratios of 4.5–5.2 per allele — risk identification is settled, testing policy is not trialled
cards.summary: Synthesis: one variant, two genome-wide studies, odds ratios of 4.5–5.2 per allele — risk identification is settled, testing policy is not trialled
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Two genome-wide association studies: a trial-based study at simvastatin 80 mg with 40 mg replication, and an independent real-world study with validation cohorts.
cards.result: Per-allele odds ratios 4.5 (2.6–7.7) and 5.15 (3.13–8.45); CC versus TT odds ratio 16.9 (4.7–61.1); over 60% of high-dose myopathy cases attributable to the variant. Both effects clear the library's twofold observational floor comfortably. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm), Tier C: observational evidence behind a harm claim, and no randomised test of genotype-guided prescribing.
cards.watchOut: Absolute risk framing matters: a 4.5-fold relative increase on a rare event at a now-unusual dose should prompt dose or statin choice awareness in carriers, not statin avoidance in everyone — untreated cardiovascular risk dwarfs myopathy risk for most patients.
cards.source: Synthesis of Link E et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2008 (PMID: 18650507); Carr DF et al. Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics. 2019 (PMID: 31220337).

shelves.title: CYP2D6-guided opioid prescribing after surgery (ADOPT-PGx): prescribing concordance rose from 27% to 64% — pain scores and opioid use did not move (SIA difference 2.8, P = .80)
shelves.question: In patients with acute postoperative pain, does CYP2D6-guided opioid selection improve pain control and reduce adverse effects versus usual opioid prescribing?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Analgesics, Opioid/pharmacokinetics/therapeutic use · Cytochrome P-450 CYP2D6/genetics/metabolism · Hydrocodone/pharmacokinetics/therapeutic use · Pain Management/methods · Pain Measurement · Postoperative Pain/diagnosis/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a well-run pragmatic trial whose intervention changed prescriptions but not outcomes. In ADOPT-PGx (Cavallari 2026, PMID: 41719044), among 351 poor or intermediate CYP2D6 metabolisers, phenotype-concordant opioid treatment was 64% in the guided arm versus 27% in controls (difference 37 percentage points, 95% CI 27 to 46; P < .001). Yet the 10-day primary outcome was identical: mean Silverman integrated analgesic assessment score 1.4 versus −1.4 (difference 2.8, 95% CI −18.3 to 23.8; P = .80), with pain intensity 5.2 versus 5.1 and opioid use 13.7 versus 13.2 morphine milligram equivalents per day. Adverse-effect differences are not reported in the record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in contemporary multimodal postoperative care, CYP2D6 guidance changed what was prescribed without improving pain or reducing opioid use. Tier C is not set — this is a null from a single large randomised trial, not a benefit or harm claim; it is flagged in the summary for the coordinator's attention on single-trial null calibration.

cards.headline: ADOPT-PGx 2026: primary outcome identical (SIA 1.4 versus −1.4; P = .80) despite concordance rising from 27% to 64%
cards.summary: ADOPT-PGx 2026: primary outcome identical (SIA 1.4 versus −1.4; P = .80) despite concordance rising from 27% to 64%
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (Cavallari 2026, ADOPT-PGx acute pain trial)
cards.people: 1,602 participants enrolled at surgery clinics in 8 US health systems before planned surgery expected to cause 7–10 days of postoperative pain (March 2021 to September 2023); the primary analysis covered the 351 participants (mean age 62; 68% female) with a CYP2D6 poor or intermediate metaboliser phenotype who proceeded to surgery — 176 guided, 175 control. The commonest operations were total knee (50%) and total hip (28%) arthroplasty. Guided participants had genotyping before surgery with recommendations to avoid tramadol, hydrocodone and codeine in poor/intermediate metabolisers.
cards.result: Concordance between prescribed opioid and CYP2D6 phenotype was 64% (112) in the guided arm versus 27% (47) in controls (difference 37 percentage points; 95% confidence interval 27 to 46; P < .001). At 10 days the mean Silverman integrated analgesic assessment score was 1.4 (SD 95.9) guided versus −1.4 (93.1) control (difference 2.8; −18.3 to 23.8; P = .80). Mean pain intensity was 5.2 (2.2) versus 5.1 (2.3) and overall opioid use 13.7 (14.9) versus 13.2 (14.7) morphine milligram equivalents per day; other secondary endpoints also did not differ.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and pragmatic: even in the guided arm 36% of actionable patients still received a non-concordant opioid, and multimodal analgesia (nerve blocks, non-opioids) may swamp any pharmacogenetic signal — the trial answers 'does routine guidance help in current practice', not 'can CYP2D6 ever matter'. Adverse-effect outcomes are not detailed in the record, so the shelf's second question half (fewer adverse effects) is unanswered rather than answered negatively.
cards.source: Cavallari LH et al. CYP2D6-Guided Opioid Management and Postoperative Pain Control: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Network Open. 2026. PMID: 41719044. Registry ID: NCT05966129. shelves.title: CYP2C19-tailored H. pylori therapy: first-line eradication 96.0% versus 70.0% with standard triple therapy — at no extra cost per cure
shelves.question: In patients with Helicobacter pylori infection, does CYP2C19 genotype-guided acid-suppression therapy improve eradication rates versus standard empirical therapy?
shelves.mesh: 2-Pyridinylmethylsulfinylbenzimidazoles/pharmacokinetics · Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage/pharmacokinetics/therapeutic use · Anti-Ulcer Agents/pharmacokinetics · Aryl Hydrocarbon Hydroxylases/genetics/metabolism · Clarithromycin/administration & dosage/pharmacokinetics/therapeutic use · Costs and Cost Analysis · Cytochrome P-450 CYP2C19 · Female · Helicobacter Infections/drug therapy/genetics/microbiology · Helicobacter pylori · Humans · Lansoprazole · Male · Mixed Function Oxygenases/genetics/metabolism · Pharmacogenetics · Polymorphism, Genetic/genetics · RNA, Ribosomal/biosynthesis/genetics
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial, a very large effect. In Furuta 2007 (PMID: 17215846), 300 H. pylori-positive patients were randomised to standard triple therapy or a regimen tailored by CYP2C19 genotype and bacterial clarithromycin susceptibility: intention-to-treat eradication was 96.0% (144/150; 95% CI 91.5 to 98.2) in the tailored group versus 70.0% (105/150; 62.2 to 77.2) on standard therapy (P < 0.001) — a 26-percentage-point absolute gain. Final cost per successful eradication was essentially identical ($669 tailored versus $657 standard), because fewer tailored patients needed second-line treatment. The catch: the tailored arm bundled two personalisations (genotype-guided acid suppression and susceptibility-guided antibiotics), so the trial cannot credit CYP2C19 alone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pharmacogenomically tailored first-line therapy eradicated H. pylori in 96% versus 70%. Tier C is set: a single trial carrying a benefit claim.

cards.headline: Furuta 2007: eradication 96.0% (144/150) tailored versus 70.0% (105/150) standard (P < 0.001); cost per cure $669 versus $657
cards.summary: Furuta 2007: eradication 96.0% (144/150) tailored versus 70.0% (105/150) standard (P < 0.001); cost per cure $669 versus $657
cards.type: Randomised trial (Furuta 2007)
cards.people: 300 Helicobacter pylori-positive patients randomly assigned to a standard regimen (lansoprazole 30 mg twice daily, clarithromycin 400 mg twice daily, amoxicillin 750 mg twice daily for 1 week) or a tailored regimen based on CYP2C19 status and bacterial clarithromycin susceptibility assessed by genetic testing, with lansoprazole dosing schedules first optimised per genotype by 24-hour intragastric pH monitoring; eradication failures received a second-line regimen.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat eradication with first-line therapy was 96.0% (95% confidence interval 91.5 to 98.2; 144/150) in the tailored group versus 70.0% (62.2 to 77.2; 105/150) in the standard group (P < 0.001) — an absolute difference of 26 percentage points. Final costs per successful eradication were $669 (tailored) and $657 (standard).
cards.watchOut: The tailored intervention combined CYP2C19-guided acid suppression with clarithromycin-susceptibility-guided antibiotic choice, so the genotype's individual contribution cannot be isolated; the study is from 2007 Japan, where genotype frequencies, clarithromycin resistance and the lansoprazole-based regimen may not match current practice elsewhere (including vonoprazan-era therapy).
cards.source: Furuta T et al. Pharmacogenomics-based tailored versus standard therapeutic regimen for eradication of H. pylori. Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics. 2007. PMID: 17215846. shelves.title: SHIVA: choosing targeted drugs from tumour profiling did not improve progression-free survival (2.3 versus 2.0 months; HR 0.88, P = 0.41) in advanced cancer
shelves.question: In adults with advanced cancer, does choosing targeted therapy from tumour molecular profiling improve progression-free survival versus conventional physician-choice therapy?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Biomarkers, Tumor/genetics/metabolism · Biopsy · Disease Progression · Disease-Free Survival · Female · France · Gene Expression Profiling · Genetic Predisposition to Disease · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Molecular Diagnostic Techniques · Molecular Targeted Therapy/adverse effects · Neoplasm Metastasis · Neoplasms/drug therapy/genetics/metabolism/mortality/pathology · Off-Label Use · Patient Selection · Phenotype · Precision Medicine · Predictive Value of Tests · Proportional Hazards Models · Risk Factors · Signal Transduction/drug effects · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the first randomised test of profile-matched prescribing was negative. In SHIVA (Le Tourneau 2015, PMID: 26342236), 195 patients with refractory metastatic solid tumours and a matchable molecular alteration were randomised to a matched targeted agent or physician's-choice treatment: median progression-free survival was 2.3 months (95% CI 1.7 to 3.8) versus 2.0 months (1.8 to 2.1), hazard ratio 0.88 (95% CI 0.65 to 1.19; P = 0.41). Grade 3–4 adverse events occurred in 43% on targeted agents versus 35% on chemotherapy (P = 0.30). Only 40% of the 741 screened patients had an alteration matching one of the trial's ten regimens at all. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): molecular profiling with the panel and drug set of this trial did not improve progression-free survival over physician's choice, and off-label matched use outside trials was discouraged by its authors.

cards.headline: SHIVA: median progression-free survival 2.3 versus 2.0 months (HR 0.88, 0.65–1.19; P = 0.41); grade 3–4 events 43% versus 35%
cards.summary: SHIVA: median progression-free survival 2.3 versus 2.0 months (HR 0.88, 0.65–1.19; P = 0.41); grade 3–4 events 43% versus 35%
cards.type: Randomised phase 2 trial (Le Tourneau 2015, SHIVA)
cards.people: 741 patients with any metastatic solid tumour refractory to standard care screened at eight French academic centres; 293 (40%) had a molecular alteration in one of three pathways (hormone receptor, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, RAF/MEK) matchable to one of ten regimens (11 targeted agents), and 195 were randomised — 99 to a matched targeted agent, 96 to treatment at physician's choice. Median follow-up was 11.3 months in both groups.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 2.3 months (95% confidence interval 1.7 to 3.8) in the experimental group versus 2.0 months (1.8 to 2.1) in the control group (hazard ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.19; P = 0.41). In the safety population, grade 3–4 adverse events occurred in 43 of 100 patients (43%) treated with a targeted agent versus 32 of 91 (35%) treated with chemotherapy (P = 0.30). The authors concluded that off-label use of molecularly targeted agents should be discouraged.
cards.watchOut: SHIVA tested one specific matching algorithm — three pathways, eleven drugs, mostly single agents used off-label in heavily pretreated patients — so its null condemns that strategy, not every modern profiling programme (which may use different panels, combinations, and earlier-line patients). Progression-free survival was not assessed by independent central review.
cards.source: Le Tourneau C et al. Molecularly targeted therapy based on tumour molecular profiling versus conventional therapy for advanced cancer (SHIVA): a multicentre, open-label, proof-of-concept, randomised, controlled phase 2 trial. Lancet Oncology. 2015. PMID: 26342236. Registry ID: NCT01771458. shelves.title: Child–parent screening at immunisation visits: 40 children and 40 parents identified per 10,095 toddlers screened — 8 people per 1,000 — a screening-yield study, not an outcomes trial
shelves.question: At routine childhood immunisation visits, does child–parent screening — testing the child for familial hypercholesterolaemia and then the parents — identify new FH cases effectively versus usual practice?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Child, Preschool · Cholesterol/blood* · Cholesterol, LDL/blood · Female · Humans · Hyperlipoproteinemia Type II/blood/diagnosis*/genetics · Infant · Male · Mass Screening* · Mutation · Parents* · Preventive Health Services · Primary Health Care*
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for case identification only; no outcome benefit was tested. In Wald DS et al. (PMID: 27783906), capillary blood samples were obtained to measure cholesterol levels and to test for familial hypercholesterolemia mutations in 10,095 children 1 to 2 years of age during routine immunization visits in primary care. Using a prespecified cholesterol cutoff value of 1.53 multiples of the median (MoM), 28 children had positive screening results for familial hypercholesterolemia (0.3% of the 10,095 children; 95% CI, 0.2 to 0.4). A lower initial cutoff strategy — 1.35 MoM plus a mutation, or two cholesterol values of at least 1.50 MoM — identified 40 children (0.4%) and 40 parents who had positive screening results. The overall mutation prevalence was 1 in 273 children (37 in 10,095; 95% CI, 1 in 198 to 1 in 388). For every 1000 children screened, 8 persons (4 children and 4 parents) were identified as having positive screening results for familial hypercholesterolemia. The study had no usual-practice comparison group and measured no cardiovascular outcomes, so it establishes the identification yield and feasibility of the strategy — not that screening this way prevents heart attacks or deaths, and not a head-to-head advantage over usual practice. This shelf is a re-card: Wald 2016 also serves as a supporting card on live shelf #476, which asks about cascade screening of relatives of people already known to have FH; child–parent screening at immunisation visits (screen the child first, then the parents) is a different screening strategy and a genuinely different question. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): child–parent screening at routine immunisation visits feasibly identifies new FH cases in both generations — 8 persons per 1,000 children screened — on the evidence of one large prospective study, with any outcome benefit unproven.

cards.headline: Wald 2016: child–parent screening at immunisation visits — 28 children (0.3%) positive at the prespecified 1.53 MoM cutoff; 40 children (0.4%) and 40 parents at the lower 1.35 MoM strategy; 8 persons identified per 1,000 children screened
cards.summary: Wald 2016: child–parent screening at immunisation visits — 28 children (0.3%) positive at the prespecified 1.53 MoM cutoff; 40 children (0.4%) and 40 parents at the lower 1.35 MoM strategy; 8 persons identified per 1,000 children screened
cards.type: Prospective screening efficacy and feasibility study in primary care (Wald 2016)
cards.people: 10,095 children 1 to 2 years of age, seen during routine immunization visits in primary care practice. Capillary blood samples were obtained to measure cholesterol levels and to test for familial hypercholesterolemia mutations. Children were considered to have positive screening results if their cholesterol level was elevated and they had either a familial hypercholesterolemia mutation or a repeat elevated cholesterol level 3 months later. A parent of each child with a positive screening result was considered to have a positive screening result if he or she had the same mutation as the child or, if no mutations were identified, had the higher cholesterol level of the two parents.
cards.result: The use of a prespecified cholesterol cutoff value of 1.53 multiples of the median (MoM, corresponding to a percentile of 99.2) identified 28 children who had positive screening results for familial hypercholesterolemia (0.3% of the 10,095 children; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.2 to 0.4), including 20 with a familial hypercholesterolemia mutation and 8 with a repeat cholesterol level of at least 1.53 MoM. A total of 17 children who had a cholesterol level of less than 1.53 MoM also had a familial hypercholesterolemia mutation. The overall mutation prevalence was 1 in 273 children (37 in 10,095; 95% CI, 1 in 198 to 1 in 388). The use of an initial cholesterol cutoff value of 1.35 MoM (95th percentile) plus a mutation, or two cholesterol values of at least 1.50 MoM (99th percentile), identified 40 children who had positive screening results for familial hypercholesterolemia (0.4% of the 10,095 children, including 32 children who had a familial hypercholesterolemia mutation and 8 who did not have the mutation) and 40 parents who had positive screening results for familial hypercholesterolemia. The authors concluded that child-parent screening was feasible in primary care practices at routine child immunization visits, and that for every 1000 children screened, 8 persons (4 children and 4 parents) were identified as having positive screening results for familial hypercholesterolemia and were consequently at high risk for cardiovascular disease.
cards.watchOut: This is a screening-yield and feasibility study, not a randomised outcomes trial: there was no usual-practice comparison group, so the record cannot show that child–parent screening identifies cases better than usual practice head-to-head — it shows the absolute yield of the strategy as delivered. No cardiovascular events, treatments started, or deaths were measured, so no outcome benefit can be claimed from this record. The yield also depends on the cutoff strategy chosen (28 children at the prespecified 1.53 MoM cutoff versus 40 at the 1.35 MoM strategy), and cholesterol alone misses mutation carriers: 17 children below the 1.53 MoM cutoff also had a familial hypercholesterolemia mutation. The fetched record carries no registry ID, and none is printed on this shelf.
cards.source: Wald DS et al. Child-Parent Familial Hypercholesterolemia Screening in Primary Care. N Engl J Med. 2016. PMID: 27783906. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large prospective study — a directly measured yield of 8 persons per 1,000 children screened, feasible at immunisation visits, with outcomes and any usual-practice comparison untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large prospective study — a directly measured yield of 8 persons per 1,000 children screened, feasible at immunisation visits, with outcomes and any usual-practice comparison untested
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One prospective screening efficacy and feasibility study of 10,095 children aged 1 to 2 years at routine immunization visits in primary care (Wald 2016), testing the child first (capillary cholesterol plus familial hypercholesterolemia mutation testing) and then the parents of screen-positive children.
cards.result: Positive screening results: 28 children (0.3%; 95% CI, 0.2 to 0.4) at the prespecified 1.53 MoM cholesterol cutoff; 40 children (0.4%) and 40 parents under the 1.35 MoM strategy. Mutation prevalence: 1 in 273 children (37 in 10,095; 95% CI, 1 in 198 to 1 in 388). Yield: 8 persons (4 children and 4 parents) identified per 1000 children screened. Cardiovascular outcomes and any comparison with usual practice: no data in the carded study. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), for identification yield only.
cards.watchOut: Re-card declaration: Wald DS et al. (PMID: 27783906) is also carded as a supporting card on live shelf #476 (Cascade screening for familial hypercholesterolemia), where it serves inside the cascade-screening question — testing the relatives of people already known to have FH. This shelf asks the child–parent question — at routine childhood immunisation visits, does screening the child first and then the parents identify new FH cases — a different screening strategy (child-first at immunisation visits, versus cascade testing outward from a known case) and a genuinely different question, built under the Nov 15 #3104 (RACING) precedent line, as applied at #3325 (STRENGTH), #3489 (CAROLINA), #3597, #3628, #3753, #3812, #3833, #3921, #3881, #3886, #3942 and #3987: a study carded elsewhere as a supporting card may anchor a new shelf when the new question is genuinely different. Tier C is set because a single study carries the shelf and the claim is a screening-yield claim; the shelf claims identification only and expressly does not claim improved cardiovascular outcomes.

shelves.title: After direct-to-consumer genomic testing (PGen): vegetable intake rose 0.11 servings a day and strength exercise 0.14 days a week — changes unrelated to the genetic results themselves
shelves.question: After direct-to-consumer personal genomic testing, do people change diet, exercise, screening, or other health behaviours — and do they share results with clinicians?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Diet · Direct-To-Consumer Screening and Testing/psychology · Exercise · Female · Genetic Testing · Genomics · Health Knowledge, Attitudes, Practice · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Surveys and Questionnaires · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — tiny average behaviour changes, driven by the experience of testing rather than by what the results said. In the PGen cohort (Nielsen 2017, PMID: 28464943; 1,002 participants with 6-month follow-up), vegetable intake rose by 0.11 servings/day (95% CI 0.05 to 0.17; P = 0.0003) and strength exercise by 0.14 days/week (0.03 to 0.25; P = 0.0153), with larger gains confined to participants who rated their health poorly at baseline; genetic results were not consistently associated with any change. On sharing and clinical contact (Carere 2017, PMID: 27657683), 5.6% (54/961) reported changing or starting a prescription medication because of their results, and 83.3% of those consulted a health-care provider first — fewer than 1% reported unsupervised changes. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): testing is followed by small, mostly healthy shifts and usually clinician-mediated medication changes, but nothing here shows the genomic information itself caused them. Tier C is set: observational survey evidence.

cards.headline: PGen (Nielsen 2017): vegetable intake +0.11 servings/day and strength exercise +0.14 days/week at 6 months; genetic results not consistently associated with change
cards.summary: PGen (Nielsen 2017): vegetable intake +0.11 servings/day and strength exercise +0.14 days/week at 6 months; genetic results not consistently associated with change
cards.type: Prospective cohort survey study (Nielsen 2017, Impact of Personal Genomics Study)
cards.people: 1,002 customers of two direct-to-consumer genomic testing companies with longitudinal survey data before receiving results and 6 months after, assessing fruit and vegetable intake and light, vigorous and strength exercise frequency.
cards.result: Significant increases were observed for vegetable intake (mean change 0.11 servings/day; 95% confidence interval 0.05 to 0.17; P = 0.0003) and strength exercise (0.14 days/week; 0.03 to 0.25; P = 0.0153). Among participants with lower self-rated health, all outcomes improved (fruit +0.11, vegetables +0.16, light exercise +0.25, vigorous +0.23, strength +0.19); among those with higher self-rated health only light exercise changed, and it fell (−0.25). Genetic results were not consistently associated with any diet or exercise change.
cards.watchOut: Self-selected, motivated testing customers reporting their own behaviour with no untested control group — expectation, regression to the mean and the act of enrolling in a study can all produce changes of this size; the absolute changes (about one extra vegetable serving every nine days) are trivial at individual level.
cards.source: Nielsen DE et al. Diet and exercise changes following direct-to-consumer personal genomic testing. BMC Medical Genomics. 2017. PMID: 28464943. cards.headline: PGen (Carere 2017): 5.6% changed a prescription medication after testing; 83.3% of them consulted a clinician; each atypical pharmacogenomic result raised the odds of a change 1.57-fold
cards.summary: PGen (Carere 2017): 5.6% changed a prescription medication after testing; 83.3% of them consulted a clinician; each atypical pharmacogenomic result raised the odds of a change 1.57-fold
cards.type: Prospective cohort survey study (Carere 2017, Impact of Personal Genomics Study)
cards.people: 961 direct-to-consumer testing customers with follow-up surveys at 6 months linked to their pharmacogenomic results; 875 (91.2%) received at least one 'atypical response' pharmacogenomic result (indicating altered risk of an adverse drug event or of therapeutic benefit).
cards.result: 54 participants (5.6%) reported changing a medication they were taking or starting a new one because of their results; 45 of these (83.3%) reported consulting a health-care provider about the change, and fewer than 1% of consumers reported unsupervised changes. For each atypical-response result received, the odds of reporting a prescription medication change increased 1.57 times (95% confidence interval 1.17 to 2.11).
cards.watchOut: Medication changes are self-reported and not verified against records, and 'consulted a provider' is not the same as the change being clinically appropriate; the study cannot show whether these changes helped or harmed.
cards.source: Carere DA et al. Prescription medication changes following direct-to-consumer personal genomic testing: findings from the Impact of Personal Genomics (PGen) Study. Genetics in Medicine. 2017. PMID: 27657683. shelves.title: Whole-genome sequencing in healthy primary-care patients (MedSeq): new clinical actions for 34% versus 16% — behaviour change no different (41% versus 30%), and 2 of 11 flagged results judged inappropriately managed
shelves.question: In healthy adults in primary care, does whole-genome sequencing added to standard care find clinically useful results and change management versus standard care alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Asymptomatic Diseases · Female · Health Behavior · Health Care Costs · Humans · Male · Medical History Taking · Middle Aged · Patient Acceptance of Health Care · Patient Reported Outcome Measures · Pilot Projects · Primary Health Care/methods · Referral and Consultation/economics · Risk Assessment · Whole Genome Sequencing
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — sequencing changed what doctors did; whether patients were better off is unknown. In the MedSeq pilot trial (Vassy 2017, PMID: 28654958), 100 generally healthy patients aged 40–65 were randomised to family-history assessment alone or family history plus an interpreted whole-genome report. Eleven of 50 sequenced patients (22%) had new monogenic disease-risk results, but only 2 (4%) had any evidence of the predicted phenotype. Physicians recommended new clinical actions for 34% of sequenced patients versus 16% of controls, while reported health-behaviour change at 6 months was 41% versus 30% — not a significant difference at this size. A clinician-geneticist panel rated management of 8 of 11 results (73%) appropriate and 2 (18%) inappropriate. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): whole-genome sequencing in healthy adults generates findings and extra clinical actions of uncertain value. Tier C is set: a single small pilot trial.

cards.headline: MedSeq: monogenic results in 22% of sequenced patients but phenotypes in only 4%; new actions recommended for 34% versus 16%; behaviour change 41% versus 30%
cards.summary: MedSeq: monogenic results in 22% of sequenced patients but phenotypes in only 4%; new actions recommended for 34% versus 16%; behaviour change 41% versus 30%
cards.type: Pilot randomised trial (Vassy 2017, MedSeq Project)
cards.people: 100 generally healthy patients aged 40 to 65 years cared for by 9 primary care physicians at academic practices, randomised to a family-history report alone or family history plus an interpreted whole-genome sequencing report (monogenic disease risk, carrier variants, pharmacogenomic associations and polygenic risk estimates), discussed with their physician; clinical outcomes and health-care use were followed for 6 months.
cards.result: Eleven sequenced patients (22%; 95% confidence interval 12% to 36%) had new monogenic disease-risk results, of whom only 2 (4%; 0.01% to 15%) had evidence of the predicted phenotypes. Physicians recommended new clinical actions for 34% (22% to 49%) of sequenced patients versus 16% (8% to 30%) of family-history-only patients. Health-behaviour change at 6 months was reported by 41% (27% to 56%) versus 30% (17% to 45%). Geneticists rated management of 8 monogenic results (73%; 39% to 99%) appropriate and 2 (18%; 3% to 52%) inappropriate.
cards.watchOut: A pilot of 100 patients at academic practices with limited ancestral and socioeconomic diversity — every interval here is wide, no clinical outcome (disease prevented, harm caused, cost) was or could be measured, and 'more actions' counts cascades of uncertain value as activity, not benefit.
cards.source: Vassy JL et al. The Impact of Whole-Genome Sequencing on the Primary Care and Outcomes of Healthy Adult Patients: A Pilot Randomized Trial. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2017. PMID: 28654958. Registry ID: NCT01736566. pilot randomised trial (vassy 2017, medseq project) 100 generally healthy patients aged 40 to 65 years cared for by 9 primary care physicians at academic practices, randomised to a family-history report alone or family history plus an interpreted whole-genome sequencing report (monogenic disease risk, carrier variants, pharmacogenomic associations and polygenic risk estimates), discussed with their physician; clinical outcomes and health-care use were followed for 6 months. eleven sequenced patients (22%; 95% confidence interval 12% to 36%) had new monogenic disease-risk results, of whom only 2 (4%; 0.01% to 15%) had evidence of the predicted phenotypes. physicians recommended new clinical actions for 34% (22% to 49%) of sequenced patients versus 16% (8% to 30%) of family-history-only patients. health-behaviour change at 6 months was reported by 41% (27% to 56%) versus 30% (17% to 45%). geneticists rated management of 8 monogenic results (73%; 39% to 99%) appropriate and 2 (18%; 3% to 52%) inappropriate. a pilot of 100 patients at academic practices with limited ancestral and socioeconomic diversity — every interval here is wide, no clinical outcome (disease prevented, harm caused, cost) was or could be measured, and 'more actions' counts cascades of uncertain value as activity, not benefit. vassy jl et al. the impact of whole-genome sequencing on the primary care and outcomes of healthy adult patients: a pilot randomized trial. annals of internal medicine. 2017. pmid: 28654958. registry id: nct01736566. mesh: adult · aged · asymptomatic diseases · female · health behavior · health care costs · humans · male · medical history taking · middle aged · patient acceptance of health care · patient reported outcome measures · pilot projects · primary health care/methods · referral and consultation/economics · risk assessment · whole genome sequencing
