shelves.title: Thrombophilia testing after a first clot: recurrence hazard ratios of 0.6–1.8 for every laboratory defect — while being male (2.7×) and having an unprovoked event (HR 1.9) actually predicted recurrence
shelves.question: In patients with a first unprovoked venous thromboembolism, does testing for inherited thrombophilia (factor V Leiden and the prothrombin G20210A mutation) change management or prevent recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anticoagulants/therapeutic use · Blood Coagulation Factors/analysis · Contraceptives, Oral · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Proportional Hazards Models · Recurrence · Risk Factors · Thrombophilia/blood/physiopathology · Venous Thrombosis/blood/epidemiology/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the laboratory results do not predict the outcome they are ordered to predict. In the Leiden follow-up cohort (Christiansen 2005, PMID: 15900005), 474 patients after a first thrombotic event were followed a mean 7.3 years; recurrence risks by laboratory abnormality ran from a hazard ratio of 0.6 (95% CI 0.3 to 1.1) for elevated factor XI to 1.8 (0.9 to 3.7) for anticoagulant deficiencies — none significant — while male sex (2.7 times the risk) and an unprovoked first event (HR 1.9, 1.2 to 2.9) did predict recurrence. In patients on warfarin (Kearon 2008, PMID: 18791166), factor V Leiden carried a recurrence hazard ratio of 0.7 (0.2 to 2.6), the prothrombin mutation 0, and one or more defects together 0.7 (0.2 to 2.3) — testing could not identify who needed stronger or longer treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): inherited-thrombophilia results after a first unprovoked clot do not usefully stratify recurrence risk, so basing anticoagulation duration on them is unsupported. Tier C is set: observational and secondary-analysis evidence.

cards.headline: Christiansen 2005: recurrence 25.9 per 1,000 patient-years; laboratory defects HR 0.6–1.8 (all non-significant) versus male sex 2.7× and unprovoked event HR 1.9
cards.summary: Christiansen 2005: recurrence 25.9 per 1,000 patient-years; laboratory defects HR 0.6–1.8 (all non-significant) versus male sex 2.7× and unprovoked event HR 1.9
cards.type: Prospective follow-up cohort (Christiansen 2005, Leiden Thrombophilia Study)
cards.people: 474 consecutive patients aged 18 to 70 without known malignancy, treated at Dutch anticoagulation clinics for a first objectively confirmed thrombotic event (enrolled 1988–1992) and followed through 2000 for a mean of 7.3 years, with 94% complete follow-up and 3,477 patient-years observed.
cards.result: Recurrence occurred in 90 patients — 25.9 per 1,000 patient-years (95% confidence interval 20.8 to 31.8), highest in the first 2 years (31.9 per 1,000). Recurrence risk was 2.7 times higher in men than women (1.8 to 4.2) and higher after an unprovoked than a provoked first event (hazard ratio 1.9; 1.2 to 2.9). By laboratory abnormality, hazard ratios ranged from 0.6 (0.3 to 1.1) for elevated factor XI to 1.8 (0.9 to 3.7) for anticoagulant deficiencies. The authors concluded prothrombotic abnormalities do not appear to play an important role in recurrence risk and testing has little consequence for prophylactic strategies.
cards.watchOut: An observational cohort from the pre-DOAC era in which anticoagulation duration was not randomised by test result — it shows the results do not predict recurrence, which is the premise any testing-guided management strategy would need; a formal trial of test-guided duration would be the direct test and is not carded here.
cards.source: Christiansen SC et al. Thrombophilia, clinical factors, and recurrent venous thrombotic events. JAMA. 2005. PMID: 15900005. cards.headline: Kearon 2008: on warfarin, recurrence was not increased by factor V Leiden (HR 0.7), the prothrombin mutation (HR 0), or any combination of defects (HR 0.7)
cards.summary: Kearon 2008: on warfarin, recurrence was not increased by factor V Leiden (HR 0.7), the prothrombin mutation (HR 0), or any combination of defects (HR 0.7)
cards.type: Thrombophilia analysis within a randomised trial cohort (Kearon 2008)
cards.people: 661 patients with unprovoked venous thromboembolism randomised to extended low-intensity (INR 1.5–1.9) or conventional-intensity (INR 2.0–3.0) warfarin, tested for thrombophilia and followed a mean of 2.3 years; one or more thrombophilic defects were present in 42%.
cards.result: The overall recurrence rate on warfarin was 0.9% per patient-year. Recurrence was not increased with factor V Leiden (hazard ratio 0.7; 95% confidence interval 0.2 to 2.6), the prothrombin 20210G>A mutation (HR 0), antithrombin deficiency (HR 0), elevated factor VIII (HR 0.7), elevated factor XI (HR 0.7) or elevated homocysteine (HR 0.7); only antiphospholipid antibody showed a trend (HR 2.9; 0.8 to 10.5). Versus no defects, recurrence was not increased with one defect (HR 0.7; 0.2 to 2.3) or more than one (HR 0.7; 0.2 to 3.4).
cards.watchOut: Event rates on treatment were low (0.9% per year), so intervals are wide and a modest effect cannot be excluded for every defect; antiphospholipid syndrome — an acquired, not inherited, thrombophilia — is the exception that trended the other way and is managed differently.
cards.source: Kearon C et al. Influence of thrombophilia on risk of recurrent venous thromboembolism while on warfarin: results from a randomized trial. Blood. 2008. PMID: 18791166. shelves.title: Genetic-risk disclosure in MI-GENES: statins started by 39% versus 22% and LDL cholesterol 96.5 versus 105.9 mg/dL at 6 months — a prescribing effect in one small trial, with no heart outcomes tested
shelves.question: Does disclosing a genetic (polygenic) risk score for coronary heart disease change statin use and LDL cholesterol versus conventional risk disclosure?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anxiety/epidemiology · Cholesterol, LDL/*blood · Comorbidity · Coronary Disease/blood/epidemiology/*genetics/psychology · Decision Making · Dietary Fats · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Genetic Counseling · Genetic Predisposition to Disease · Genotype · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Minnesota/epidemiology · Motor Activity · Patient Participation · Physician-Patient Relations · Polymorphism, Single Nucleotide · Probability · Risk Assessment · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for prescribing and a cholesterol number, not for heart outcomes. In MI-GENES (Kullo IJ et al., PMID: 26915630), 203 people aged 45–65 years at intermediate risk for coronary heart disease and not on statins were randomly assigned to receive their 10-year probability of coronary heart disease based either on a conventional risk score alone (n=100) or on the conventional score plus a genetic risk score (n=103); risk was disclosed by a genetic counselor followed by shared decision making regarding statin therapy with a physician. At 6 months the genetic-score group had a lower LDL cholesterol than the conventional group (96.5±32.7 versus 105.9±33.3 mg/dL; P=0.04), a difference of 9.4 mg/dL, and statins had been initiated more often in the genetic-score group (39% versus 22%, P<0.01). The LDL difference was concentrated in participants with a high genetic risk score (92.3±32.9 mg/dL; P=0.02 versus the conventional group), while participants with an average/low genetic risk score did not differ significantly (100.9±32.2 mg/dL; P=0.18). No significant differences in dietary fat intake or physical activity levels were noted, so the LDL effect ran through statin prescribing, not through lifestyle change. The trial measured no heart attacks, strokes, or deaths, and this shelf claims behaviour and LDL effects only — no outcome benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in one small randomised trial, disclosing coronary risk that incorporated a genetic risk score led to more statin initiation and a modestly lower LDL cholesterol at 6 months than conventional risk disclosure alone.

cards.headline: Kullo 2016 (MI-GENES): LDL cholesterol at 6 months 96.5 mg/dL with genetic-risk disclosure versus 105.9 mg/dL with conventional disclosure (P=0.04) — statins initiated by 39% versus 22% (P<0.01)
cards.summary: Kullo 2016 (MI-GENES): LDL cholesterol at 6 months 96.5 mg/dL with genetic-risk disclosure versus 105.9 mg/dL with conventional disclosure (P=0.04) — statins initiated by 39% versus 22% (P<0.01)
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (Kullo 2016, MI-GENES)
cards.people: 203 participants (mean age 59.4±5 years; 48% men; mean 10-year coronary heart disease risk 8.5±4.1%), aged 45–65 years, at intermediate risk for coronary heart disease and not on statins, randomly assigned to receive their 10-year probability of coronary heart disease based either on a conventional risk score (CRS, n=100) or on CRS plus a genetic risk score ((+)GRS, n=103). Participants in the (+)GRS group were stratified as having high or average/low GRS. Risk was disclosed by a genetic counselor followed by shared decision making regarding statin therapy with a physician, and the primary end point was LDL cholesterol levels at 6 months.
cards.result: At the end of the study period, the (+)GRS group had a lower LDL cholesterol than the CRS group (96.5±32.7 versus 105.9±33.3 mg/dL; P=0.04), a difference of 9.4 mg/dL. Participants with high GRS had lower LDL cholesterol levels (92.3±32.9 mg/dL) than CRS participants (P=0.02) but participants with average/low GRS did not differ significantly (100.9±32.2 mg/dL; P=0.18). Statins were initiated more often in the (+)GRS group than in the CRS group (39% versus 22%, P<0.01), the absolute rates printed alongside. No significant differences in dietary fat intake and physical activity levels were noted. The authors concluded that disclosure of coronary heart disease risk estimates that incorporated genetic risk information led to lower LDL cholesterol levels than disclosure of risk based on conventional risk factors alone.
cards.watchOut: One small single-centre trial (n=203) with a surrogate primary endpoint — LDL cholesterol at 6 months — and a borderline P value (P=0.04); the LDL difference was driven by the high-genetic-risk subgroup, while the average/low subgroup showed no significant difference (P=0.18). The mechanism was prescribing, not behaviour: statin initiation rose, dietary fat intake and physical activity did not change. Disclosure was delivered by a genetic counselor with physician shared decision making, an intensive format that routine disclosure may not reproduce. No heart attacks, strokes, or deaths were measured, so nothing here shows that genetic-risk disclosure prevents events.
cards.source: Kullo IJ et al. Incorporating a Genetic Risk Score Into Coronary Heart Disease Risk Estimates: Effect on Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol Levels (the MI-GENES Clinical Trial). Circulation. 2016. PMID: 26915630. Registry ID: NCT01936675. cards.headline: Synthesis: one small randomised trial — genetic-risk disclosure moved statin prescribing and LDL at 6 months, through prescribing rather than lifestyle, with no outcome evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small randomised trial — genetic-risk disclosure moved statin prescribing and LDL at 6 months, through prescribing rather than lifestyle, with no outcome evidence
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One randomised clinical trial of 203 adults aged 45–65 years at intermediate coronary heart disease risk and not on statins (MI-GENES), comparing disclosure of a conventional risk score plus a genetic risk score (n=103) against a conventional risk score alone (n=100), with risk disclosed by a genetic counselor followed by shared decision making with a physician and follow-up to 6 months.
cards.result: LDL cholesterol at 6 months: 96.5±32.7 mg/dL with genetic-risk disclosure versus 105.9±33.3 mg/dL with conventional disclosure (P=0.04), a difference of 9.4 mg/dL; high genetic risk score subgroup 92.3±32.9 mg/dL (P=0.02 versus conventional), average/low subgroup 100.9±32.2 mg/dL (P=0.18). Statin initiation: 39% versus 22% (P<0.01). Dietary fat intake and physical activity: no significant differences. Heart attacks, strokes, and deaths: not measured. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Re-card declaration: MI-GENES (Kullo IJ et al., PMID: 26915630) is also carded as a supporting card on live shelf #440, which asks the broad question “Do polygenic risk scores improve prediction or prevention enough to belong in clinical care?” This shelf asks MI-GENES' exact trial question — whether disclosing a genetic (polygenic) risk score for coronary heart disease changes statin use and LDL cholesterol versus conventional risk disclosure — a genuinely different, narrower question, built under the Nov 15 #3104 (RACING) precedent, as applied at #3325 (STRENGTH), #3489 (CAROLINA), and #3597 (PROPATRIA): a study carded elsewhere as a supporting card may anchor a new shelf when the new question is genuinely different. Cross-point: for whether polygenic scores belong in clinical care at all — prediction increment, ancestry transport, and the absence of outcome evidence — see live shelf #440; this shelf claims behaviour and LDL effects only and no outcome benefit. Tier C is set because a single trial carries the shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kullo IJ et al. Circulation. 2016 (PMID: 26915630).

shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1093, which homes the primary phase 3 report of setmelanotide in POMC/LEPR deficiency; that report is cross-pointed here, not re-carded, and this shelf homes the placebo-comparison question it cannot answer. The honest answer is that the 'versus placebo' comparison does not exist: every POMC report in the records fetched is single-arm and open-label, with no placebo group at any point. What the free reports add is corroboration around that gap. A 2023 review of the phase 3 programme (Trapp 2023) records that 10 participants with POMC/PCSK1 deficiency were enrolled and 80% of POMC participants achieved at least 10% weight loss at 1 year. The natural-history analysis (Wabitsch 2022) shows the untreated trajectory these patients were on — above the 95th weight percentile throughout childhood with continuous gain and no long-term loss from diet, surgery or exercise — and that setmelanotide attenuated the trajectory over 1 year (POMC n = 8 of 17 analysed). Quality-of-life data from the two phase 3 trials (Kühnen 2022) show impaired baseline quality of life improving on treatment in most adults assessed. The trials also enrolled children and adolescents, so the evidence is not adults-only, and the total POMC evidence base is the pivotal cohort of 10 — both limits are printed on the stamp. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm evidence only, total N = 10 with POMC deficiency: substantial weight loss occurred on treatment against a documented history of continuous gain, but with no placebo-controlled trial the size of any placebo-adjusted effect is unknown.

cards.headline: Trapp 2023: in the open-label phase 3 POMC trial, 80% of POMC participants achieved at least 10% weight loss at 1 year — from a cohort of 10 POMC/PCSK1 participants, with no placebo group (cohort N on the face)
cards.summary: Trapp 2023: in the open-label phase 3 POMC trial, 80% of POMC participants achieved at least 10% weight loss at 1 year — from a cohort of 10 POMC/PCSK1 participants, with no placebo group (cohort N on the face)
cards.type: Review of the phase 3 programme (Trapp 2023)
cards.people: Participants in open-label phase 3 trials of setmelanotide enrolled February 2017 to September 2018 at 10 centres: 10 participants with proopiomelanocortin (POMC)/proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 1 (PCSK1) deficiency and 11 with leptin receptor (LEPR) deficiency, spanning adults and children aged 6 years and over. This card is a review's summary of that programme; the programme's primary report is homed on live shelf #1093 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: 80% of POMC participants and 45% of LEPR participants achieved at least 10% weight loss at 1 year. Significant changes in hunger scores were seen for both cohorts. Setmelanotide was well tolerated, with injection site reactions and hyperpigmentation the most common adverse events. On the basis of these single-arm data the drug was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration in 2020 for chronic weight management in adult and pediatric patients 6 years of age and older with POMC, LEPR or PCSK1 deficiency. The record reports no placebo comparison and no mean weight-change figure for the POMC cohort.
cards.watchOut: A responder proportion (80% reaching 10% loss) in 10 uncontrolled patients cannot separate drug effect from regression to the mean, trial support, or expectancy — and this is a secondary review of the trials, carded because the primary report is homed on shelf #1093; the shelf's claim rests on the single-arm design being all that exists, not on this summary being strong evidence.
cards.source: Trapp CM et al. Setmelanotide: a promising advancement for pediatric patients with rare forms of genetic obesity. Current Opinion in Endocrinology, Diabetes and Obesity. 2023. PMID: 36722447. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wabitsch 2022: before treatment, patients with POMC deficiency gained weight continuously and did not lose long-term with diet, surgery or exercise; on setmelanotide the weight trajectory was attenuated over 1 year (POMC n = 8 of 17 analysed — subgroup N on the face)
cards.summary: Wabitsch 2022: before treatment, patients with POMC deficiency gained weight continuously and did not lose long-term with diet, surgery or exercise; on setmelanotide the weight trajectory was attenuated over 1 year (POMC n = 8 of 17 analysed — subgroup N on the face)
cards.type: Natural-history and on-treatment trajectory analysis (Wabitsch 2022)
cards.people: 17 patients with historical weight and height data from the two pivotal single-arm, open-label phase 3 trials of setmelanotide: POMC n = 8, PCSK1 n = 1, LEPR n = 8. Historical measured weight and height were obtained at screening to reconstruct each patient's pre-treatment trajectory; there was no concurrent control group.
cards.result: Before setmelanotide treatment, patients with obesity due to POMC/PCSK1 or LEPR deficiency were above the 95th percentile for weight throughout childhood, demonstrated continuous weight gain, and did not show long-term weight loss upon interventions such as diet, surgery or exercise. Setmelanotide treatment attenuated weight and body mass index trajectories over the observation period of 1 year. The record reports no numerical weight-change values, so none are printed here. The authors conclude traditional interventions had limited impact on this obesity, while setmelanotide attenuated trajectories and led to weight loss in most individuals.
cards.watchOut: Each patient is their own historical control: trajectories can flatten with age, puberty or trial participation itself, and with only 8 POMC patients and no numbers in the record this card supports the direction of the programme's findings, not a quantified effect.
cards.source: Wabitsch M et al. Natural History of Obesity Due to POMC, PCSK1, and LEPR Deficiency and the Impact of Setmelanotide. Journal of the Endocrine Society. 2022. PMID: 35528826. Registry ID: NCT02896192 and NCT03287960 (as printed in the record). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Kühnen 2022: quality of life was impaired at baseline in the phase 3 POMC/LEPR trials and improved on setmelanotide in most adults assessed (5 of 6 adults with week-52 scores had a clinically meaningful improvement, +24.2 points on average) — supportive, not weight, evidence
cards.summary: Kühnen 2022: quality of life was impaired at baseline in the phase 3 POMC/LEPR trials and improved on setmelanotide in most adults assessed (5 of 6 adults with week-52 scores had a clinically meaningful improvement, +24.2 points on average) — supportive, not weight, evidence
cards.type: Quality-of-life outcomes report of two phase 3 trials (Kühnen 2022)
cards.people: The two pivotal phase 3 trials of setmelanotide in obesity due to POMC deficiency or LEPR deficiency, enrolling 21 patients in total (both trials combined); quality of life was assessed in adults (n = 7) with the Impact of Weight on Quality of Life-Lite and in children and adolescents with the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory, alongside depression scores. The record does not separate the POMC-only quality-of-life results.
cards.result: Adults had moderate-to-severe impairment at baseline (mean Impact of Weight on Quality of Life-Lite total score 60.3 of 100). Improvement was observed as early as week 5; among adults with week-52 scores, 5 of 6 experienced a clinically meaningful improvement, with mean total scores up from baseline by 24.2 (standard deviation 12.1) points. In children and adolescents, 3 of 5 with scores experienced clinically meaningful improvement. Baseline depression scores (mean Patient Health Questionnaire-9 5.3 in those 12 and over) were generally maintained. The authors suggest the quality-of-life gains may relate to reduced hunger and body weight on treatment.
cards.watchOut: Quality of life in an open-label trial is the outcome most exposed to expectancy effects, the POMC and LEPR cohorts are pooled, and only 6 adults had week-52 scores — this card corroborates that patients felt better on treatment; it is not evidence about weight versus placebo.
cards.source: Kühnen P et al. Quality of life outcomes in two phase 3 trials of setmelanotide in patients with obesity due to LEPR or POMC deficiency. Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases. 2022. PMID: 35123544. Registry ID: NCT02896192 and NCT03287960 (as printed in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: setmelanotide produced large weight loss in the single-arm POMC programme (80% of 10 participants lost at least 10% at 1 year) against a documented natural history of continuous gain — but no placebo-controlled trial exists, so 'versus placebo' is unanswerable as posed
cards.summary: Synthesis: setmelanotide produced large weight loss in the single-arm POMC programme (80% of 10 participants lost at least 10% at 1 year) against a documented natural history of continuous gain — but no placebo-controlled trial exists, so 'versus placebo' is unanswerable as posed
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: a review summarising the phase 3 programme (POMC/PCSK1 cohort n = 10; LEPR n = 11), a natural-history trajectory analysis (17 patients; POMC n = 8), and the trials' quality-of-life report (21 patients, both trials). Unique participants with POMC deficiency across the programme total 10 — the pivotal cohort — and the stamp carries that N. The primary phase 3 report is homed on live shelf #1093 and cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.result: On treatment, 80% of POMC participants achieved at least 10% weight loss at 1 year (Trapp 2023); pre-treatment trajectories showed continuous gain without long-term loss from diet, surgery or exercise, and trajectories attenuated on treatment (Wabitsch 2022); quality of life improved in most assessed patients (Kühnen 2022). No carded or fetched record contains a placebo arm. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm evidence only, total N = 10 with POMC deficiency.
cards.watchOut: The population also fails the question's frame in a second way: the trials enrolled patients from age 6, not adults only, and the record set contains no adults-only POMC analysis — the shelf answers for POMC deficiency obesity as studied, and flags both the missing placebo and the mixed ages rather than smoothing either over.
cards.source: Synthesis of Trapp CM et al. Current Opinion in Endocrinology, Diabetes and Obesity. 2023 (PMID: 36722447); Wabitsch M et al. Journal of the Endocrine Society. 2022 (PMID: 35528826); Kühnen P et al. Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases. 2022 (PMID: 35123544).

shelves.title: Cascade screening for familial hypercholesterolemia — the treatment-uptake slice (PARTIAL completion of live #476): identified relatives start treatment (39% to 93% in the Dutch programme), but routine care still leaves most below target
shelves.question: Does cascade screening for familial hypercholesterolemia improve early treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adult · DNA Mutational Analysis · Female · Humans · Hyperlipoproteinemia Type II · Male · Mass Screening · Middle Aged · Netherlands · ROC Curve · Receptors, LDL · Retrospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (observational) — this pack is a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #476, which already homes cascade identification (Wald child–parent screening; the CATCH randomised programme trial) and the absence of cardiovascular-outcome evidence. The slice built here is the middle link #476 leaves open: once relatives are identified, do they actually start treatment early? The Dutch national programme's first-five-years report is the anchor: among 2,039 relatives identified as heterozygotes, the share receiving lipid-lowering treatment rose from 39% at identification to 93% one year later (Umans-Eckenhausen 2001). A Turkish paediatric cascade series shows the same mechanism in miniature — screening children led to statins being started in 18 previously undiagnosed parents and 7 siblings (Kose 2020). The counterweight is a 2023 UK health-technology assessment: in linked primary–secondary care data, 70% of people coded with familial hypercholesterolemia did not achieve target treatment levels, so identification alone does not guarantee adequate treatment (Qureshi 2023). Every report here is observational or programme data — no trial has randomised relatives to cascade identification versus not and measured treatment — so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational. Whether earlier treatment started this way prevents heart attacks remains the unproven inference fenced on #476.

cards.headline: Dutch national cascade programme 2001: relatives identified with familial hypercholesterolemia went from 39% on lipid-lowering treatment at identification to 93% one year later
cards.summary: Dutch national cascade programme 2001: relatives identified with familial hypercholesterolemia went from 39% on lipid-lowering treatment at identification to 93% one year later
cards.type: National screening programme report (retrospective, Netherlands)
cards.people: 5,442 relatives of 237 index patients with a functional LDL-receptor mutation, screened in the first 5 years of the Netherlands national programme (from 1994) by DNA analysis and cholesterol measurement; 2,039 were identified as heterozygotes for familial hypercholesterolemia.
cards.result: At the time of examination, 667 of the identified adults with familial hypercholesterolemia (39%) were receiving some form of lipid-lowering treatment; 1 year later this had risen to 93%. Diagnosis by cholesterol measurement alone (sex- and age-specific 90th percentiles) would have misdiagnosed 18% of carriers and non-carriers, which is why the programme used DNA analysis. The authors conclude most identified patients sought treatment and were successfully started on cholesterol-lowering therapy.
cards.watchOut: A before–after programme figure with no comparison group: some of the rise from 39% to 93% would reflect ordinary clinical follow-up of people told they carry a mutation, and the programme cannot separate the effect of identification itself from the treatment offer that came with it.
cards.source: Umans-Eckenhausen MA et al. Review of first 5 years of screening for familial hypercholesterolaemia in the Netherlands. Lancet (London, England). 2001. PMID: 11213091. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · DNA Mutational Analysis · Female · Humans · Hyperlipoproteinemia Type II · Male · Mass Screening · Middle Aged · Netherlands · ROC Curve · Receptors, LDL · Retrospective Studies

cards.headline: Turkish paediatric cascade series 2020: screening 51 children with familial hypercholesterolemia newly diagnosed 7 parents — and statins were started in 18 parents and 7 siblings
cards.summary: Turkish paediatric cascade series 2020: screening 51 children with familial hypercholesterolemia newly diagnosed 7 parents — and statins were started in 18 parents and 7 siblings
cards.type: Retrospective cascade-screening case series (single clinic, Turkey)
cards.people: 51 children (mean age 9.8 years, all with heterozygous LDLR mutations) diagnosed with familial hypercholesterolemia at a paediatric metabolism clinic in Turkey under the national school-age lipid screening programme begun in 2016, with cascade screening of their families; retrospective evaluation.
cards.result: Cascade screening diagnosed familial hypercholesterolemia in 7 parents (13.7%) who had not previously been diagnosed. After the screening programme, statin treatment was initiated in 18 parents (35.3%) and 7 siblings (16.3%). Among the children themselves, 22 (43.1%) were started on a statin and mean LDL cholesterol fell from 204.1 mg/dL to 137.0 mg/dL; dietary intervention alone lowered LDL cholesterol by 14.5%. Uptake was not universal: parents refused statin treatment for 8 children (15.7%).
cards.watchOut: A small single-clinic retrospective series (51 index children); the treatment-initiation counts for parents and siblings are descriptive, with no comparison against families who were not cascade-screened.
cards.source: Kose E et al. Cascade screening and treatment of children with familial hypercholesterolemia in Turkey. Journal of pediatric endocrinology & metabolism : JPEM. 2020. PMID: 32829317. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: UK health-technology assessment 2023: cascade testing finds relatives, but in linked routine-care data 70% of people with familial hypercholesterolemia did not achieve target treatment levels
cards.summary: UK health-technology assessment 2023: cascade testing finds relatives, but in linked routine-care data 70% of people with familial hypercholesterolemia did not achieve target treatment levels
cards.type: Health technology assessment: systematic reviews and routine-data analyses (UK)
cards.people: Systematic reviews plus three UK data sets analysed for the NIHR assessment of alternative cascade-testing protocols: hospital familial hypercholesterolemia databases (PASS), the Clinical Practice Research Datalink linked to Hospital Episode Statistics, and a specialist familial hypercholesterolemia register.
cards.result: Across 4 of 24 protocol studies, a combined direct-plus-indirect contact approach tested slightly more relatives (40%, 95% CI 37% to 42%) than direct (33%, 95% CI 28% to 39%) or indirect (34%, 95% CI 30% to 37%) approaches alone, and directly contacted relatives were more likely to complete testing (P < 0.01). The CPRD–HES data set indicated that 70% of people with familial hypercholesterolemia did not achieve target treatment levels and carried increased cardiovascular risk versus controls (hazard ratio 9.14, 95% CI 8.55 to 9.76); the specialist register confirmed excessive cardiovascular morbidity (standardised morbidity ratio 7.17, 95% CI 6.79 to 7.56).
cards.watchOut: The 70%-not-at-target figure comes from primary-care coding, and the assessors note only a proportion of coded familial hypercholesterolemia is likely to be true familial hypercholesterolemia, so the treatment gap may be over- or under-stated; it measures treatment adequacy after identification, not whether identification happened.
cards.source: Qureshi N et al. Alternative cascade-testing protocols for identifying and managing patients with familial hypercholesterolaemia: systematic reviews, qualitative study and cost-effectiveness analysis. Health technology assessment (Winchester, England). 2023. PMID: 37924278. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cholesterol · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Cost-Effectiveness Analysis · Hyperlipoproteinemia Type II · Systematic Reviews as Topic

cards.headline: Synthesis: identification reliably converts into treatment starting — 39% to 93% in the Dutch programme — but routine-care data show treatment often stays inadequate, and no trial isolates the cascade step
cards.summary: Synthesis: identification reliably converts into treatment starting — 39% to 93% in the Dutch programme — but routine-care data show treatment often stays inadequate, and no trial isolates the cascade step
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: one national programme report (5,442 relatives screened, 2,039 heterozygotes identified), one paediatric cascade series (51 children and their families), and one UK health-technology assessment drawing on three routine data sets and 24 protocol studies. Total carded participants are in the thousands, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: The Dutch programme shows identified relatives overwhelmingly starting lipid-lowering treatment within a year (39% treated at identification, 93% at one year); the Turkish series shows the same cascade mechanism starting statins in previously undiagnosed parents (35.3%) and siblings (16.3%); the UK assessment confirms relatives are found and tested but finds 70% of identified patients not at treatment targets in routine care. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): cascade screening improves early treatment uptake, on programme and cohort evidence only — the cardiovascular-outcome question stays homed, and unanswered, on live shelf #476.
cards.watchOut: Uptake is not outcome: this shelf deliberately does not claim fewer heart attacks or deaths, because no carded report — here or on #476 — measures them for the screening strategy itself.
cards.source: Synthesis of Umans-Eckenhausen MA et al. Lancet (London, England). 2001 (PMID: 11213091); Kose E et al. Journal of pediatric endocrinology & metabolism : JPEM. 2020 (PMID: 32829317); Qureshi N et al. Health technology assessment (Winchester, England). 2023 (PMID: 37924278).

shelves.title: BRCA testing in women with a strong family history (PARTIAL completion of live #478): testing triggers surveillance, surgery and early-stage detection — but the mortality link for testing itself has never been measured directly
shelves.question: Does genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 in women with a strong family history reduce cancer deaths through earlier intervention?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Breast Neoplasms · Fallopian Tube Neoplasms · Female · Genes, BRCA1 · Genes, BRCA2 · Genetic Counseling · Genetic Testing · Heterozygote · Humans · Middle Aged · Mutation · Ovarian Neoplasms · Ovariectomy · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (observational) — this pack is a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #478, which homes risk-reducing surgery in women already known to carry BRCA mutations; the slice built here is the step before: the testing itself, offered to women because of a strong family history, and whether the chain it starts — identification, intensified surveillance, risk-reducing surgery — reaches cancer deaths. No trial has randomised women to genetic testing versus no testing and counted deaths; the USPSTF evidence review states the chain's benefit is inferred from intervention studies in identified carriers (Nelson 2014). The prospective testing-programme cohort is the closest direct evidence: after testing, surveillance intensified, 29 women chose risk-reducing mastectomy and 90 risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy, the cancers found were early-stage, and no stage III or IV cancer was detected after test results (Scheuer 2002). In European familial surveillance programmes, cancers arising in tested women were mostly detected early, with 5-year survival of 96% in BRCA2 carriers and 92% in mutation-negative women — but only 73% in BRCA1 carriers, whose tumour biology stays aggressive even when found early (Moller 2007). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): testing plausibly reduces cancer deaths through earlier intervention, on cohort evidence for each link and none for the whole chain. Population-wide BRCA testing (a different strategy) is homed on live shelf #808 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Scheuer 2002: after BRCA testing, surveillance intensified, 29 women chose risk-reducing mastectomy and 90 salpingo-oophorectomy — and no stage III or IV cancer was detected after test results
cards.summary: Scheuer 2002: after BRCA testing, surveillance intensified, 29 women chose risk-reducing mastectomy and 90 salpingo-oophorectomy — and no stage III or IV cancer was detected after test results
cards.type: Prospective cohort (single-centre testing programme)
cards.people: 251 individuals with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations identified through genetic counselling and testing at a single comprehensive cancer centre (1995–2000), all at hereditary risk because of family history, given uniform screening and preventive-surgery recommendations and followed for a mean of 24.8 months.
cards.result: Frequency of cancer surveillance by physical examination and imaging increased after genetic counselling and testing. Twenty-one breast, ovarian, primary peritoneal or fallopian tube cancers were detected after receipt of test results: screening detected six breast cancers (five stage 0/I), one early-stage primary peritoneal cancer and three stage I or II ovarian cancers, and physical examination found six further breast cancers between screening intervals (four stage I). Among 29 individuals choosing risk-reducing mastectomy, two occult intraductal breast cancers were found; among 90 undergoing risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy, one early-stage ovarian and one early-stage fallopian tube neoplasm were found. No stage III or stage IV malignancies were detected after genetic testing.
cards.watchOut: Follow-up averaged only about 2 years and there is no untested comparison group: 'no advanced cancers after testing' shows early detection happened, not that deaths were prevented — lead-time alone produces exactly this picture.
cards.source: Scheuer L et al. Outcome of preventive surgery and screening for breast and ovarian cancer in BRCA mutation carriers. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2002. PMID: 11870168. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Moller 2007: in familial surveillance programmes, 5-year survival after breast cancer was 96% for BRCA2 carriers and 92% for mutation-negative women — but 73% for BRCA1 carriers
cards.summary: Moller 2007: in familial surveillance programmes, 5-year survival after breast cancer was 96% for BRCA2 carriers and 92% for mutation-negative women — but 73% for BRCA1 carriers
cards.type: Prospective surveillance-programme cohort (Norway and UK)
cards.people: Women with a family history of breast cancer enrolled in familial breast cancer surveillance programmes at collaborating centres in Norway and the UK, analysed by the mutation status established through testing (BRCA1-positive, BRCA2-positive, or no mutation detected); 442 breast cancers were diagnosed and followed for a total of 2,095 years.
cards.result: Eighty-nine cancers (20%) were in BRCA1 carriers, 35 (8%) in BRCA2 carriers and 318 (72%) in mutation-negative women. Five-year survival was 73% in BRCA1 carriers compared with 96% in BRCA2 carriers and 92% in mutation-negative women (P = 0.000). Among BRCA1 carriers, 5-year survival was 67% for carcinoma in situ, 84% for node-negative invasive cancer and 58% with nodal involvement — early detection did not equalise their outcomes, a difference the authors attribute to tumour biology.
cards.watchOut: There is no unscreened control group, so the good survival in BRCA2 and mutation-negative women cannot be credited to surveillance alone (lead-time and length bias both flatter screen-detected survival); the BRCA1 result is the card's hard core — testing and surveillance do not erase BRCA1 biology.
cards.source: Moller P et al. Surveillance for familial breast cancer: Differences in outcome according to BRCA mutation status. International journal of cancer. 2007. PMID: 17471561. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: USPSTF evidence review 2014: no trial has tested whether BRCA testing itself reduces cancer deaths — the benefit is a chain: testing identifies carriers, and surgery in carriers reduced breast cancer mortality by 81% to 100% in the intervention studies reviewed
cards.summary: USPSTF evidence review 2014: no trial has tested whether BRCA testing itself reduces cancer deaths — the benefit is a chain: testing identifies carriers, and surgery in carriers reduced breast cancer mortality by 81% to 100% in the intervention studies reviewed
cards.type: Systematic review (USPSTF evidence synthesis)
cards.people: Systematic review for the US Preventive Services Task Force of risk assessment, genetic counselling and genetic testing for BRCA-related cancer in women, covering studies from 2004 to July 2013 across MEDLINE, PsycINFO, the Cochrane registers and other databases.
cards.result: No trials evaluated the effectiveness of intensive screening in mutation carriers, and efficacy trials of the testing strategy were lacking. Among high-risk women and mutation carriers, the reviewed intervention studies found risk-reducing mastectomy decreased breast cancer incidence by 85% to 100% and breast cancer mortality by 81% to 100% compared with women without surgery, and risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy decreased breast cancer incidence by 37% to 100%, ovarian cancer by 69% to 100%, and all-cause mortality by 55% to 100%. Harms ran the other way for screening itself: false-positive rates, unneeded imaging and unneeded surgeries were higher with intensive screening.
cards.watchOut: The mortality percentages come from observational intervention studies in already-identified carriers — the very evidence homed on live shelf #478 — so this review documents the chain's plausibility, not an independent demonstration that offering the test saves lives.
cards.source: Nelson HD et al. Risk assessment, genetic counseling, and genetic testing for BRCA-related cancer in women: a systematic review to update the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendation. Annals of internal medicine. 2014. PMID: 24366442. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: testing demonstrably triggers earlier intervention and early-stage detection, but the final link — fewer cancer deaths from testing itself — has never been measured directly — POSSIBLE (observational)
cards.summary: Synthesis: testing demonstrably triggers earlier intervention and early-stage detection, but the final link — fewer cancer deaths from testing itself — has never been measured directly — POSSIBLE (observational)
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: one prospective testing-programme cohort (251 identified carriers), one familial surveillance cohort (442 cancers by mutation status), and one USPSTF systematic review. Total carded participants are in the hundreds for the direct cohorts, with the review spanning the wider literature; no small-N stamp labelling applies to the stamp, but the direct evidence base is cohort-sized, not trial-sized.
cards.result: After testing, surveillance intensified and risk-reducing surgery was taken up (29 mastectomies, 90 salpingo-oophorectomies in Scheuer's cohort), cancers found were early-stage with no stage III/IV disease detected after results, and surveillance-detected cancers carried 5-year survival of 92–96% except in BRCA1 carriers (73%). The USPSTF review confirms no trial of the testing strategy itself exists and that mortality benefit is inferred from intervention effects in carriers. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): genetic testing in women with a strong family history plausibly reduces cancer deaths through earlier intervention, with each link observed and the whole chain untested. Surgery efficacy in known carriers stays homed on live shelf #478; population testing stays homed on live shelf #808.
cards.watchOut: Anyone quoting this shelf as 'testing saves lives' overstates it: the defensible claim is that testing starts a chain whose later links (early detection, risk-reducing surgery) are associated with fewer deaths, while BRCA1 carriers remind us the chain leaks.
cards.source: Synthesis of Scheuer L et al. Journal of clinical oncology. 2002 (PMID: 11870168); Moller P et al. International journal of cancer. 2007 (PMID: 17471561); Nelson HD et al. Annals of internal medicine. 2014 (PMID: 24366442).

shelves.title: Alirocumab in children and adolescents with heterozygous FH: LDL fell 43.3% (every-2-weeks) and 33.8% (every-4-weeks) more than placebo at 24 weeks in the phase 3 trial - a single programme, capped at POSSIBLE
shelves.question: In children and adolescents with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, does alirocumab, compared with placebo on background statin, lower LDL cholesterol safely?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Child · Male · Cholesterol, LDL · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · Hyperlipoproteinemia Type II/drug therapy · Hypercholesterolemia/chemically induced,drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Anticholesteremic Agents/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), single-programme cap. PREMISE VERIFIED: home #1415 is the evolocumab HAUSER-RCT shelf in paediatric heterozygous FH - a different antibody; the tree's other alirocumab packs concern adults (limb events, FH event extrapolation). The alirocumab paediatric programme: ODYSSEY KIDS (phase 2, 42 children aged 8-17) found the higher-dose cohorts lowered LDL cholesterol by 45-46% at week 8. The phase 3 trial (Santos 2024; 153 children aged 8-17 with LDL at least 130 mg/dL on statins or other lipid therapy) found least-squares mean LDL differences against placebo of -43.3% (every-2-weeks dosing) and -33.8% (every-4-weeks dosing) at week 24 (both P<.001), with no significant difference in adverse-event incidence and two discontinuations for adverse events on alirocumab. A 2024 meta-analysis pooling the paediatric PCSK9 trials (320 children in 3 RCTs, evolocumab and alirocumab together) found a weighted mean LDL difference of -37.92% and general tolerability. LDL is a surrogate - appropriately so in FH, where lifetime exposure is the disease mechanism - but long-term paediatric safety beyond the trial horizons is unproven, hence POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Phase 3 trial 2024: alirocumab lowered LDL cholesterol by -43.3% (every 2 weeks) and -33.8% (every 4 weeks) relative to placebo at week 24 in 153 children and adolescents with heterozygous FH
cards.summary: Phase 3 trial 2024: alirocumab lowered LDL cholesterol by -43.3% (every 2 weeks) and -33.8% (every 4 weeks) relative to placebo at week 24 in 153 children and adolescents with heterozygous FH
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Santos 2024) - 153 patients aged 8-17
cards.people: 153 patients aged 8 to 17 years with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia and LDL cholesterol of at least 130 mg/dL despite statins or other lipid-lowering therapy, at 43 centres in 24 countries (mean age 12.9 years; 56.9% female), randomised 2:1 to subcutaneous alirocumab or placebo in every-2-weeks (Q2W) or every-4-weeks (Q4W) cohorts, with weight-based dosing adjusted at week 12 if week-8 LDL remained at least 110 mg/dL; a 24-week double-blind period was followed by an optional 80-week open-label period.
cards.result: At week 24, the least-squares mean difference in percentage LDL change against placebo was -43.3% (97.5% CI -56.0% to -30.7%; P<.001) in the Q2W cohort and -33.8% (97.5% CI -46.4% to -21.2%; P<.001) in the Q4W cohort (percentage-point differences in percent change, as reported). Secondary lipid parameters also improved significantly at weeks 12 and 24. Two patients on alirocumab Q4W had adverse events leading to discontinuation; no significant difference in adverse-event incidence was observed between groups, and open-label findings were consistent with the double-blind period.
cards.watchOut: A 24-week surrogate-endpoint trial: the LDL effect is large and matches the adult programme, but neither cardiovascular outcomes (not feasible in children) nor multi-year growth and development safety are in this record. Dosing was weight-banded with mid-trial adjustment, so the result is for the titration strategy, not a fixed dose.
cards.source: Santos RD et al. Alirocumab in Pediatric Patients With Heterozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA pediatrics. 2024. PMID: 38315470. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03510884, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: ODYSSEY KIDS phase 2 (2020): in 42 children with heterozygous FH, the higher alirocumab dose cohorts lowered LDL cholesterol by -46% and -45% at week 8
cards.summary: ODYSSEY KIDS phase 2 (2020): in 42 children with heterozygous FH, the higher alirocumab dose cohorts lowered LDL cholesterol by -46% and -45% at week 8
cards.type: Phase 2 open-label dose-finding study (ODYSSEY KIDS, 2020) - 42 patients aged 8-17
cards.people: 42 patients aged 8-17 years with heterozygous FH, body weight at least 25 kg and LDL cholesterol at least 130 mg/dL despite optimal statin or other lipid-modifying therapy (mean age 12.4 years; 95% on a statin), enrolled in four weight- and interval-based dose cohorts: 30/50 mg Q2W, 40/75 mg Q2W, 75/150 mg Q4W and 150/300 mg Q4W (lower dose under 50 kg). The primary endpoint was LDL percentage change at week 8.
cards.result: Baseline LDL ranged from 160.0 to 188.9 mg/dL across cohorts. At week 8, the higher-dose cohorts showed the greatest LDL reductions (-46% in cohort 2, Q2W; -45% in cohort 4, Q4W), with free PCSK9 lowest in those cohorts (42.2 and 8.6 ng/mL). Adverse events were reported in 50-90% of patients across cohorts and 2 patients discontinued for adverse events. Alirocumab was generally well tolerated at all doses, and the study selected the doses carried into phase 3.
cards.watchOut: An uncontrolled, open-label dose-finding study with about 10 children per cohort: its percentage reductions have no placebo comparator and its role is dose selection and preliminary tolerability, not proof of efficacy - that comes from the phase 3 card above.

cards.headline: Paediatric PCSK9 meta-analysis 2024: pooled LDL reduction was -37.92% (weighted mean difference) across the evolocumab and alirocumab trials in children with FH, with general tolerability
cards.summary: Paediatric PCSK9 meta-analysis 2024: pooled LDL reduction was -37.92% (weighted mean difference) across the evolocumab and alirocumab trials in children with FH, with general tolerability
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of paediatric PCSK9 inhibitor studies (2024) - 9 unique studies; 3 RCTs with 320 patients (pools evolocumab with alirocumab - flagged)
cards.people: Systematic review of interventional studies of evolocumab or alirocumab in paediatric familial hypercholesterolaemia to July 2024: 14 articles reporting 9 unique studies, including 3 randomised trials with 320 patients in total, one crossover trial and five single-arm or observational studies. This review pools both antibodies - the alirocumab-specific estimates are the two cards above - and is carded as programme-level support, flagged as such.
cards.result: Pooled results showed significant LDL cholesterol reduction (weighted mean difference -37.92%, 95% CI -43.06% to -32.78%; I2=0.0%), apolipoprotein B reduction (-33.67%, 95% CI -38.12% to -29.22%) and lipoprotein(a) reduction (-16.94%, 95% CI -26.20% to -7.69%) - differences in percentage change, as reported. Effects in heterozygous FH were consistent between studies, while homozygous FH responses varied dramatically. The inhibitors were generally well tolerated, in line with adult studies.
cards.watchOut: Pooling two different antibodies means this card cannot be read as an alirocumab estimate; it also inherits the short horizons of its component trials. Its value here is showing the paediatric class effect is consistent and that no safety signal emerges when the small trials are combined.

cards.headline: Synthesis: POSSIBLE (benefit) - alirocumab lowers LDL cholesterol substantially and without a short-term safety signal in children and adolescents with heterozygous FH on background therapy; home #1415 (evolocumab) verified as a different antibody
cards.summary: Synthesis: POSSIBLE (benefit) - alirocumab lowers LDL cholesterol substantially and without a short-term safety signal in children and adolescents with heterozygous FH on background therapy; home #1415 (evolocumab) verified as a different antibody
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence is the alirocumab paediatric programme - ODYSSEY KIDS phase 2 (42 children) and the phase 3 randomised trial (153 children) - plus a 2024 meta-analysis pooling the paediatric PCSK9 trials of both antibodies (320 children in RCTs). Home #1415 was verified this session: it is the evolocumab HAUSER-RCT shelf, so the alirocumab slice was genuinely uncovered.
cards.result: Against placebo on background statin, alirocumab reduced LDL cholesterol by 43.3% (Q2W) and 33.8% (Q4W) more than placebo at 24 weeks in phase 3, consistent with the phase 2 dose-finding reductions of 45-46% at the selected doses and with the pooled class estimate of -37.92%. Adverse-event incidence did not differ significantly from placebo in phase 3; discontinuations for adverse events were few (2 in phase 3, 2 in phase 2). No outcome or long-term developmental data exist in the carded records.
cards.watchOut: Single-programme cap and surrogate endpoint: one sponsor's two-study programme, 24 weeks of blinded treatment. In FH the LDL surrogate carries unusual weight because lifetime exposure drives risk, but the stamp stays POSSIBLE until independent or longer-term paediatric data exist.
cards.source: Synthesis of Santos RD et al. JAMA pediatrics. 2024 (PMID: 38315470, NCT03510884); Daniels S et al. Journal of clinical lipidology. 2020 (PMID: 32331936, NCT02890992); Xiao G et al. Medicina (Kaunas, Lithuania). 2024 (PMID: 39459433). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Taliglucerase alfa in type 1 Gaucher disease (one programme, small N): spleen volume −26.9% / −38.0% relative at 30 / 60 U/kg in 29 adults; switch patients stable
shelves.question: In children and adults with type 1 Gaucher disease, does enzyme replacement with taliglucerase alfa (plant cell-expressed glucocerebrosidase), compared between its own two doses or after switching from imiglucerase, improve haemoglobin, platelet counts and spleen volume?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a small-N rare-disease base, with the counts leading: one programme, three reports. The randomised base is a single dose-comparison trial in which 29 treatment-naïve adults completed the protocol — spleen volume fell −26.9% relative at 30 U/kg and −38.0% relative at 60 U/kg over 9 months, with gains in haemoglobin, liver volume and (at 60 U/kg) platelets — but there was NO placebo or active-comparator arm, so the gains are uncontrolled. A 31-patient open-label switch study (from imiglucerase) and a 15-child extension report show stability / within-group improvement only. Endpoints are haematological and organ-volume surrogates; no fracture, bone-crisis or mortality trial exists. The tested product is named as the publications give it — taliglucerase alfa (Protalix Biotherapeutics, Carmiel, Israel), plant cell-expressed — for clarification, not promotion.

cards.headline: Pivotal dose-comparison phase 3 trial (Zimran 2011): in 29 treatment-naïve adults who completed the protocol, spleen volume fell −26.9% relative (95% CI −31.9 to −21.8) at 30 U/kg and −38.0% relative (95% CI −43.4 to −32.8) at 60 U/kg over 9 months (both P < 0.0001) — no placebo arm
cards.summary: Pivotal dose-comparison phase 3 trial (Zimran 2011): in 29 treatment-naïve adults who completed the protocol, spleen volume fell −26.9% relative (95% CI −31.9 to −21.8) at 30 U/kg and −38.0% relative (95% CI −43.4 to −32.8) at 60 U/kg over 9 months (both P < 0.0001) — no placebo arm
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind dose-comparison trial (30 vs 60 U/kg), no placebo or active-comparator arm, 9 months
cards.people: Treatment-naïve adults with type 1 Gaucher disease, splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia, in a phase 3 double-blind randomised parallel-group dose-comparison trial (taliglucerase alfa 30 vs 60 U/kg per infusion every other week, 20 infusions over 9 months) at 11 centres; 29 patients completed the protocol. The tested product is named as the publication gives it: taliglucerase alfa (Protalix Biotherapeutics, Carmiel, Israel), a plant cell-expressed recombinant human β-glucocerebrosidase.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, reduction in spleen volume by MRI, was statistically significant at 9 months at both doses: −26.9% relative (95% CI −31.9 to −21.8) at 30 U/kg and −38.0% relative (95% CI −43.4 to −32.8) at 60 U/kg (both P < 0.0001) — percent changes are relative measures, printed as such. All secondary measures (haemoglobin, liver volume, platelet counts) improved significantly except platelet counts at the lower dose. There were no serious adverse events; drug-related events were mild/moderate and transient; 2 patients (6%) developed non-neutralising IgG antibodies and 2 (6%) developed hypersensitivity reactions.
cards.watchOut: Small-N on the face: 29 completers, and with no placebo or comparator arm the within-group gains are uncontrolled — this trial compares two doses of the same enzyme, it does not estimate an effect against no treatment or against another enzyme.
cards.source: Zimran A et al. Pivotal trial with plant cell-expressed recombinant glucocerebrosidase, taliglucerase alfa, a novel enzyme replacement therapy for Gaucher disease. Blood. 2011. PMID: 21900191. Registry ID: NCT00376168. cards.headline: Switchover phase 3 trial (Pastores 2014): in 31 patients (26 adult, 5 paediatric) stable on imiglucerase for ≥2 years, spleen and liver volumes, haemoglobin, platelet counts and biomarkers remained stable 9 months after switching to the same dose of taliglucerase alfa
cards.summary: Switchover phase 3 trial (Pastores 2014): in 31 patients (26 adult, 5 paediatric) stable on imiglucerase for ≥2 years, spleen and liver volumes, haemoglobin, platelet counts and biomarkers remained stable 9 months after switching to the same dose of taliglucerase alfa
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre open-label switchover trial (from imiglucerase), 9 months
cards.people: 31 patients (26 adult, 5 paediatric) with Gaucher disease treated with imiglucerase for at least the previous 2 years and with stable disease, switched open-label to taliglucerase alfa at the same dose (9–60 U/kg) and every-other-week regimen for 9 months.
cards.result: Disease parameters (spleen and liver volumes, haemoglobin concentration, platelet count and biomarker levels) remained stable through 9 months of treatment in adults and children after the switch. All treatment-related adverse events were mild or moderate in severity and transient. Exploratory measures of linear growth and development in the paediatric patients were positive. The authors conclude the findings support the efficacy and safety profile of taliglucerase alfa in patients previously treated with imiglucerase.
cards.watchOut: Open-label stability after a switch in already-stable patients is maintenance evidence, not efficacy against a comparator: regression to a stable baseline and survivor selection are built into the design, and N = 31 (only 5 children).
cards.source: Pastores GM et al. A Phase 3, multicenter, open-label, switchover trial to assess the safety and efficacy of taliglucerase alfa, a plant cell-expressed recombinant human glucocerebrosidase, in adult and pediatric patients with Gaucher disease previously treated with imiglucerase. cards.headline: Paediatric long-term report (Zimran 2018) — an extension report of the programme's paediatric studies, labelled as such: in 10 treatment-naïve children, spleen volume fell −18.6 and −26.0 multiples of normal at 30 and 60 U/kg, haemoglobin rose +2.0 and +2.3 g/dL and platelets rose +38,200 and +138,250/mm³ over up to 36 months; 5 switched children remained stable
cards.summary: Paediatric long-term report (Zimran 2018) — an extension report of the programme's paediatric studies, labelled as such: in 10 treatment-naïve children, spleen volume fell −18.6 and −26.0 multiples of normal at 30 and 60 U/kg, haemoglobin rose +2.0 and +2.3 g/dL and platelets rose +38,200 and +138,250/mm³ over up to 36 months; 5 switched children remained stable
cards.type: Extension report of the programme's paediatric studies (same programme — not an independent trial), up to 36 months
cards.people: 15 children with Gaucher disease in a multicentre extension study: 10 treatment-naïve (taliglucerase alfa 30 or 60 U/kg every other week) and 5 previously treated with imiglucerase (switched at the same dose), treated for up to 36 months in total (33 months for the switched group).
cards.result: In treatment-naïve children, taliglucerase alfa at 30 and 60 U/kg respectively reduced mean spleen volume (−18.6 and −26.0 multiples of normal), reduced liver volume (−0.8 and −0.9 multiples of normal) and chitotriosidase activity (−72.7% and −84.4%, relative changes), and increased mean haemoglobin (+2.0 and +2.3 g/dL) and mean platelet count (+38,200 and +138,250/mm³) from baseline through 36 months. In switched children, disease parameters remained stable through 33 months. Most adverse events were mild/moderate and treatment was well tolerated, with no new safety signals.
cards.watchOut: Fifteen children, open-label and uncontrolled, in an extension report: the naïve-child gains are within-group changes over 3 years (growth itself changes organ volumes and counts in children), and the switched-child result is stability, as in the adult switch trial.
cards.source: Zimran A et al. Long-term safety and efficacy of taliglucerase alfa in pediatric Gaucher disease patients who were treatment-naïve or previously treated with imiglucerase. cards.result: Small-N rare-disease base — the counts lead, and they are printed on the face of every card: the randomised base is a single 29-completer dose-comparison trial with no placebo or active-comparator arm, so its within-group gains are uncontrolled; the switch (N = 31) and paediatric extension (N = 15) reports are open-label reports of the same programme, labelled as such, and the programme's further reports (adult switch extension, 5-year naïve report, pooled safety review) are support only and not carded, as the commissioning row directs. Endpoints are haemoglobin, platelet counts and spleen / liver volumes — surrogates; no fracture, bone-crisis or mortality outcomes trial exists. The tested product is named as the publications give it — taliglucerase alfa, plant cell-expressed (Protalix Biotherapeutics, Carmiel, Israel) — for clarification, not promotion, because enzyme products from different expression systems are not interchangeable on this evidence. Its Gaucher siblings are homed separately (eliglustat live #1402; velaglucerase S18-1-10) and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards: no number on this shelf comes from a placebo-controlled comparison, and total carded N across the programme is 29 + 31 + 15, with the reports overlapping one programme.

shelves.title: Cipaglucosidase alfa + miglustat in late-onset Pompe (PROPEL): the phase 3 primary endpoint was MISSED (+13.6 m, 95% CI −2.8 to 29.9); open-label reports show stability, not proven superiority
shelves.question: In adults with late-onset Pompe disease, does the two-component enzyme therapy cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat, compared with alglucosidase alfa, improve walking distance and respiratory function (the PROPEL programme: one randomised trial and its labelled extension and phase 1/2 reports)?
shelves.mesh: 1-Deoxynojirimycin · Adolescent · Double-Blind Method · Glycogen Storage Disease Type II · Humans · Treatment Outcome · alpha-Glucosidases
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), on one programme of three reports / two trials — labelled as such. PROPEL, the only randomised trial (125 randomised), MISSED its primary endpoint: 6-minute walk distance improved by 20.8 m on cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat versus 7.2 m on alglucosidase alfa plus placebo, a between-group difference of 13.6 m (95% CI −2.8 to 29.9), and the abstract's own conclusion is that the combination did not achieve statistical superiority. The two remaining reports are open-label and uncontrolled: the PROPEL extension (118 patients to 104 weeks) showed maintained or stable walk distance and forced vital capacity rather than decline, and the phase 1/2 ATB200-02 report (29 adults to 48 months) showed within-group gains with shrinking denominators (n = 9 remaining at 48 months in the pooled experienced ambulatory cohorts). Respiratory and subgroup signals in PROPEL are, in the abstract's own framing, hypothesis-generating. The missed primary endpoint leads this shelf; the combination is not presented as proven superior to alglucosidase alfa. Cross-point: avalglucosidase alfa versus alglucosidase alfa is a different agent and question, homed at pack #5194.

cards.headline: PROPEL phase 3 RCT (Schoser 2021): the primary endpoint was NOT met — 6-minute walk distance difference 13.6 m (95% CI −2.8 to 29.9) for cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat versus alglucosidase alfa
cards.summary: PROPEL phase 3 RCT (Schoser 2021): the primary endpoint was NOT met — 6-minute walk distance difference 13.6 m (95% CI −2.8 to 29.9) for cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat versus alglucosidase alfa
cards.type: Phase 3 international randomised double-blind trial (PROPEL), cipaglucosidase alfa + miglustat vs alglucosidase alfa + placebo
cards.people: 125 adults with late-onset Pompe disease (85 cipaglucosidase alfa 20 mg/kg plus oral miglustat, 40 alglucosidase alfa 20 mg/kg plus oral placebo, every 2 weeks for 52 weeks; 62 centres in 24 countries), either enzyme-replacement-therapy (ERT)-experienced for at least 2 years or ERT-naïve; 123 received at least one dose and 117 completed the study.
cards.result: Mean change in 6-minute walk distance at week 52 was 20.8 m (SE 4.6) on the combination versus 7.2 m (SE 6.6) on alglucosidase alfa — a between-group difference of 13.6 m (95% CI −2.8 to 29.9), which did not achieve statistical superiority on the primary endpoint. At least one treatment-emergent adverse event occurred in 95% of the combination group and 97% of the comparator group; 12 serious adverse events occurred in 8 combination patients, only one (anaphylaxis) deemed drug-related, and there were no deaths. The authors state that further studies should investigate longer-term effects and possible respiratory and ERT-experienced-subgroup benefits suggested by secondary and subgroup analyses.
cards.watchOut: A negative superiority trial on its primary endpoint: the numerically favourable walk-distance difference is compatible with no difference (CI −2.8 to 29.9 m). Secondary and subgroup respiratory signals are hypothesis-generating only, as the abstract itself frames them.
cards.source: Schoser B et al. Safety and efficacy of cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat versus alglucosidase alfa plus placebo in late-onset Pompe disease (PROPEL): an international, randomised, double-blind, parallel-group, phase 3 trial. The Lancet. Neurology. 2021. PMID: 34800400. Registry ID: NCT03729362. MeSH: 1-Deoxynojirimycin · Adolescent · Double-Blind Method · Glycogen Storage Disease Type II · Humans · Treatment Outcome · alpha-Glucosidases

cards.headline: PROPEL open-label extension (Schoser 2024): an extension report of the PROPEL trial, labelled as such — walk distance and FVC were maintained or stable to 104 weeks on the combination, with no comparator arm
cards.summary: PROPEL open-label extension (Schoser 2024): an extension report of the PROPEL trial, labelled as such — walk distance and FVC were maintained or stable to 104 weeks on the combination, with no comparator arm
cards.type: Programme report: open-label extension of the PROPEL randomised trial (same programme as the card above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: 118 patients from PROPEL treated in the open-label extension: 81 who continued cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat (61 ERT-experienced, 20 ERT-naïve before PROPEL) and 37 who switched from alglucosidase alfa plus placebo (29 ERT-experienced, 8 ERT-naïve); outcomes are changes from PROPEL baseline to 104 weeks.
cards.result: Mean (SD) change in % predicted 6-minute walk distance was +3.1 (8.1) in the continued-combination group and −0.5 (7.8) in ERT-experienced switchers, and +8.6 (8.6) and +8.9 (11.7) respectively in ERT-naïve patients. Mean (SD) change in % predicted forced vital capacity was −0.6 (7.5) (continued) and −3.8 (6.2) (experienced switchers), and −4.8 (6.5) and −3.1 (6.7) in ERT-naïve patients. Creatine kinase and hexose tetrasaccharide levels improved in both groups. Three patients discontinued for infusion-associated reactions and no new safety signals were identified.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and uncontrolled: stability over 104 weeks in patients who stayed in the programme cannot be separated from natural history, survivor effects or expectation, and it does not repair the parent trial's missed primary endpoint.
cards.source: Schoser B et al. 104-week efficacy and safety of cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat in adults with late-onset Pompe disease: a phase III open-label extension study (ATB200-07). Journal of neurology. 2024. PMID: 38418563. Registry ID: NCT04138277. cards.headline: Phase 1/2 long-term report ATB200-02 (Byrne 2024): 29 adults in 4 cohorts treated open-label to 48 months — walk distance improved within group in ambulatory cohorts, with only 9 experienced ambulatory patients remaining at 48 months
cards.summary: Phase 1/2 long-term report ATB200-02 (Byrne 2024): 29 adults in 4 cohorts treated open-label to 48 months — walk distance improved within group in ambulatory cohorts, with only 9 experienced ambulatory patients remaining at 48 months
cards.type: Phase 1/2 open-label long-term programme report (ATB200-02), 4 cohorts, no comparator
cards.people: 29 adults with Pompe disease in 4 cohorts: 6 non-ambulatory ERT-experienced patients and 23 ambulatory patients (11 ERT-experienced 2–6 years, 6 ERT-experienced at least 7 years, 6 ERT-naïve), all receiving cipaglucosidase alfa 20 mg/kg plus miglustat 260 mg every 2 weeks.
cards.result: In the pooled ambulatory ERT-experienced cohorts, mean (SD) change in % predicted 6-minute walk distance was +6.1 (7.84) at 12 months (n = 16), +5.4 (10.56) at 24 months (n = 13), +3.4 (14.66) at 36 months (n = 12) and +5.9 (17.36) at 48 months (n = 9); in the small ERT-naïve cohort the corresponding gains were +10.7 to +11.7 with n = 6 falling to n = 4. % predicted forced vital capacity was generally stable in ERT-experienced cohorts and improved in the naïve cohort (+8.3 (4.50) at 48 months, n = 4). Biomarkers improved in ambulatory cohorts and the safety profile was described as like alglucosidase alfa.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled, with very small and shrinking denominators (n = 9 and n = 4 at 48 months in the ambulatory cohorts): within-group changes over 4 years carry no comparative weight against alglucosidase alfa.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one randomised trial exists (PROPEL, 125 randomised) and it missed its primary endpoint — the extension and phase 1/2 reports show stability on open-label treatment, not proven superiority over alglucosidase alfa
cards.summary: Synthesis: one randomised trial exists (PROPEL, 125 randomised) and it missed its primary endpoint — the extension and phase 1/2 reports show stability on open-label treatment, not proven superiority over alglucosidase alfa
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The randomised record is a single trial: cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat improved 6-minute walk distance by 13.6 m more than alglucosidase alfa (95% CI −2.8 to 29.9), a non-significant difference the investigators themselves report as superiority not achieved. The open-label extension (118 patients, 104 weeks) and the phase 1/2 report (29 patients, 48 months) show maintained walk distance and generally stable respiratory function on the combination, with similar adverse-event incidence to the comparator in PROPEL (95% vs 97% with at least one event; one drug-related serious event, anaphylaxis). Endpoints throughout are walk distance and forced vital capacity — functional measures; no mortality trial exists. A further PROPEL patient-reported-outcomes paper is a report of the same trial, is support only, and is not carded or counted here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Diazoxide choline ER in Prader-Willi hyperphagia (DESTINY): phase 3 primary MISSED (P = 0.198); severe subgroup and withdrawal study in prior responders positive
shelves.question: In children and adults with Prader-Willi syndrome and hyperphagia, does diazoxide choline extended-release (DCCR), compared with placebo or with its own withdrawal, reduce hyperphagia (the DESTINY PWS programme: one phase 3 trial, its labelled open-label report, and a randomised withdrawal study)?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Prader-Willi Syndrome · Diazoxide · COVID-19 · Obesity · Hyperphagia
shelves.balance: SPLIT, on one programme of three reports — labelled as such. DESTINY PWS, the phase 3 placebo-controlled trial (127 randomised), MISSED its primary endpoint: Hyperphagia Questionnaire for Clinical Trials (HQ-CT) change was −5.94 on diazoxide choline extended-release (DCCR) versus −4.27 on placebo (P = 0.198). The affirmative evidence sits in narrower frames: a significant result in the severe-baseline-hyperphagia subgroup (−9.67 vs −4.26, P = 0.012), a pre-COVID sensitivity analysis that met the primary endpoint (P = 0.037), significant secondary endpoints (Clinical Global Impression of Improvement, P = 0.029; fat mass, P = 0.023), uncontrolled open-label improvement over up to 52 weeks (HQ-CT −9.9 within group), and a positive randomised-withdrawal study (77 prior responders/completers after 2.5–4.5 years of open-label treatment: HQ-CT worsened +2.6 on continued DCCR versus +7.6 on switched-to-placebo, P = 0.0022) — a design that enriches for patients already tolerating and apparently benefiting from the drug and does not re-establish the primary endpoint in an unselected population. The agent was approved in the US in 2025 on this totality; the approval and the missed primary are printed together here. Hyperglycaemia — an on-mechanism harm of a diazoxide product — is on the face of the open-label card. HQ-CT is a caregiver-reported questionnaire score, not a weight or survival outcome.

cards.headline: DESTINY PWS phase 3 RCT (Miller 2023): the primary endpoint was NOT met — HQ-CT hyperphagia change −5.94 on DCCR versus −4.27 on placebo (P = 0.198)
cards.summary: DESTINY PWS phase 3 RCT (Miller 2023): the primary endpoint was NOT met — HQ-CT hyperphagia change −5.94 on DCCR versus −4.27 on placebo (P = 0.198)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (DESTINY PWS), DCCR vs placebo
cards.people: 127 participants with Prader-Willi syndrome aged 4 years and older with hyperphagia, randomised 2:1 to diazoxide choline extended-release (DCCR) or placebo for 13 weeks.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — change in hyperphagia on the Hyperphagia Questionnaire for Clinical Trials (HQ-CT) — was not significantly different: least-squares mean (SE) −5.94 (0.879) on DCCR versus −4.27 (1.145) on placebo (P = 0.198). In participants with severe baseline hyperphagia the difference was significant (−9.67 vs −4.26, P = 0.012), and two of three secondary endpoints improved (Clinical Global Impression of Improvement, P = 0.029; fat mass, P = 0.023). In a pre-COVID analysis the primary endpoint was met (P = 0.037) and all secondary endpoints improved. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 83.3% on DCCR versus 73.8% on placebo (not significant).
cards.watchOut: The primary analysis is negative; the severe-subgroup and pre-COVID results are subgroup and sensitivity analyses of a trial that missed its primary endpoint, and must not be read as the trial having succeeded.
cards.source: Miller JL et al. Diazoxide Choline Extended-Release Tablet in People With Prader-Willi Syndrome: A Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2023. PMID: 36639249. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Prader-Willi Syndrome · Diazoxide · COVID-19 · Obesity · Hyperphagia

cards.headline: Long-term open-label report (Miller 2024): an uncontrolled extension report of the DESTINY programme, labelled as such — HQ-CT improved −9.9 within group over up to 52 weeks; hypertrichosis, peripheral oedema and hyperglycaemia were the common adverse events
cards.summary: Long-term open-label report (Miller 2024): an uncontrolled extension report of the DESTINY programme, labelled as such — HQ-CT improved −9.9 within group over up to 52 weeks; hypertrichosis, peripheral oedema and hyperglycaemia were the common adverse events
cards.type: Programme report: long-term open-label extension of the DESTINY PWS programme (same programme as the card above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: 125 participants with Prader-Willi syndrome aged 4 years and older who had enrolled in DESTINY PWS and received DCCR for up to 52 weeks across the trial and its open-label extension.
cards.result: HQ-CT improved by a mean (SE) −9.9 (0.77) within group (P < 0.0001), with larger improvements in those with more severe baseline hyperphagia; aggression, anxiety and compulsivity scores improved (all P < 0.0001), leptin, insulin and insulin resistance fell, adiponectin rose (all P < 0.004), and lean body mass increased (P < 0.0001). Common treatment-emergent adverse events were hypertrichosis, peripheral oedema and hyperglycaemia; 7.2% discontinued for adverse events.
cards.watchOut: No comparator: within-group improvement over a year in families and clinicians who know the drug is being taken cannot distinguish drug effect from expectation, maturation or regression to the mean. Hyperglycaemia is an on-mechanism harm of a diazoxide product and is printed here on the face.
