cards.headline: Randomised withdrawal study (Miller 2026): in prior DCCR responders/completers, hyperphagia worsened far less on continued DCCR than on switch to placebo (HQ-CT +2.6 vs +7.6, P = 0.0022)
cards.summary: Randomised withdrawal study (Miller 2026): in prior DCCR responders/completers, hyperphagia worsened far less on continued DCCR than on switch to placebo (HQ-CT +2.6 vs +7.6, P = 0.0022)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind withdrawal study, continued DCCR vs switch to placebo, in prior programme participants
cards.people: 77 children and adults with Prader-Willi syndrome and hyperphagia who had previously completed the randomised DESTINY PWS study and then received open-label DCCR for 2.5–4.5 years, randomised 1:1 (38 continued DCCR, 39 switched to placebo) for 16 weeks.
cards.result: HQ-CT worsened in both groups but significantly less on continued DCCR: least-squares mean (SE) change +2.6 (1.12) versus +7.6 (1.09) on placebo (P = 0.0022). The placebo group gained more weight (least-squares mean difference −1.6 kg, 95% CI −3.1 to −0.1, favouring continued treatment) and BMI z-score rose more (difference −0.09, 95% CI −0.17 to −0.01). Clinical Global Impression scores favoured DCCR but were not significantly changed. Adverse events were similar between groups, with no serious adverse events in the DCCR arm.
cards.watchOut: A withdrawal design enriches for responders: every participant had already tolerated and apparently benefited from years of open-label DCCR, so this result shows the drug's effect persists in that selected group — it does not re-establish the missed primary endpoint in an unselected population.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the phase 3 primary endpoint was missed in the unselected population (P = 0.198); the programme's affirmative evidence is a severe-subgroup result, a pre-COVID sensitivity analysis, uncontrolled open-label improvement, and a positive withdrawal study in prior responders

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: DESTINY PWS (127 randomised) did not significantly improve hyperphagia on its primary analysis. Over up to 52 weeks of open-label treatment, hyperphagia and behavioural scores improved within group, with hypertrichosis, peripheral oedema and hyperglycaemia the common adverse events and 7.2% discontinuing for adverse events. In the withdrawal study, stopping DCCR after 2.5–4.5 years of open-label treatment led to significantly greater worsening of hyperphagia than continuing it (+7.6 vs +2.6 HQ-CT points, P = 0.0022). The programme's phase 2 pilot (13 participants) is programme support only, is sub-floor-sized for this shelf's purposes, and is not carded or counted. The agent's 2025 US approval rests on this totality — a missed primary endpoint plus supportive narrower analyses — and this shelf presents both together.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Olipudase alfa for ASMD (ASCEND programme): adults — DLCO +22% vs +3.0%, spleen volume −39% vs +0.5% and liver volume −28% vs −1.5% at 52 weeks in the one randomised trial (36 adults); children — single-arm, spleen and liver volumes improved by over 40%
shelves.question: In children and adults with chronic acid sphingomyelinase deficiency (ASMD), does enzyme replacement with olipudase alfa, compared with placebo (adults) or within-patient change (children), improve lung diffusion capacity and spleen and liver volumes (the ASCEND programme)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Carbon Monoxide/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Enzyme Replacement Therapy/methods · Humans · Niemann-Pick Disease, Type A · Recombinant Proteins · Sphingomyelin Phosphodiesterase · Splenomegaly · Adolescent · Child · Child, Preschool · Enzyme Replacement Therapy · Infant · Liver · Niemann-Pick Disease, Type A/drug therapy,genetics · Recombinant Proteins/therapeutic use · Sphingomyelin Phosphodiesterase/genetics · Sphingomyelin Phosphodiesterase/therapeutic use · Niemann-Pick Diseases
shelves.balance: One programme, three reports carded and labelled as such — the counts lead. The randomised base is a single 36-adult trial (ASCEND): at 52 weeks percent-predicted DLCO rose +22% vs +3.0% (P = 0.0004), spleen volume fell −39% vs +0.5% (P < 0.0001) and liver volume fell −28% vs −1.5% (P < 0.0001) — percent changes as published, with the placebo-arm changes beside them — while the splenomegaly-related score did not differ (P = 0.64). The paediatric evidence (ASCEND-Peds, 20 children) is open-label and single-arm: spleen and liver volumes improved by over 40% within patient, DLCO improved +32.9% in those able to perform it, and height Z-scores improved +0.56. The adult open-label extension (35 of 36 continuing) shows the former placebo group paralleling the original group after crossover and continued gains to year 2. Endpoints are organ volumes and DLCO — disease-pathology surrogates; no mortality or hospitalisation trial exists. Per the standing product-naming rule the tested product is named as published: olipudase alfa, recombinant human acid sphingomyelinase — clarification, not promotion. Its lysosomal sibling sebelipase alfa is homed at live #1408 (cross-point only). PROPOSED STAMP: LIKELY (benefit).

cards.headline: ASCEND adult trial (Wasserstein 2022): 36 adults randomised — percent-predicted DLCO +22% vs +3.0% (P = 0.0004), spleen volume −39% vs +0.5% (P < 0.0001) and liver volume −28% vs −1.5% (P < 0.0001) at 52 weeks; the splenomegaly-related score did NOT differ (P = 0.64)
cards.summary: ASCEND adult trial (Wasserstein 2022): 36 adults randomised — percent-predicted DLCO +22% vs +3.0% (P = 0.0004), spleen volume −39% vs +0.5% (P < 0.0001) and liver volume −28% vs −1.5% (P < 0.0001) at 52 weeks; the splenomegaly-related score did NOT differ (P = 0.64)
cards.type: Phase 2/3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (ASCEND), olipudase alfa vs placebo in adults with ASMD — the programme's only randomised trial
cards.people: 36 adults with chronic acid sphingomyelinase deficiency randomised 1:1 in a phase 2/3 international double-blind placebo-controlled trial (ASCEND) to intravenous olipudase alfa or placebo every 2 weeks for 52 weeks, with intrapatient dose escalation to 3 mg/kg. Primary endpoints: percent change in percent-predicted diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO) and spleen volume (combined with the splenomegaly-related score in the United States).
cards.result: Least-squares mean percent change from baseline to week 52 favoured olipudase alfa over placebo for percent-predicted DLCO (22% vs 3.0% increases, P = 0.0004), spleen volume (39% decrease vs 0.5% increase, P < 0.0001) and liver volume (28% vs 1.5% decreases, P < 0.0001) — percent changes as published, placebo changes beside them. The splenomegaly-related score decreased in both groups (P = 0.64). Other clinical outcomes (liver function and sphingomyelin content, pulmonary imaging and function, platelets, lipids) improved in the olipudase group compared with placebo. There were no treatment-related serious adverse events or adverse-event discontinuations; most adverse events were mild.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-six patients is the whole randomised base: the effects are large and internally consistent, but every estimate rests on 18 patients per arm, and the one patient-reported limb (splenomegaly-related score) was null.

cards.headline: ASCEND-Peds trial (Diaz 2021): 20 children, open-label SINGLE-ARM — spleen and liver volumes improved by over 40% within patient (P < 0.0001), percent-predicted DLCO improved +32.9% in those able to perform it, height Z-scores improved +0.56; infusion reactions in 11 patients and one anaphylactic reaction managed by desensitisation
cards.summary: ASCEND-Peds trial (Diaz 2021): 20 children, open-label SINGLE-ARM — spleen and liver volumes improved by over 40% within patient (P < 0.0001), percent-predicted DLCO improved +32.9% in those able to perform it, height Z-scores improved +0.56; infusion reactions in 11 patients and one anaphylactic reaction managed by desensitisation
cards.type: Phase 1/2 open-label single-arm trial (ASCEND-Peds), olipudase alfa in children with ASMD — no comparator
cards.people: 20 children with chronic ASMD enrolled in a phase 1/2 international multicentre open-label trial (ASCEND-Peds): four adolescents (12–17 years), nine children (6–11 years) and seven infants / early children (1–5 years). Intravenous olipudase alfa every 2 weeks with intrapatient dose escalation to 3 mg/kg; primary outcome safety through week 64, with efficacy outcomes through week 52. There is no control group — all changes are within-patient.
cards.result: Mean splenomegaly and hepatomegaly improved by >40% (P < 0.0001). Mean percent-predicted DLCO improved by 32.9% (P = 0.0053) in patients able to perform the test. Lipid profiles and elevated liver transaminases normalised, and mean height Z-scores improved by 0.56 (P < 0.0001). Most adverse events were mild or moderate, including infusion-associated reactions (primarily urticaria, pyrexia and/or vomiting) in 11 patients. Three patients had serious treatment-related events: transient asymptomatic alanine aminotransferase increases in one, urticaria and rash (antidrug-antibody positive) in another, and an anaphylactic reaction (antidrug-antibody positive) in a third, who underwent desensitisation and reached the 3 mg/kg maintenance dose.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: in a progressive disease, within-patient improvement over 52–64 weeks is suggestive, not controlled evidence, and the DLCO figure covers only the children old enough to perform the test. This card supports, and cannot substitute for, the adult randomised trial.

cards.headline: ASCEND open-label extension (Wasserstein 2023) — an extension report of the SAME adult trial, labelled as such: after crossover the former placebo group's DLCO rose +28.0% and spleen volume fell −36.0% in its first treatment year, paralleling the original group, whose spleen volume had fallen −47.0% by year 2
cards.summary: ASCEND open-label extension (Wasserstein 2023) — an extension report of the SAME adult trial, labelled as such: after crossover the former placebo group's DLCO rose +28.0% and spleen volume fell −36.0% in its first treatment year, paralleling the original group, whose spleen volume had fallen −47.0% by year 2
cards.type: Open-label extension report of the ASCEND randomised trial (same programme and patients as the first card — not an independent trial)
cards.people: 35 of the 36 ASCEND participants continued into the open-label extension and 33 completed year 2; the placebo group crossed over to olipudase alfa and the original olipudase group continued treatment. Results are least-squares mean percent changes ± SEM from baseline.
cards.result: In the crossover group after 1 year of treatment, percent-predicted DLCO increased by 28.0 ± 6.2%, spleen volume decreased by 36.0 ± 3.0% and liver volume decreased by 30.7 ± 2.5% — paralleling the original group's first-year results. In those with 2 years of olipudase alfa, percent-predicted DLCO increased by 28.5 ± 6.2%, spleen volume decreased by 47.0 ± 2.7% and liver volume decreased by 33.4 ± 2.2%. Lipid profiles and elevated transaminases improved or normalised by 1 year and remained stable. Overall 99% of treatment-emergent adverse events were mild or moderate, with one treatment-related serious adverse event (extrasystoles, in previously documented cardiomyopathy); no one discontinued for an adverse event.
cards.watchOut: The crossover replication is the extension's real content — the former placebo patients reproduced the treatment pattern once treated — but from crossover onward there is no untreated comparator, so year-2 figures are durability data, not efficacy data.
cards.source: Wasserstein MP et al. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: One programme (ASCEND), three reports carded: the randomised adult trial (36 patients; DLCO +22% vs +3.0%, spleen −39% vs +0.5%, liver −28% vs −1.5% at 52 weeks, all significant; splenomegaly-related score null), the single-arm paediatric trial (20 children; organ volumes improved by over 40% within patient), and the adult extension (crossover replication and continued gains to year 2, spleen −47.0%). The paediatric long-term report and the 5-year adult report of this same programme are further programme reports — support only, not counted. LIKELY (benefit) for the non-central-nervous-system manifestations of chronic ASMD, on organ-volume and DLCO surrogates; no trial measures mortality or hospitalisation. The tested product is named as published — olipudase alfa, recombinant human acid sphingomyelinase. Cross-point only: sebelipase alfa for lysosomal acid lipase deficiency at live #1408.

shelves.balance: One programme, three reports carded and labelled as such — the small-N rare-disease counts lead. The randomised base is one phase 3 trial of 32 patients (PEACE, 21 pegzilarginase vs 11 placebo, 24 weeks, on individualised disease management): geometric-mean plasma arginine fell from 354.0 to 86.4 µmol/L on pegzilarginase vs 464.7 to 426.6 µmol/L on placebo (P < 0.0001) and normalised in 90.5% vs 0%; the abstract reports clinically relevant functional mobility improvements on the key secondary endpoints (GMFM-E, 2-minute walk) without printing their magnitudes, and none are claimed here. The primary endpoint is biochemical (plasma arginine). The earlier phase 1/2 report (16 patients, open-label) showed a median arginine fall of 277 µmol/L after 20 cumulative doses with improvement in at least one mobility assessment in 79%. The long-term extensions (Study 102A, n = 14, up to 5 years; PEACE extension, n = 31, up to 3 years) show sustained arginine control and spasticity improvement in 21 of 25 (84%), but some walk-test cells rest on n = 6 and n = 2, printed on the face. No trial measures survival or developmental outcomes against control beyond 24 weeks. Per the standing product-naming rule the tested product is named as published — pegzilarginase, recombinant human arginase 1 — clarification, not promotion. PROPOSED STAMP: LIKELY (benefit).

cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (PEACE), pegzilarginase vs placebo added to individualised disease management — the programme's only randomised trial
cards.people: 32 patients with arginase 1 deficiency randomised 2:1 (21 pegzilarginase, 11 placebo) in 7 countries (United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Austria, France, Germany, Italy), receiving once-weekly intravenous/subcutaneous pegzilarginase or placebo together with their individualised disease management, from May 2019 to March 2021. Primary endpoint: change from baseline in plasma arginine at week 24. Key secondaries: Gross Motor Function Measure part E (GMFM-E) and the 2-minute walk test.
cards.result: Pegzilarginase lowered geometric-mean plasma arginine from 354.0 µmol/L to 86.4 µmol/L at week 24 vs 464.7 to 426.6 µmol/L for placebo (P < 0.0001) and normalised levels in 90.5% of patients vs 0% with placebo. Clinically relevant functional mobility improvements were demonstrated on the key secondary endpoints — the fetched record reports that conclusion without printing the GMFM-E or 2-minute-walk magnitudes, and this card claims none. Effects were sustained through a further 24 weeks of exposure. Pegzilarginase was well tolerated, with adverse events mostly transient and mild/moderate in severity. This record carries no MeSH terms (see source line).
cards.watchOut: The randomised base is 32 patients and its primary endpoint is a metabolite, not a clinical outcome; the mobility secondaries carry the clinical claim and their magnitudes are not in the fetched record, so they are described, never numbered, on this shelf.

cards.headline: Phase 1/2 report (Diaz 2021): 16 patients, open-label — median plasma arginine fell 277 µmol/L after 20 cumulative doses, reaching the normal range (40–115 µmol/L) in 50% at 168 hours post-dose, with improvement in at least one mobility assessment in 79%; seven hypersensitivity reactions in four patients across 162 infusions
cards.summary: Phase 1/2 report (Diaz 2021): 16 patients, open-label — median plasma arginine fell 277 µmol/L after 20 cumulative doses, reaching the normal range (40–115 µmol/L) in 50% at 168 hours post-dose, with improvement in at least one mobility assessment in 79%; seven hypersensitivity reactions in four patients across 162 infusions
cards.type: Phase 1/2 open-label study report (studies 101A / 102A), pegzilarginase in arginase 1 deficiency — no comparator
cards.people: 16 paediatric and adult patients with arginase 1 deficiency in the phase 1/2 study 101A and the first 12 weeks of its open-label extension 102A, receiving once-weekly intravenous pegzilarginase on top of standard disease management. Baseline burden was substantial: lower-limb spasticity in 75%, developmental delay in 56% and previous hyperammonaemic episodes in 44%; baseline plasma arginine was elevated (median 389 µmol/L, range 238–566).
cards.result: Once-weekly repeat dosing produced a median decrease in plasma arginine of 277 µmol/L after 20 cumulative doses (n = 14), with plasma arginine in the normal range (40 to 115 µmol/L) in 50% of patients at 168 hours post-dose (mean dose 0.10 mg/kg). Arginine lowering was accompanied by improvements in one or more key mobility assessments (6-minute walk, GMFM-D and GMFM-E) in 79% of patients. In study 101A, seven hypersensitivity reactions occurred in four patients out of 162 infusions administered; other common treatment-related adverse events included vomiting, hyperammonaemia, pruritus and abdominal pain, and the treatment-related serious adverse events in five patients all occurred in 101A.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and first-in-human: the 79% mobility figure is an any-assessment improvement count in 16 uncontrolled patients, and the hypersensitivity signal (7 reactions in 4 patients) belongs on the face beside the efficacy, as here.
cards.source: Diaz GA et al. Clinical effect and safety profile of pegzilarginase in patients with arginase 1 deficiency. Journal of inherited metabolic disease. 2021. PMID: 33325055. cards.headline: Long-term extension report (McNutt 2025) — extension reports of the programme's two studies, labelled as such: 37 of 39 evaluable participants met the composite motor response; spasticity improved in 21 of 25 (84%); arginine control was sustained (means <115 µmol/L through week 96 in the PEACE extension, n = 11 remaining) — with some walk-test cells as small as n = 6 and n = 2, printed here
cards.summary: Long-term extension report (McNutt 2025) — extension reports of the programme's two studies, labelled as such: 37 of 39 evaluable participants met the composite motor response; spasticity improved in 21 of 25 (84%); arginine control was sustained (means <115 µmol/L through week 96 in the PEACE extension, n = 11 remaining) — with some walk-test cells as small as n = 6 and n = 2, printed here
cards.type: Long-term open-label extension report (studies 102A and PEACE LTE) — same programme's patients, labelled as such; not an independent trial
cards.people: Two international multicentre open-label extensions of the same programme: Study 102A (n = 14, up to 5 years) and the PEACE long-term extension (n = 31, up to 3 years), with weekly pegzilarginase given with standard care. Outcomes included walk tests (2-/6-minute), GMFM-D/E, spasticity (Modified Ashworth Scale), plasma arginine and guanidino compounds.
cards.result: Of 39 evaluable participants, 37 (95%) met the composite response or achieved the maximum score in at least one motor domain. In 102A, mean 6-minute walk improved to 68.2 m (+19%; n = 12) and GMFM-D/E rose by 2.7/3.7. In the PEACE extension, 2-minute walk improved to 16.5 m (+25%; n = 6) in those treated with pegzilarginase throughout and 13.5 m (+16%; n = 2) in those who crossed from placebo — denominators printed, as the row requires. Spasticity improved in 21 of 25 (84%), with 12 reaching a Modified Ashworth score of 0. Arginine control was sustained: 102A mean 118 µmol/L at week 192 (n = 9); PEACE extension means <115 µmol/L through week 96 (n = 11). Most adverse events were mild/moderate, with no treatment-related discontinuations or persistent antibodies.
cards.watchOut: Extension survivors are a selected remainder: by week 96 only 11 PEACE-extension participants contribute arginine values and one walk-test cell has n = 2, so the percentages describe who stayed and could be measured, not the randomised cohort.
cards.source: McNutt M et al. Long-Term Efficacy and Tolerability of Pegzilarginase in Arginase 1 Deficiency: Results of Two International Multicentre Open-Label Extension Studies. Journal of inherited metabolic disease. 2025. PMID: 40714964. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.question: In children and adults with neuronopathic mucopolysaccharidosis II (Hunter syndrome), does pabinafusp alfa (iduronate-2-sulfatase fused to an anti-transferrin-receptor antibody, JR-141), compared with within-patient baseline, reduce cerebrospinal-fluid heparan sulfate and stabilise neurocognitive development?

shelves.balance: No controlled efficacy trial exists — the flag leads. The entire clinical base is one programme of 62 patients in total (Japan and Brazil): a single-arm open-label phase 2/3 trial in 28 Japanese patients (cerebrospinal-fluid heparan sulfate fell significantly from baseline, P < 0.001; neurocognitive evaluations showed positive changes in 21 of 28 patients — a within-patient judgement without a comparator in a variably progressive disease) and a 26-week open-label dose-randomised trial in Brazil (1.0 / 2.0 / 4.0 mg/kg/week; the 2.0 mg/kg group showed marked reductions in CSF, serum and urine substrate and was judged the best dose; the record prints no N for this trial and none is claimed on its card), summarised in an integrated analysis of the programme. The primary clinical evidence is a CSF substrate surrogate plus uncontrolled neurocognitive readings. The agent is approved in Japan and not in the US/EU — a single-region programme (Japan/Brazil). Per the standing product-naming rule the tested product and its development code are named as the publications give them — pabinafusp alfa, JR-141 — clarification, not promotion. The homed MPS II shelf is conventional idursulfase (live #1405), which does not cross the blood-brain barrier — a different agent and question, cross-point only. PROPOSED STAMP: MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Japanese phase 2/3 trial (Okuyama 2021): 28 patients, SINGLE-ARM open-label — cerebrospinal-fluid heparan sulfate fell significantly from baseline (P < 0.001) over 52 weeks at 2.0 mg/kg weekly, and neurocognitive evaluations showed positive changes in 21 of 28 patients (no comparator)
cards.summary: Japanese phase 2/3 trial (Okuyama 2021): 28 patients, SINGLE-ARM open-label — cerebrospinal-fluid heparan sulfate fell significantly from baseline (P < 0.001) over 52 weeks at 2.0 mg/kg weekly, and neurocognitive evaluations showed positive changes in 21 of 28 patients (no comparator)
cards.type: Phase 2/3 multicentre single-arm open-label trial, pabinafusp alfa in MPS II (Japan) — no placebo and no comparator arm
cards.people: 28 Japanese patients with mucopolysaccharidosis II (Hunter syndrome) in a multicentre single-arm open-label phase 2/3 trial of intravenous pabinafusp alfa 2.0 mg/kg weekly for 52 weeks. Primary efficacy endpoint: change in heparan sulfate concentration in cerebrospinal fluid. Secondaries: neurocognitive development (central efficacy) and plasma heparan and dermatan sulfate (peripheral efficacy).
cards.result: Heparan sulfate concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid decreased significantly from baseline to week 52 (P < 0.001) — the record reports the significance without a numeric magnitude, and none is claimed here — suggesting continued inhibition of substrate accumulation in the central nervous system. Evaluations of neurocognitive development showed positive changes in 21 of the 28 patients. Serum heparan and dermatan sulfate, liver and spleen volumes and other assessments suggested peripheral efficacy comparable to that of idursulfase. Drug-related adverse events were mild or moderate in severity, transient and manageable.
cards.watchOut: 'Positive changes in 21 of 28' is an uncontrolled within-patient judgement in a variably progressive disease: without a control group it cannot distinguish treatment effect from natural variation, and the CSF heparan sulfate endpoint is a substrate surrogate, not a clinical outcome.

cards.type: Phase 2 open-label dose-randomised parallel-group trial, pabinafusp alfa in MPS II (Brazil) — dose comparison only, no placebo
cards.people: Patients with MPS II in Brazil in a 26-week open-label randomised parallel-group phase 2 study of intravenous pabinafusp alfa at 1.0, 2.0 or 4.0 mg/kg/week. Randomisation was between doses only — there is no placebo or untreated arm. The abstract prints no number of patients, and none is claimed on this card (the programme total of 62 patients comes from the integrated analysis carded next).
cards.result: The safety profiles in the three dosage groups were similar. Neurodevelopmental evaluation suggested positive neurocognitive signals despite the relatively short study period. The 2.0 mg/kg group, which demonstrated marked reductions in substrate concentrations in the cerebrospinal fluid, serum and urine, was considered to provide the best combination of safety and efficacy signals. The record gives no numeric substrate magnitudes, and none are claimed here.
cards.watchOut: Dose-randomised is not placebo-controlled: every patient was treated, so this trial can rank doses but cannot estimate efficacy against no treatment, and 26 weeks is short for neurodevelopmental claims in this disease.

cards.headline: Integrated analysis (Giugliani 2021) — a summary analysis of the programme, labelled as such: the Japan and Brazil trials together enrolled 62 patients; to date pabinafusp alfa is the only approved intravenous enzyme therapy with demonstrated CSF substrate reduction in MPS II (as published)
cards.summary: Integrated analysis (Giugliani 2021) — a summary analysis of the programme, labelled as such: the Japan and Brazil trials together enrolled 62 patients; to date pabinafusp alfa is the only approved intravenous enzyme therapy with demonstrated CSF substrate reduction in MPS II (as published)
cards.type: Integrated analysis / programme summary of the pabinafusp alfa preclinical and clinical data (labelled — a summary of the two trials carded above, not a third trial)
cards.people: A summary and integrated analysis of the preclinical and clinical evidence for pabinafusp alfa, covering the mouse-model work and the clinical trials in Japan and Brazil carded above. This card carries only its clinical-programme summary; the preclinical (animal) data in the same paper are not clinical evidence and are not carded as such.
cards.result: Intravenously administered enzymes cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, so conventional enzyme replacement is ineffective against the neurodegeneration of neuronopathic MPS. Pabinafusp alfa — human iduronate-2-sulfatase fused with a blood-brain-barrier-crossing anti-transferrin-receptor antibody — showed central and peripheral efficacy in a mouse model, and subsequent clinical trials in a total of 62 patients with MPS II in Japan and Brazil substantiated this dual efficacy with an acceptable safety profile. To date, as published, pabinafusp alfa is the only approved intravenous enzyme replacement therapy effective against both the somatic and central nervous system symptoms of MPS II.
cards.watchOut: A programme summary written from within the programme: its 'only approved intravenous therapy' statement is the authors' published claim and prints as such. It adds no patients beyond the 62 in the two trials and must never be counted as independent confirmation.

cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: One programme, 62 patients in total, no placebo-controlled trial — stated on the face, as the row requires. The Japanese single-arm trial (28 patients, 52 weeks) showed a significant within-patient fall in CSF heparan sulfate and positive neurocognitive changes in 21 of 28; the Brazilian open-label dose-ranging trial (26 weeks) identified 2.0 mg/kg/week as the best dose on substrate reductions, with no N in its record; the integrated analysis summarises the same programme and adds no patients. MAYBE (weak evidence) for clinical benefit: the CSF substrate reduction is demonstrated within-patient, but every clinical reading is uncontrolled in a variably progressive disease, and the agent's approval is in Japan, not the US/EU. Cross-point only: conventional idursulfase at live #1405, which does not cross the blood-brain barrier and answers a different (somatic) question.
cards.watchOut: Do not upgrade within-patient substrate and neurocognitive signals into demonstrated clinical efficacy: there is no comparator anywhere in this base, and that absence — not the size of the CSF effect — sets the stamp.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Sepiapterin in phenylketonuria: phenylalanine −63% vs +1% vs placebo and greater than sapropterin — in responder-enriched phase 3 trials, on a surrogate endpoint
shelves.question: In children and adults with phenylketonuria, does oral sepiapterin (a synthetic tetrahydrobiopterin precursor), compared with placebo or with sapropterin, lower blood phenylalanine?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Administration, Oral · Double-Blind Method · Phenylalanine/blood · Phenylketonurias/drug therapy,blood · Pterins/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Cross-Over Studies · Biopterins/analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use,adverse effects · Pterins · Biopterins/analogs & derivatives,cerebrospinal fluid · Phenylalanine/administration & dosage,blood · Phenylketonurias/blood,drug therapy · Pterins/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit, blood phenylalanine only) — a biochemical-surrogate base in enriched populations, and both flags lead. Both phase 3 trials randomised only patients already shown to respond to sepiapterin in an open-label run-in (73% in APHENITY), so the placebo contrast (−63% vs +1% percent changes; −395.9 µmol/L) and the sapropterin contrast (−437.0 vs −256.6 µmol/L; 70% relative greater reduction) apply to responders, not all-comers. The only unenriched report is 24 adults treated 7 days per period. No trial measures neurocognitive outcomes. Product named as published: sepiapterin, formerly PTC923 / CNSA-001.

cards.headline: APHENITY phase 3 (Muntau 2024): in the primary analysis set of 98 responder-enriched participants, blood phenylalanine fell −63% vs +1% on placebo (percent changes) after 6 weeks of sepiapterin — least-squares mean change −395.9 µmol/L (SE 33.8, P < 0.0001)
cards.summary: APHENITY phase 3 (Muntau 2024): in the primary analysis set of 98 responder-enriched participants, blood phenylalanine fell −63% vs +1% on placebo (percent changes) after 6 weeks of sepiapterin — least-squares mean change −395.9 µmol/L (SE 33.8, P < 0.0001)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 6 weeks (primary analysis set N = 98, responder-enriched)
cards.people: 157 enrolled at 34 sites in 13 countries (187 assessed for eligibility); after a 14-day open-label responsiveness assessment in 156 participants, 114 (73%) were sepiapterin-responsive, and the primary analysis set of 98 participants (49 sepiapterin / 49 placebo) — those with at least a 30% phenylalanine reduction in part 1 who took at least one dose in part 2 — was randomised to 6 weeks of sepiapterin (forced escalation 20 / 40 / 60 mg/kg/day) or placebo. The tested product is named as the publication gives it: sepiapterin, formerly PTC923 / CNSA-001 (clarification, not promotion).
cards.result: Blood phenylalanine fell −63% (SD 20) on sepiapterin vs +1% (SD 29) on placebo — percent changes, with the absolute least-squares mean change −395.9 µmol/L (SE 33.8, P < 0.0001) printed beside them. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 59% (33 of 56) on sepiapterin vs 33% (18 of 54) on placebo, mostly mild gastrointestinal events; there were no deaths and no serious or severe adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Responder-enriched by design: only patients already shown to respond in an open-label run-in (73% of those assessed) were randomised, so this placebo contrast applies to responders, not to all-comers with phenylketonuria; blood phenylalanine is a biochemical surrogate — no neurocognitive outcome is measured.
cards.source: Muntau AC et al. Effects of oral sepiapterin on blood Phe concentration in a broad range of patients with phenylketonuria (APHENITY): results of an international, phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2024. PMID: 39368841. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05099640; EudraCT 2021-000474-29. cards.headline: AMPLIPHY phase 3 (Giżewska 2026): in 58 primary-analysis participants, sepiapterin 60 mg/kg/day lowered phenylalanine by a least-squares mean −437.0 µmol/L vs −256.6 µmol/L on sapropterin 20 mg/kg/day — a difference of −180.4 µmol/L (95% CI −229.5 to −131.4, P < 0.0001), a 70% relative greater reduction
cards.summary: AMPLIPHY phase 3 (Giżewska 2026): in 58 primary-analysis participants, sepiapterin 60 mg/kg/day lowered phenylalanine by a least-squares mean −437.0 µmol/L vs −256.6 µmol/L on sapropterin 20 mg/kg/day — a difference of −180.4 µmol/L (95% CI −229.5 to −131.4, P < 0.0001), a 70% relative greater reduction
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised crossover open-label active-controlled trial vs sapropterin (62 randomised in part 2; primary analysis set N = 58, responder-enriched)
cards.people: 82 enrolled; participants responsive to sepiapterin in part 1 entered part 2, in which 62 were randomised to crossover sequences of sepiapterin 60 mg/kg/day and sapropterin 20 mg/kg/day for 4 weeks each with a 14-day washout; the primary analysis set was 58 (those with at least a 30% phenylalanine reduction in part 1). Open-label, active-controlled.
cards.result: Least-squares mean (SE) phenylalanine reduction was −437.0 (28.0) µmol/L on sepiapterin vs −256.6 (28.2) µmol/L on sapropterin, a least-squares mean difference of −180.4 µmol/L (95% CI −229.5 to −131.4, P < 0.0001) — described in the record as a relative 70% greater reduction with sepiapterin, printed here as a relative measure with the absolute µmol/L changes beside it. Mean baseline phenylalanine was 725.8 µmol/L before sepiapterin and 790.4 µmol/L before sapropterin in the primary set. Both treatments were well tolerated, with no new safety signals.
cards.watchOut: Also responder-enriched (only sepiapterin responders entered the crossover) and open-label: the 70% figure is relative — the absolute separation is 180.4 µmol/L on a surrogate endpoint, over 4-week treatment periods.
cards.source: Giżewska M et al. cards.headline: Phase 2 crossover trial (Bratkovic 2022): in 24 all-comers adults, least-squares mean phenylalanine changes were −206.4 µmol/L on sepiapterin 60 mg/kg (P < 0.0001), −146.9 on 20 mg/kg (P = 0.0010) and −91.5 µmol/L on sapropterin (P = 0.0339), 7 days per period; only the 60 mg/kg dose reduced phenylalanine in classical PKU (n = 11, P = 0.0287)
cards.summary: Phase 2 crossover trial (Bratkovic 2022): in 24 all-comers adults, least-squares mean phenylalanine changes were −206.4 µmol/L on sepiapterin 60 mg/kg (P < 0.0001), −146.9 on 20 mg/kg (P = 0.0010) and −91.5 µmol/L on sapropterin (P = 0.0339), 7 days per period; only the 60 mg/kg dose reduced phenylalanine in classical PKU (n = 11, P = 0.0287)
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised three-period crossover open-label active-controlled all-comers trial (N = 24 adults, 7 days per period)
cards.people: 24 adults (18–60 years) with phenylketonuria and hyperphenylalaninaemia, all-comers regardless of PAH variants, in a three-period open-label crossover of PTC923 (sepiapterin) 20 and 60 mg/kg/day and sapropterin 20 mg/kg/day, 7 days each with 7-day washouts, on their usual diet. This is the only unenriched report on this shelf.
cards.result: Least-squares mean (SE) phenylalanine changes were −206.4 (41.8) µmol/L for sepiapterin 60 mg/kg (P < 0.0001), −146.9 (41.8) for 20 mg/kg (P = 0.0010) and −91.5 (41.7) µmol/L for sapropterin (P = 0.0339); the 60 mg/kg effect vs sapropterin was significantly larger (P = 0.0098). Only sepiapterin 60 mg/kg reduced phenylalanine in classical PKU subjects (n = 11, P = 0.0287). Adverse events were mostly mild to moderate and transient, similar across groups, with no serious adverse events or discontinuations.
cards.watchOut: The unenriched evidence is 24 adults treated for 7 days per period — the phase 3 responder-enriched results must never be generalised to all-comers on the strength of this shelf without this card beside them.

cards.headline: Synthesis: sepiapterin lowers blood phenylalanine more than placebo and more than sapropterin — but the base is a biochemical surrogate in enriched populations, and both flags lead: both phase 3 trials randomised only open-label responders, and no trial here measures neurocognitive outcomes

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Three trials are carded: APHENITY (primary set 98, 6 weeks — phenylalanine −63% vs +1% percent changes, least-squares mean −395.9 µmol/L, P < 0.0001, vs placebo), AMPLIPHY (primary set 58, crossover — −437.0 vs −256.6 µmol/L vs sapropterin, difference −180.4 µmol/L, a 70% relative greater reduction) and the phase 2 all-comers crossover (24 adults, 7 days per period — −206.4 µmol/L at 60 mg/kg vs −91.5 µmol/L on sapropterin). Sapropterin itself and pegvaliase are homed on their own shelves — different agents, cross-points only; this shelf asks only about the newer precursor, named as the publications give it (sepiapterin, formerly PTC923 / CNSA-001). Tolerability was broadly similar across reports, with mostly mild gastrointestinal events in APHENITY (treatment-emergent events 59% vs 33%) and no deaths or serious adverse events there.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards: responder enrichment (73% in APHENITY) and a surrogate endpoint bound every claim on this shelf; phenylalanine values are printed in µmol/L as the records print them.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Cerliponase alfa in CLN2 disease: far slower decline than historical controls in a single-arm programme of 23 children — no concurrent control exists
shelves.question: In children with neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis type 2 (CLN2 disease), does intracerebroventricular cerliponase alfa (recombinant human tripeptidyl peptidase 1), compared with untreated historical controls, slow decline in motor and language function?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small N = 23 efficacy population (24 enrolled), with no randomised or concurrent control anywhere in the base: every efficacy contrast is against a historical natural-history cohort, so the effect sizes (including hazard ratio 0.14, a relative measure) carry the full bias risk of non-concurrent comparison in a variably progressing disease. Delivery requires a surgically implanted intracerebroventricular device, with device-related infections in nine participants in the extension. Single-arm bases sit at POSSIBLE at best, with the uncontrolled base stated — as here. Product named as published: cerliponase alfa, recombinant human TPP1.

cards.headline: Pivotal single-arm study (Schulz 2018): in 23 efficacy-population children, the median time to a 2-point decline in motor-language score was not reached on cerliponase alfa vs 345 days in 42 historical controls, and the mean rate of decline was 0.27 ± 0.35 vs 2.12 ± 0.98 points per 48 weeks (mean difference 1.85, P < 0.001)
cards.summary: Pivotal single-arm study (Schulz 2018): in 23 efficacy-population children, the median time to a 2-point decline in motor-language score was not reached on cerliponase alfa vs 345 days in 42 historical controls, and the mean rate of decline was 0.27 ± 0.35 vs 2.12 ± 0.98 points per 48 weeks (mean difference 1.85, P < 0.001)
cards.type: Single-arm open-label study vs historical controls (24 enrolled, 23 efficacy population; 42 historical controls) — no concurrent control
cards.people: 24 children enrolled (23 in the efficacy population), ages 3–16 years with CLN2 disease, given cerliponase alfa (recombinant human tripeptidyl peptidase 1) 300 mg intraventricularly every 2 weeks for at least 96 weeks, compared with 42 historical controls. There is no concurrent control anywhere in this programme — that flag leads this shelf. The tested product is named as the publication gives it (cerliponase alfa, recombinant human TPP1; funded by BioMarin Pharmaceutical) — clarification, not promotion.
cards.result: The median time until a 2-point decline in the motor-language score was not reached for treated patients and was 345 days for historical controls. The mean (± SD) rate of decline per 48-week period was 0.27 ± 0.35 points on treatment vs 2.12 ± 0.98 points in historical controls (mean difference 1.85, P < 0.001). Common adverse events included convulsions, pyrexia, vomiting, hypersensitivity reactions and failure of the intraventricular device; in 2 patients, infections developed in the intraventricular device, requiring antibiotic treatment and device replacement.
cards.watchOut: Every efficacy contrast on this card is against a non-concurrent natural-history cohort in a variably progressing disease, so the effect sizes carry the full bias risk of historical comparison; delivery requires a surgically implanted intraventricular device.
cards.source: Schulz A et al. Study of Intraventricular Cerliponase Alfa for CLN2 Disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2018. PMID: 29688815. cards.headline: Open-label extension report (Schulz 2024) — an extension report of the same study, labelled as such: 23 participants treated for a mean of 272.1 weeks were less likely than historical untreated controls to have an unreversed 2-point decline or a score of 0 (hazard ratio 0.14, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.33, P < 0.0001 — a relative measure); nine participants experienced device-related infections
cards.summary: Open-label extension report (Schulz 2024) — an extension report of the same study, labelled as such: 23 participants treated for a mean of 272.1 weeks were less likely than historical untreated controls to have an unreversed 2-point decline or a score of 0 (hazard ratio 0.14, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.33, P < 0.0001 — a relative measure); nine participants experienced device-related infections
cards.type: Open-label extension report of the same single-arm study (N = 23, mean 272.1 weeks) vs historical controls — not an independent trial
cards.people: 23 participants from the same primary study enrolled in the extension and received 300 mg cerliponase alfa intracerebroventricularly every 2 weeks for a mean of 272.1 weeks (range 162.1–300.1); 17 completed the extension and six discontinued prematurely. Historical untreated controls came from the DEM-CHILD database. This report adds follow-up time, not new patients.
cards.result: Treated patients were significantly less likely than historical untreated controls to have an unreversed 2-point decline or a score of 0 in the combined motor and language domains (hazard ratio 0.14, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.33, P < 0.0001) — a hazard ratio is a relative measure, printed as such, against a historical comparator. All participants experienced at least one adverse event and 21 (88%) a serious adverse event; nine participants experienced intracerebroventricular device-related infections, with nine events in six participants resulting in device replacement. There were no discontinuations because of an adverse event and no deaths.
cards.watchOut: An extension of the same 23 patients: the hazard ratio of 0.14 must never be counted as a second, independent confirmation, and its comparator is still historical, not concurrent.

cards.headline: Immunogenicity report (Cherukuri 2018) — a report of the same phase 1/2 programme, labelled as such: anti-drug antibodies in serum of 19 of 24 (79%) and cerebrospinal fluid of 6 of 24 (25%), no neutralising antibodies in CSF, no anaphylaxis, and no correlation between antibody titres and motor-language change or hypersensitivity
cards.summary: Immunogenicity report (Cherukuri 2018) — a report of the same phase 1/2 programme, labelled as such: anti-drug antibodies in serum of 19 of 24 (79%) and cerebrospinal fluid of 6 of 24 (25%), no neutralising antibodies in CSF, no anaphylaxis, and no correlation between antibody titres and motor-language change or hypersensitivity
cards.type: Immunogenicity report of the same phase 1/2 programme (N = 24) — support only, not an efficacy report
cards.people: 24 subjects with CLN2 disease in the same phase 1/2 programme, over a mean exposure of 96.4 weeks (range 0.1–129 weeks). This is a programme report about antibody response, not an efficacy trial, and is carded as support only.
cards.result: Treatment was associated with anti-drug antibody production in cerebrospinal fluid in 6 of 24 (25%) and in serum in 19 of 24 (79%) subjects. Neutralising antibodies were not detected in the CSF of any subject, and no events of anaphylaxis were reported. Neither serum antibody presence nor drug-specific immunoglobulin E was associated with the incidence or severity of hypersensitivity adverse events, and serum and CSF antibody titres did not correlate with change in motor-language score.
cards.watchOut: Support only: this card answers an antibody question about the same patients and adds no efficacy evidence; the programme's treated population remains 24 enrolled / 23 in the efficacy population.
cards.source: Cherukuri A et al. Immunogenicity to cerliponase alfa intracerebroventricular enzyme replacement therapy for CLN2 disease: Results from a Phase 1/2 study. shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, weekly dosing only) — one programme, labelled, and one randomised trial is the controlled base: the count leads. The placebo-controlled benefit is a 22.5-metre 6-minute-walk difference on the weekly regimen only at 24 weeks, with the stair-climb secondary null on both regimens and the every-other-week regimen null on the primary; everything beyond 24 weeks is open-label extension data compared with a natural-history cohort. Endpoints are endurance, lung-function and questionnaire measures — no mortality outcome has been randomised. Product named as published: elosulfase alfa, BMN 110.

cards.headline: MOR-004 phase 3 trial (Hendriksz 2014): in 176 randomised patients the primary 6-minute walk test improved by an estimated +22.5 m (95% CI 4.0 to 40.9, P = 0.017) on weekly elosulfase alfa only — the every-other-week estimate was +0.5 m (P = 0.954) and the 3-minute stair climb did not improve on either regimen

cards.headline: Multi-domain report (Hendriksz 2015) — a further report of the same MOR-004 trial, labelled as such: the trial was not powered for tertiary outcomes; the largest weekly-dose effects were on maximal voluntary ventilation, the MPS Health Assessment Questionnaire, height and growth rate, and the prespecified composite endpoint showed a modest positive impact (P = 0.053)
cards.summary: Multi-domain report (Hendriksz 2015) — a further report of the same MOR-004 trial, labelled as such: the trial was not powered for tertiary outcomes; the largest weekly-dose effects were on maximal voluntary ventilation, the MPS Health Assessment Questionnaire, height and growth rate, and the prespecified composite endpoint showed a modest positive impact (P = 0.053)
cards.type: Multi-domain / tertiary-endpoint report of the same MOR-004 randomised trial — not an independent trial
cards.people: The same MOR-004 population as the card above (weekly n = 58, every other week n = 59, placebo n = 59), reported for tertiary and composite endpoints: respiratory function, activities of daily living (MPS-HAQ), anthropometric, echocardiographic and radiographic measures, hearing and corneal clouding. This report adds outcomes, not patients.
cards.result: For most tertiary endpoints, weekly-dose subjects improved more than placebo; the largest treatment effects were on maximal voluntary ventilation, MPS-HAQ, height and growth rate, and the every-other-week group appeared similar to placebo. The prespecified composite endpoint (6-minute walk, 3-minute stair climb and maximal voluntary ventilation z-scores, equally weighted) showed a modest positive impact for weekly dosing vs placebo (P = 0.053); a prespecified supportive O'Brien Rank Sum composite also favoured weekly dosing (P = 0.011), and post-hoc combinations were explored. The study was not designed to have sufficient power for any tertiary outcome.
cards.watchOut: Tertiary and composite findings from an underpowered-for-those-outcomes trial, including post-hoc combinations: supportive colour for the weekly regimen, never a second confirmation of the primary result.

cards.headline: MOR-005 extension ADL report (Hendriksz 2018) — an open-label extension report of the same programme, labelled as such: in 173 patients followed to 120 weeks from MOR-004 baseline, activities-of-daily-living domain scores improved vs baseline at 2 years (mobility −0.5, P = 0.002; self-care −0.4, P = 0.001; caregiver assistance −1.0, P = 0.06), while a comparable untreated natural-history cohort (MorCAP, n = 94) showed no improvement
cards.summary: MOR-005 extension ADL report (Hendriksz 2018) — an open-label extension report of the same programme, labelled as such: in 173 patients followed to 120 weeks from MOR-004 baseline, activities-of-daily-living domain scores improved vs baseline at 2 years (mobility −0.5, P = 0.002; self-care −0.4, P = 0.001; caregiver assistance −1.0, P = 0.06), while a comparable untreated natural-history cohort (MorCAP, n = 94) showed no improvement
cards.type: Open-label extension report (MOR-005, N = 173) vs a natural-history cohort (MorCAP, N = 94) — uncontrolled extension data
cards.people: 173 patients with Morquio A syndrome in the 96-week open-label MOR-005 extension of MOR-004, evaluated over 120 weeks from MOR-004 baseline (intent-to-treat population 169, including 158 with 2 years of follow-up); the comparator cohort is the MorCAP natural-history study (intent-to-treat 94, including 37 with 2 years of follow-up) — a non-concurrent, untreated cohort, printed as such.
cards.result: At week 120, least-squares mean (SE) changes from baseline were −0.5 (0.1) for mobility (P = 0.002), −0.4 (0.1) for self-care (P = 0.001) and −1.0 (0.5) for caregiver assistance (P = 0.06), where reductions represent improvements. The MorCAP cohort showed no improvement over 2 years, with two of three domains worsening; changes differed significantly between MOR-005 and MorCAP for mobility (−0.7, SE 0.4, P = 0.0490) and self-care (−0.7, SE 0.3, P = 0.0146) at 2 years.
cards.watchOut: Everything beyond 24 weeks is open-label extension data compared with a natural-history cohort: it can show durability and direction, not a controlled treatment effect, and no mortality outcome has been randomised in this programme.

shelves.title: Laronidase in mucopolysaccharidosis I: FVC and walk improved in a 45-patient trial — walk endpoint significant by one analysis, not the other
shelves.question: In children and adults with mucopolysaccharidosis I, does enzyme replacement with laronidase (recombinant human α-L-iduronidase), compared with placebo, improve respiratory function and walking capacity?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small-N rare-disease base, and the counts lead. The placebo-controlled base is 45 patients over 26 weeks, one co-primary endpoint (6-minute walk) is significant by one analysis and not the other (P = .066 / .039 — both printed), and the long-term data are uncontrolled. The trial population had attenuated phenotypes; intravenous laronidase does not address the central-nervous-system disease of severe (Hurler) MPS I, and no wording may imply that it does. Product named as published: laronidase, recombinant human α-L-iduronidase.

cards.headline: Phase 3 trial (Wraith 2004): in 45 randomised patients, percent-predicted forced vital capacity improved by a mean of 5.6 percentage points (median 3.0, P = .009) and 6-minute walk distance by a mean of 38.1 m (median 38.5; P = .066 by rank-sum, P = .039 by analysis of covariance) on laronidase over 26 weeks
cards.summary: Phase 3 trial (Wraith 2004): in 45 randomised patients, percent-predicted forced vital capacity improved by a mean of 5.6 percentage points (median 3.0, P = .009) and 6-minute walk distance by a mean of 38.1 m (median 38.5; P = .066 by rank-sum, P = .039 by analysis of covariance) on laronidase over 26 weeks
cards.type: Randomised double-blinded placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, 26 weeks (N = 45 randomised) — the programme's placebo-controlled base
cards.people: 45 patients with mucopolysaccharidosis I randomised (22 laronidase 100 U/kg [0.58 mg/kg] weekly / 23 placebo) for 26 weeks in a multinational double-blinded study; the co-primary endpoints were median change in percent-predicted forced vital capacity and 6-minute walk distance. Small-N rare-disease base — the counts lead on this shelf. The tested product is named as the publications give it: laronidase, recombinant human α-L-iduronidase (Aldurazyme in the dose trial) — clarification, not promotion.
cards.result: After 26 weeks, laronidase vs placebo showed mean improvements of 5.6 percentage points in percent-predicted forced vital capacity (median 3.0, P = .009) and 38.1 metres in 6-minute walk distance (median 38.5; P = .066 by Wilcoxon rank-sum, P = .039 by analysis of covariance) — both P values for the walk endpoint are printed, as the row directs. Laronidase also significantly reduced hepatomegaly and urinary glycosaminoglycans and, in more severely affected patients, improved sleep apnea / hypopnea and shoulder flexion. Nearly all treated patients developed IgG antibodies, without apparent clinical effect.
cards.watchOut: The placebo-controlled base is 45 patients over 26 weeks, and one co-primary endpoint (6-minute walk) is significant by one analysis and not the other (P = .066 / .039) — both printed, never cherry-picked.

cards.headline: Dose-optimization trial (Giugliani 2009) — a second randomised trial of the programme, on the dose question, labelled as such: in 33 patients no regimen differed significantly in urinary glycosaminoglycan reduction or liver-volume change, the approved 0.58 mg/kg/week regimen had the lowest drug-related adverse-event incidence (38% vs 63–75%), and one patient died of respiratory failure 6 hours after a first infusion, in the setting of acute bronchitis
cards.summary: Dose-optimization trial (Giugliani 2009) — a second randomised trial of the programme, on the dose question, labelled as such: in 33 patients no regimen differed significantly in urinary glycosaminoglycan reduction or liver-volume change, the approved 0.58 mg/kg/week regimen had the lowest drug-related adverse-event incidence (38% vs 63–75%), and one patient died of respiratory failure 6 hours after a first infusion, in the setting of acute bronchitis
cards.type: Randomised open-label dose-optimization trial, 26 weeks (N = 33 randomised) — dose question only
cards.people: 33 patients with mucopolysaccharidosis I randomised open-label for 26 weeks to the approved laronidase dose (0.58 mg/kg/week) or three alternative regimens (1.2 mg/kg every 2 weeks; 1.2 mg/kg every week; 1.8 mg/kg every 2 weeks). This trial answers a dose question, not a placebo question, and is labelled as such.
cards.result: The four regimens showed no significant differences in reduction of urinary glycosaminoglycan excretion or liver volume. Infusion-associated reactions were the most common drug-related adverse events (by patient, pyrexia 21%, vomiting 15%, rash 15%, urticaria 12%). The approved-dose group had the lowest incidence of drug-related adverse events (38% vs 63–75%) and was judged to give near-maximal storage reduction with the best benefit-to-risk ratio. There was one death: a patient with acute bronchitis died of respiratory failure 6 hours after completing the first laronidase infusion, as printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: A dose-comparison trial with no placebo arm: it supports the approved regimen's benefit-to-risk position and cannot add efficacy-vs-placebo evidence; the single post-infusion death, in acute bronchitis, prints on the face as the record gives it.
cards.source: Giugliani R et al. A dose-optimization trial of laronidase (Aldurazyme) in patients with mucopolysaccharidosis I. Molecular genetics and metabolism. 2009. PMID: 19038563. cards.summary: Long-term extension report (Clarke 2009) — an extension report of the phase 3 trial, labelled as such: all 45 patients entered a 3.5-year open-label extension; percent-predicted FVC remained broadly stable (slope −0.78 percentage points per year) and the 6-minute walk gain was 17.1 ± 16.8 m at final assessment; one anaphylactic reaction occurred
cards.type: Open-label extension report of the phase 3 trial (all 45 patients, 3.5 years) — uncontrolled long-term data
cards.people: All 45 patients who completed the 26-week placebo-controlled trial entered the 3.5-year open-label extension; mean age at baseline 16 years (range 6–43), with attenuated disease (84% Hurler-Scheie, 16% Scheie phenotypes) — that population prints on the face of this shelf. 40 patients (89%) completed and received at least 80% of scheduled infusions.
cards.result: Urinary glycosaminoglycan levels decreased within the first 12 weeks and liver volume within the first year. Percent-predicted forced vital capacity remained stable, with a linear slope of −0.78 percentage points per year. The 6-minute walk distance increased 31.7 ± 10.2 m in the first 2 years, with a final gain of 17.1 ± 16.8 m. Infusion-associated reactions occurred in 53% of patients, were mostly mild and decreased markedly after 6 months; one patient experienced an anaphylactic reaction, and one patient died of an upper respiratory infection unrelated to treatment, as printed. Antibodies developed in 93% of patients.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled extension data in an attenuated-phenotype population: intravenous laronidase does not address the central-nervous-system disease of severe (Hurler) MPS I, and no wording on this shelf may imply that it does.
cards.source: Clarke LA et al. Long-term efficacy and safety of laronidase in the treatment of mucopolysaccharidosis I. Pediatrics. 2009. PMID: 19117887. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00146770. cards.result: One programme, three reports, labelled throughout: the phase 3 trial (45 randomised — respiratory function and walking capacity improved vs placebo, with the walk endpoint's split significance printed in full), the dose-optimization trial (33 randomised, open-label, no placebo — no significant regimen differences in glycosaminoglycan or liver-volume reduction; approved dose lowest drug-related adverse-event incidence, 38% vs 63–75%; one death from respiratory failure 6 hours after a first infusion in acute bronchitis) and the extension (all 45 phase 3 patients, 3.5 years — FVC broadly stable at −0.78 percentage points per year, final walk gain 17.1 ± 16.8 m, one anaphylactic reaction). The trial population had attenuated phenotypes (84% Hurler-Scheie, 16% Scheie). The repeated Cochrane versions of this literature are one review in successive versions, not evidence, and are not counted here. Product named as published: laronidase, recombinant human α-L-iduronidase.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards: small N, one split co-primary, and no central-nervous-system claim — intravenous enzyme replacement in attenuated MPS I only, as carded.

shelves.title: Vestronidase alfa in MPS VII: whole programme is 23 patients — 12-patient blind-start trial plus sub-floor reports of 3 and 8, on a urinary surrogate
shelves.question: In children and adults with mucopolysaccharidosis VII (Sly syndrome), does enzyme replacement with vestronidase alfa (recombinant human β-glucuronidase), compared with placebo (blind-start) or within-patient baseline, reduce urinary glycosaminoglycans and improve clinical measures?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small N = 23 across the whole programme: the entire programme enrolled 23 patients across its three reports, the count leads, and two of the three reports are sub-floor (N = 3 and N = 8, printed on their faces) and are never load-bearing alone. The only randomised evidence is a 12-patient blind-start crossover whose primary clinical readout is a responder index with no magnitude printed in its abstract; the paediatric evidence is a urinary biomarker change without a comparator. Urinary glycosaminoglycan is a surrogate endpoint throughout. Product named as published: vestronidase alfa, recombinant human β-glucuronidase.

cards.headline: Phase 3 blind-start trial + extension, in a single paper (Wang 2020) — labelled as such: 12 subjects aged 8–25 completed a randomised placebo-controlled blind-start single-crossover study of vestronidase alfa 4 mg/kg, which showed significantly reduced urinary glycosaminoglycans and clinical improvement on a multi-domain responder index (no effect magnitude for the responder index is printed in the abstract, and none is claimed here), then entered an open-label extension for up to a further 144 weeks
cards.summary: Phase 3 blind-start trial + extension, in a single paper (Wang 2020) — labelled as such: 12 subjects aged 8–25 completed a randomised placebo-controlled blind-start single-crossover study of vestronidase alfa 4 mg/kg, which showed significantly reduced urinary glycosaminoglycans and clinical improvement on a multi-domain responder index (no effect magnitude for the responder index is printed in the abstract, and none is claimed here), then entered an open-label extension for up to a further 144 weeks
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised placebo-controlled blind-start single-crossover trial (N = 12) and its open-label extension, reported in one paper — the programme's only randomised report
cards.people: 12 subjects aged 8–25 years with mucopolysaccharidosis VII (Sly syndrome) completed the blind-start study (24–48 weeks of vestronidase alfa 4 mg/kg intravenously) and enrolled in the long-term open-label extension; 3 (25%) completed all 144 extension weeks, 8 (67%) stopped early to switch to commercially available vestronidase alfa, and 1 discontinued for non-compliance after one extension infusion. This is the only randomised evidence in the programme, and it is 12 patients. The tested product is named as the publication gives it: vestronidase alfa, recombinant human β-glucuronidase — clarification, not promotion.
cards.result: The blind-start study showed significantly reduced urinary glycosaminoglycans and clinical improvement in a multi-domain responder index (assessments in pulmonary function, motor function, range of motion, mobility and visual acuity); the abstract prints no magnitude for the responder index and none is claimed here. In the extension, subjects on continuous treatment showed sustained urinary GAG reduction and clinical response on the same index, and reduction in fatigue was maintained. Most adverse events were mild to moderate; there were no treatment or study discontinuations due to adverse events. Of 11 subjects testing positive for anti-drug antibodies at any time, 7 tested positive for neutralising antibodies and all 7 continued to show urinary GAG reduction.
cards.watchOut: A 12-patient blind-start crossover whose primary clinical readout is a responder index with no magnitude printed in its abstract: urinary glycosaminoglycan is a surrogate endpoint, and this card must never be read as a conventionally powered phase 3 result.
cards.source: Wang RY et al. The long-term safety and efficacy of vestronidase alfa, rhGUS enzyme replacement therapy, in subjects with mucopolysaccharidosis VII. Molecular genetics and metabolism. 2020. PMID: 32063397. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02377921 and NCT02432144. cards.headline: Paediatric phase 2 study (Lau 2022): 8 subjects under 5 years, printed as such — open-label vestronidase alfa 4 mg/kg every other week for 48 weeks; the primary endpoint, urinary GAG dermatan-sulfate excretion, fell by a least-squares mean −61% (percent change) at week 48 (P < 0.0001 at each visit), with positive trends in height Z-score and hepatosplenomegaly. N = 8 is below the ~10-human reference floor: this card is labelled sub-floor on its face and is never load-bearing alone
cards.summary: Paediatric phase 2 study (Lau 2022): 8 subjects under 5 years, printed as such — open-label vestronidase alfa 4 mg/kg every other week for 48 weeks; the primary endpoint, urinary GAG dermatan-sulfate excretion, fell by a least-squares mean −61% (percent change) at week 48 (P < 0.0001 at each visit), with positive trends in height Z-score and hepatosplenomegaly. cards.type: Open-label paediatric phase 2 study (N = 8 under 5 years — sub-floor, never load-bearing alone), 48 weeks, no comparator
cards.people: 8 paediatric subjects under 5 years of age with mucopolysaccharidosis VII — N = 8, sub-floor, printed on the face — in an open-label multicentre study, with an offered continuation period after the 48-week treatment period. There is no comparator in this study.
cards.result: Statistically significant reductions in urinary GAG dermatan-sulfate excretion were observed at each visit (P < 0.0001), with a least-squares mean (SE) percentage change of −60% (6.6) at week 4 and −61% (6.41) at week 48 — percent changes from baseline, with no control group. Positive trends were observed in standing height Z-score (mean −2.630 at baseline, n = 8, to −2.045 at week 48, n = 7) and growth velocity, and hepatomegaly resolved in 3 of 3 subjects assessed by ultrasound. Mild-to-moderate infusion-associated reactions occurred in 4 (50%) subjects; no new safety signals were identified.
cards.watchOut: Sub-floor (N = 8) and uncontrolled: a urinary biomarker percent change without a comparator cannot establish clinical benefit in children under 5, however consistent the biomarker direction.

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the event-rate evidence is entirely before/after, and that flag leads. The single randomised trial is a 32-patient, 4-month, active-comparator study whose positive endpoints are echocardiographic measures, with its event outcome (rhabdomyolysis) null; the dramatic event-rate reductions come from uncontrolled pre/post comparisons in extension and compassionate-use cohorts, where regression to the mean and survivorship cannot be excluded. All percent reductions on this shelf are relative measures, labelled as such with absolutes beside them. Product named as published: triheptanoin.

cards.headline: Randomised trial (Gillingham 2017): in 32 subjects, left-ventricular ejection fraction rose 7.4% (percent change, P = 0.046) and resting LV wall mass fell 20% (percent change, P = 0.041) on triheptanoin (C7) vs trioctanoin (C8), with a lower heart rate at the same workload — and NO difference in total energy expenditure, phosphocreatine recovery, body composition, rhabdomyolysis incidence or any secondary outcome
cards.summary: Randomised trial (Gillingham 2017): in 32 subjects, left-ventricular ejection fraction rose 7.4% (percent change, P = 0.046) and resting LV wall mass fell 20% (percent change, P = 0.041) on triheptanoin (C7) vs trioctanoin (C8), with a lower heart rate at the same workload — and NO difference in total energy expenditure, phosphocreatine recovery, body composition, rhabdomyolysis incidence or any secondary outcome
cards.type: Double-blind randomised controlled trial vs trioctanoin, 4 months (N = 32 randomised) — the programme's one randomised trial
cards.people: 32 subjects with long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders (carnitine palmitoyltransferase-2, very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, trifunctional protein or long-chain 3-hydroxy acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency) randomised double-blind to diets with 20% of energy from triheptanoin (C7) or trioctanoin (C8) for 4 months. This is the programme's single randomised trial, and it is an active-comparator trial, not a placebo trial. The tested product is named as the publication gives it: triheptanoin, an anaplerotic odd-chain triglyceride — clarification, not promotion.
cards.result: Patients in the C7 group increased left ventricular ejection fraction by 7.4% (P = 0.046) and experienced a 20% (P = 0.041) decrease in LV wall mass on resting echocardiogram — percent changes as printed in the record — and required a lower heart rate for the same amount of work during moderate-intensity exercise testing. There was no difference in total energy expenditure, phosphocreatine recovery, body composition, incidence of rhabdomyolysis, or any secondary outcome measures between the groups.
cards.watchOut: Positive endpoints are echocardiographic measures in 32 patients over 4 months, and the event outcome that matters clinically — rhabdomyolysis incidence — was null: never print the ejection-fraction change as an event benefit.
cards.source: Gillingham MB et al. Triheptanoin versus trioctanoin for long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders: a double blinded, randomized controlled trial. Journal of inherited metabolic disease. 2017. PMID: 28871440. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01379625. cards.headline: Long-term extension final report (Vockley 2023) — an open-label extension report of the programme, labelled as such: in 94 patients, the triheptanoin-naïve cohort's median major-clinical-event rate fell from 2.00 to 0.28 events/patient/year on treatment (an 86% relative reduction, P = 0.0343) and the rollover cohort's mean rate fell 43% relative (P = 0.0347) — both before/after comparisons without a concurrent control
cards.summary: Long-term extension final report (Vockley 2023) — an open-label extension report of the programme, labelled as such: in 94 patients, the triheptanoin-naïve cohort's median major-clinical-event rate fell from 2.00 to 0.28 events/patient/year on treatment (an 86% relative reduction, P = 0.0343) and the rollover cohort's mean rate fell 43% relative (P = 0.0347) — both before/after comparisons without a concurrent control
cards.type: Open-label long-term extension final report (N = 94, in three cohorts) — before/after comparisons, no concurrent control
cards.people: 94 patients with long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders in the open-label extension: 33 triheptanoin-naïve, 24 rollover from the earlier study, and 37 from investigator-sponsored trials / expanded-access programmes; mean treatment durations 27.4, 46.9 and 49.6 months respectively. The primary endpoint was the annualised rate of major clinical events (rhabdomyolysis, hypoglycemia, cardiomyopathy).
cards.result: In the naïve cohort, the median (IQR) major-clinical-event rate fell from 2.00 (0.67–3.33) to 0.28 (0.00–1.43) events/patient/year (P = 0.0343) — an 86% relative reduction, printed as a relative measure with the absolute rates beside it. In the rollover cohort, the mean rate fell from 1.76 ± 1.64 to 1.00 ± 1.00 events/patient/year (P = 0.0347) — a 43% relative reduction, with absolutes beside it. Treatment-related treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 68.1% of patients, mostly mild / moderate; five patients had seven serious treatment-related events, all resolved.
cards.watchOut: Before/after event-rate comparisons in extension cohorts: regression to the mean, survivorship and era effects cannot be excluded, so the 86% and 43% relative reductions must always travel with their absolute rates and their uncontrolled design.
cards.source: Vockley J et al. Triheptanoin for the treatment of long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders: Final results of an open-label, long-term extension study. Journal of inherited metabolic disease. 2023. PMID: 37276053. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02214160 and NCT01886378. cards.headline: Retrospective chart review (Vockley 2015): in 20 compassionate-use patients treated for up to 12.5 years, mean hospitalisation days/year fell 67% relative after triheptanoin initiation (5.76 vs 17.55, P = 0.0242), with a non-significant trend to a 35% relative lower hospitalisation event rate (P = 0.1126)
cards.summary: Retrospective chart review (Vockley 2015): in 20 compassionate-use patients treated for up to 12.5 years, mean hospitalisation days/year fell 67% relative after triheptanoin initiation (5.76 vs 17.55, P = 0.0242), with a non-significant trend to a 35% relative lower hospitalisation event rate (P = 0.1126)
cards.type: Retrospective chart review of a compassionate-use cohort (N = 20) — before/after comparison, no concurrent control
cards.people: 20 patients with long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders (of 24 in the compassionate-use protocol) treated with triheptanoin for up to 12.5 years, in a retrospective comprehensive medical-record review comparing periods before and after initiation; these 20 patients had 320 hospitalisations from birth to the study end date.
cards.result: Mean hospitalisation days/year decreased by 67% relative after initiation (n = 15; 5.76 vs 17.55 days/year, P = 0.0242) — a relative measure with the absolute days beside it — and a trend toward a 35% relative lower hospitalisation event rate was observed (n = 16 subjects over 6 months of age; 1.26 vs 1.94, P = 0.1126, not significant). The hypoglycemia event rate in 9 subjects fell 96% relative (0.04 vs 0.92 per year, P = 0.0091), while the rhabdomyolysis hospital event rate in 11 affected subjects was similar before and after. Gastrointestinal symptoms were the most commonly reported side effects. The authors themselves note heterogeneity in routine care and natural variation in the disease course over time.
cards.watchOut: A retrospective before/after review spanning up to 12.5 years of changing routine care: the 67% relative fall in hospital days is hypothesis-supporting, not confirmatory, and its non-significant event-rate trend (P = 0.1126) prints beside it.
cards.source: Vockley J et al. Long-term major clinical outcomes in patients with long chain fatty acid oxidation disorders before and after transition to triheptanoin treatment--A retrospective chart review. Molecular genetics and metabolism. 2015. PMID: 26116311. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Miglustat in Niemann-Pick disease type C (one programme, three reports): the 29-patient randomised trial's surrogate primary — saccadic eye-movement velocity — was significant only after excluding benzodiazepine users (P = 0.028); extensions report stabilisation
shelves.question: In children and adults with Niemann-Pick disease type C, does miglustat monotherapy (substrate reduction), compared with standard care, slow neurological progression?
shelves.mesh: 1-Deoxynojirimycin/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Adolescent · Adult · Age Factors · Analysis of Variance · Child · Child, Preschool · Cohort Studies · Deglutition/drug effects · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Enzyme Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Male · Niemann-Pick Disease, Type C/drug therapy/physiopathology · Retrospective Studies · Saccades/drug effects · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one programme, three reports, labelled as such. The single randomised trial (29 patients aged ≥12 years) found its primary endpoint — horizontal saccadic eye-movement velocity, a surrogate chosen for its correlation with progression — improved on miglustat vs standard care, reaching significance only when patients taking benzodiazepines were excluded (P = 0.028); swallowing improved, auditory acuity was stable and ambulatory deterioration was slower. The two other reports are open-label extensions of the same programme (adult/juvenile and paediatric), not independent confirmations. No trial measures survival. The control was standard care, not placebo.

cards.headline: Randomised trial (Patterson 2007): 29 patients aged ≥12 years — the primary endpoint, horizontal saccadic eye-movement velocity (a surrogate), improved on miglustat vs standard care, significant only after excluding benzodiazepine users (P = 0.028)
cards.summary: Randomised trial (Patterson 2007): 29 patients aged ≥12 years — the primary endpoint, horizontal saccadic eye-movement velocity (a surrogate), improved on miglustat vs standard care, significant only after excluding benzodiazepine users (P = 0.028)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, miglustat vs standard care in Niemann-Pick disease type C (with a parallel non-randomised paediatric cohort)
cards.people: 29 patients aged 12 years or older with Niemann-Pick disease type C, randomised to miglustat 200 mg three times daily (n = 20) or standard care (n = 9) for 12 months; a parallel non-randomised cohort of 12 children younger than 12 received miglustat at body-surface-area-adjusted doses. All participants were then treated with miglustat for an additional year in an extension study.
cards.result: At 12 months, horizontal saccadic eye-movement (HSEM) velocity had improved in patients treated with miglustat versus standard care; results were significant when patients taking benzodiazepines were excluded (p = 0.028). Children showed an improvement in HSEM velocity of similar size at 12 months. Improvement in swallowing capacity, stable auditory acuity, and a slower deterioration in ambulatory index were also seen in treated patients older than 12 years. Safety and tolerability at 200 mg three times a day were consistent with previous trials in type I Gaucher disease, where half this dose was used.
cards.watchOut: SURROGATE PRIMARY, stated on the face: HSEM velocity was chosen for its correlation with disease progression, and its headline significance depends on excluding benzodiazepine users. The control is standard care, not placebo. This is the programme's only randomised trial — the two reports below are its extensions, never independent confirmations.
cards.source: Patterson MC et al. Miglustat for treatment of Niemann-Pick C disease: a randomised controlled study. The Lancet. Neurology. 2007. PMID: 17689147. Registry ID: ISRCTN26761144.
