results were significant when patients taking benzodiazepines were excluded (p = 0.028). children showed an improvement in hsem velocity of similar size at 12 months. improvement in swallowing capacity, stable auditory acuity, and a slower deterioration in ambulatory index were also seen in treated patients older than 12 years. safety and tolerability at 200 mg three times a day were consistent with previous trials in type i gaucher disease, where half this dose was used. surrogate primary, stated on the face: hsem velocity was chosen for its correlation with disease progression, and its headline significance depends on excluding benzodiazepine users. the control is standard care, not placebo. this is the programme's only randomised trial — the two reports below are its extensions, never independent confirmations. patterson mc et al. miglustat for treatment of niemann-pick c disease: a randomised controlled study. the lancet. neurology. 2007. pmid: 17689147. registry id: isrctn26761144. mesh: 1-deoxynojirimycin/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · adolescent · adult · age factors · analysis of variance · child · child, preschool · cohort studies · deglutition/drug effects · double-blind method · drug administration schedule · enzyme inhibitors/therapeutic use · female · humans · male · niemann-pick disease, type c/drug therapy/physiopathology · retrospective studies · saccades/drug effects · severity of illness index

cards.headline: Adult/juvenile extension report of the same trial (Wraith 2010), labelled as such: 21 patients completed 12 months of miglustat and 15 completed 24 months — swallowing improved or stable in 86% (12 months) and up to 93% (24 months); exploratory stability in 13 of 19 (68%)
cards.summary: Adult/juvenile extension report of the same trial (Wraith 2010), labelled as such: 21 patients completed 12 months of miglustat and 15 completed 24 months — swallowing improved or stable in 86% (12 months) and up to 93% (24 months); exploratory stability in 13 of 19 (68%)
cards.type: Open-label extension report of the Patterson 2007 randomised trial (same programme, labelled) — miglustat (named Zavesca in this report) in adult and juvenile Niemann-Pick disease type C
cards.people: Extension report of the randomised trial carded above: from the 29 patients in the randomised phase, 21 completed 12 months of therapy with miglustat (17 from the miglustat-randomised group, 4 from the extension phase) and 15 patients (all from the miglustat-randomised group) completed 24 months on miglustat, in a non-controlled open-label extension.
cards.result: Mean HSEM velocity indicated improvement in the 12-month miglustat group and stabilisation in the 24-month group; swallowing was improved or stable in 86% and in up to 93%, respectively, and ambulation was stabilised in both groups. In an exploratory disease-stability analysis of prospective data on key parameters (HSEM, swallowing, ambulation and cognition), 13 of 19 patients (68%) receiving ≥12 months of miglustat therapy had stable disease. Among all patients receiving ≥1 dose of miglustat (n = 28), the most frequent adverse events were diarrhoea, weight decrease, flatulence and tremor.
cards.watchOut: An extension report of the trial above, not a second trial: open-label, non-controlled, and 'stability' here is an exploratory composite. The tested product is named as the publication gives it (miglustat; Zavesca in this report) for clarification, not promotion.

cards.type: Open-label extension report of the programme's paediatric cohort (same programme, labelled) — miglustat in children with Niemann-Pick disease type C
cards.people: Extension report of the programme's paediatric cohort: children aged 4 to 12 years with Niemann-Pick disease type C received open-label miglustat (dose adjusted for body surface area) for an initial 12 months, a further 12-month extension, and a long-term continued extension phase; 10 children completed 24 months' treatment.
cards.result: Horizontal saccadic eye movement, ambulation, and swallowing were stabilised at 24 months. Analysis of key parameters of disease progression showed disease stability in 8 of 10 patients (80%). Safety and tolerability were comparable to those observed in adults and juveniles.
cards.watchOut: An extension report of the same programme's non-randomised paediatric cohort, not a randomised comparison: 10 completers, open-label, with stability as the readout. It adds duration, not independent confirmation.

cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the randomised trial (29 patients aged ≥12 years, plus a parallel non-randomised cohort of 12 children) and its adult/juvenile and paediatric extension reports — one programme, counted once.
cards.result: Miglustat improved or stabilised several markers of Niemann-Pick type C severity in this single programme: the surrogate primary (HSEM velocity) reached significance only after benzodiazepine users were excluded (P = 0.028), swallowing improved, auditory acuity was stable and ambulatory deterioration was slower over 12 months, and the extensions report stabilisation in most completers (exploratory stability 68% adult/juvenile, 80% paediatric). The cross-point shelves are the arimoclomol shelf (pack #7036, where miglustat is background therapy) and the levacetylleucine shelf (pack #7037) — different agent questions, never counted here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Agalsidase alfa and beta in Fabry disease: a 123-patient placebo-controlled base across two products — pain and cardiac-mass signals for alfa, and a beta event trial whose primary analysis missed significance (HR 0.47, P = 0.06)
shelves.question: In children and adults with Fabry disease, does enzyme replacement therapy with agalsidase alfa or agalsidase beta, compared with placebo, improve neuropathic pain, kidney function, cardiac mass or clinical-event outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Analysis of Variance · Arrhythmias, Cardiac · Body Weight · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Fabry Disease/drug therapy,physiopathology · Heart Rate · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Kidney Function Tests · Male · Pain Measurement · Trihexosylceramides/metabolism · alpha-Galactosidase/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Aged · Cardiovascular Diseases/etiology · Cerebrovascular Disorders/etiology · Disease Progression · Fabry Disease/complications,drug therapy,physiopathology · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Isoenzymes/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Kidney Diseases/etiology · Middle Aged · Proteinuria/etiology · Treatment Outcome · alpha-Galactosidase/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Cardiomyopathies/drug therapy,metabolism · Chromatography, High Pressure Liquid · Echocardiography · Electrocardiography · Fabry Disease/drug therapy · Heart Conduction System/enzymology · Hypertrophy, Left Ventricular/drug therapy · Magnetic Resonance Angiography · Myocardium/chemistry · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left/drug therapy · alpha-Galactosidase/metabolism,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: A small, old, two-product base — the counts lead. The placebo-controlled evidence for agalsidase itself is 123 patients across three trials of two different products (alfa 0.2 mg/kg; beta 1 mg/kg) that have never been compared head-to-head in this base: alfa reduced neuropathic pain and improved biopsy/creatinine-clearance measures in 26 men (inulin clearance null), alfa reduced MRI left ventricular mass in 15 men (myocardial substrate change null), and beta's clinical-event trial — the only event-outcome trial — missed significance on its primary intention-to-treat analysis (hazard ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.21 to 1.03, P = 0.06, a relative measure; absolute events 27% vs 42%), with the protocol-adherent analysis significant (HR 0.39, P = 0.034). Both analyses are printed on the face. Product names are given exactly as the publications give them — clarification, not promotion.

cards.headline: Agalsidase alfa pain/renal trial (Schiffmann 2001, N = 26): alpha-galactosidase A 0.2 mg/kg every other week reduced Brief Pain Inventory neuropathic pain severity from 6.2 (SE 0.46) to 4.3 (0.73) vs no significant change on placebo (P = .02); glomeruli with mesangial widening changed −12.5% on treatment vs +16.5% on placebo (P = .01) and creatinine clearance rose 2.1 mL/min vs a fall of 16.1 mL/min (P = .02), while inulin clearance did not differ significantly (P = .19)
cards.summary: Agalsidase alfa pain/renal trial (Schiffmann 2001, N = 26): alpha-galactosidase A 0.2 mg/kg every other week reduced Brief Pain Inventory neuropathic pain severity from 6.2 (SE 0.46) to 4.3 (0.73) vs no significant change on placebo (P = .02); glomeruli with mesangial widening changed −12.5% on treatment vs +16.5% on placebo (P = .01) and creatinine clearance rose 2.1 mL/min vs a fall of 16.1 mL/min (P = .02), while inulin clearance did not differ significantly (P = .19)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, agalsidase alfa (alpha-galactosidase A 0.2 mg/kg) in Fabry disease — pain and renal outcomes
cards.people: 26 hemizygous male patients aged ≥18 years with Fabry disease confirmed by alpha-galactosidase A assay, in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial at the NIH Clinical Research Center (December 1998 to August 1999): alpha-gal A 0.2 mg/kg intravenously every other week, 12 doses.
cards.result: Neuropathic pain severity fell on treatment with no significant change on placebo (P = .02); pain-related quality of life also improved (P = .05). Kidney biopsy mesangial widening and creatinine clearance favoured treatment (P = .01 and P = .02), inulin clearance did not differ significantly (P = .19), plasma glycosphingolipid levels fell by approximately 50%, and cardiac conduction and body weight improved significantly.
cards.watchOut: 26 patients, one centre, 12 doses: the renal findings rest on biopsy percentages and creatinine clearance (a surrogate that moved opposite to the inulin-clearance result, which was null) — not on clinical renal events. The tested product is named as the publication gives it (agalsidase alfa / alpha-galactosidase A 0.2 mg/kg) — clarification, not promotion.
cards.source: Schiffmann et al. Enzyme replacement therapy in Fabry disease: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2001. PMID: 11386930. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Agalsidase beta clinical-event trial (Banikazemi 2007, N = 82): clinical events (renal, cardiac, cerebrovascular or death) in 14 of 51 (27%) on agalsidase beta vs 13 of 31 (42%) on placebo; the primary intention-to-treat analysis gave a hazard ratio of 0.47 (95% CI 0.21 to 1.03; P = 0.06) — a relative measure that did NOT reach significance — while the protocol-adherent analysis gave 0.39 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.93; P = 0.034)
cards.summary: Agalsidase beta clinical-event trial (Banikazemi 2007, N = 82): clinical events (renal, cardiac, cerebrovascular or death) in 14 of 51 (27%) on agalsidase beta vs 13 of 31 (42%) on placebo; the primary intention-to-treat analysis gave a hazard ratio of 0.47 (95% CI 0.21 to 1.03; P = 0.06) — a relative measure that did NOT reach significance — while the protocol-adherent analysis gave 0.39 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.93; P = 0.034)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, agalsidase beta 1 mg/kg in advanced Fabry disease — composite clinical-event outcome (NCT00074984)
cards.people: 82 adults with advanced Fabry disease and mild-to-moderate kidney disease at 41 referral centres in 9 countries, randomised 2:1 to agalsidase beta 1 mg/kg or placebo intravenously every 2 weeks for up to 35 months (median 18.5); 74 were protocol-adherent and some patients withdrew or transitioned to open-label/commercial therapy before an event.
cards.result: The primary intention-to-treat analysis, adjusted for baseline proteinuria, showed agalsidase beta delayed time to first clinical event with hazard ratio 0.47 (95% CI 0.21 to 1.03; P = 0.06) — the absolute event proportions beside it are 27% (14/51) vs 42% (13/31). The protocol-adherent analysis gave HR 0.39 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.93; P = 0.034), and a subgroup analysis suggested larger effects at baseline eGFR > 55 mL/min/1.73 m² (HR 0.19) than at or below it (HR 0.85), with the formal interaction test non-significant (P = 0.09). Infusion-associated reactions occurred in 55% on agalsidase beta vs 23% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Both analyses are printed because the primary one missed significance (P = 0.06): the hazard ratios are relative measures and travel with the absolute proportions (27% vs 42%). The protocol-adherent and subgroup analyses are secondary and cannot upgrade the primary result. The tested product is named as the publication gives it (agalsidase beta 1 mg/kg) — clarification, not promotion.
cards.source: Banikazemi et al. Agalsidase-beta therapy for advanced Fabry disease: a randomized trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2007. PMID: 17179052. Registry ID: NCT00074984. cards.headline: Agalsidase alfa cardiac trial (Hughes 2008, N = 15): left ventricular mass by MRI was significantly reduced on agalsidase alfa vs placebo at 6 months (p = 0.041); myocardial globotriaosylceramide content fell by a mean 20% on treatment vs a 10% increase on placebo, NOT significant (p = 0.42)
cards.summary: Agalsidase alfa cardiac trial (Hughes 2008, N = 15): left ventricular mass by MRI was significantly reduced on agalsidase alfa vs placebo at 6 months (p = 0.041); myocardial globotriaosylceramide content fell by a mean 20% on treatment vs a 10% increase on placebo, NOT significant (p = 0.42)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, agalsidase alfa in Fabry cardiomyopathy — left ventricular mass outcome (6 months)
cards.people: 15 adult male patients with Anderson-Fabry disease in a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial of agalsidase alfa over 6 months, followed by a 2-year open-label extension (extension results are not the placebo-controlled finding and are not claimed here).
cards.result: Left ventricular mass measured by MRI was significantly reduced after 6 months of agalsidase alfa compared with placebo (p = 0.041). Myocardial Gb3 content changed by a mean −20% on treatment vs +10% on placebo (p = 0.42, not significant). The abstract prints no absolute left-ventricular-mass values, and none are claimed here.
cards.watchOut: 15 patients and an imaging surrogate: the significant result is an MRI mass difference without printed absolute values, and the tissue-substrate result in the same trial was null. This card supports, and cannot carry, the shelf.

randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, agalsidase alfa in fabry cardiomyopathy — left ventricular mass outcome (6 months) 15 adult male patients with anderson-fabry disease in a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial of agalsidase alfa over 6 months, followed by a 2-year open-label extension (extension results are not the placebo-controlled finding and are not claimed here). left ventricular mass measured by mri was significantly reduced after 6 months of agalsidase alfa compared with placebo (p = 0.041). myocardial gb3 content changed by a mean −20% on treatment vs +10% on placebo (p = 0.42, not significant). the abstract prints no absolute left-ventricular-mass values, and none are claimed here. 15 patients and an imaging surrogate: the significant result is an mri mass difference without printed absolute values, and the tissue-substrate result in the same trial was null. this card supports, and cannot carry, the shelf. hughes et al. effects of enzyme replacement therapy on the cardiomyopathy of anderson-fabry disease: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial of agalsidase alfa. heart (british cardiac society). 2008. pmid: 17483124. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · aged · cardiomyopathies/drug therapy,metabolism · chromatography, high pressure liquid · double-blind method · echocardiography · electrocardiography · fabry disease/drug therapy · heart conduction system/enzymology · humans · hypertrophy, left ventricular/drug therapy · magnetic resonance angiography · male · middle aged · myocardium/chemistry · trihexosylceramides/metabolism · ventricular dysfunction, left/drug therapy · alpha-galactosidase/metabolism,therapeutic use

cards.headline: Synthesis: the placebo-controlled agalsidase base is 123 patients across three trials of two different products never compared head-to-head in this base — pain and biopsy/clearance signals for alfa in 26 men, an MRI mass signal for alfa in 15 men, and for beta a clinical-event result whose primary intention-to-treat analysis missed significance (HR 0.47, P = 0.06, relative) with a significant protocol-adherent analysis (HR 0.39)

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: Schiffmann 2001 (agalsidase alfa, N = 26), Banikazemi 2007 (agalsidase beta, N = 82, NCT00074984) and Hughes 2008 (agalsidase alfa, N = 15) — 123 patients in total. The Fabry family's other homed slices are different questions: pegunigalsidase alfa vs agalsidase beta (pack #5192, where agalsidase beta is the comparator, not the subject), migalastat chaperone therapy and lucerastat substrate reduction (homed / trigger records) — no other shelf asks whether agalsidase itself works against placebo.
cards.result: Products and doses are kept separate throughout: alfa 0.2 mg/kg and beta 1 mg/kg are different products at different doses, and no pooled 'enzyme replacement works' number is printed. The only clinical-event evidence is the beta trial, printed with both its analyses and its absolute event proportions (27% vs 42%).
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. Product names are given exactly as the publications give them — clarification, not promotion.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
